headings: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency VBI / Vertebral Artery Dissection VAD
AHA/ASA Scientific Statement Biller et al., 2014
content: Overview & Pathophysiology The current IFOMPT terminology is vascular pathologies of the neck . The historical label "cervical artery dysfunction" is retained in this route for continuity, but should not be read as a single diagnostic entity. Internal carotid and vertebral artery pathology can masquerade as musculoskeletal neck pain or headache and requires careful history, neurological examination and clinical reasoning. This is a critical safety topic for all physiotherapists performing cervical assessment and treatment. Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency VBI / Vertebral Artery Dissection VAD - Vertebral arteries VA : Arise from subclavian arteries; enter transverse foramina at C6, ascend through C6–C1, pierce dura, enter skull via foramen magnum, and unite to form basilar artery - Internal carotid arteries ICA : Ascend anterior to VA; enter petrous canal; supply anterior circulation - VA supplies posterior brain circulation: brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobe, medial temporal lobe Pathology: 1. Atherosclerotic VBI : Progressive stenosis of VA/basilar artery; older patients >55 ; embolic or haemodynamic ischaemia; symptoms often positional but mechanical compression less important than atheroma/embolism 2. Vertebral Artery Dissection VAD : Intimal tear → intramural haematoma → stenosis, occlusion, or thromboembolism; may be spontaneous or trauma-related whiplash, manipulation, trivial trauma ; peak incidence 40s 3. Internal Carotid Artery Dissection ICAD : Similar mechanism; anterior circulation TIA/stroke; classically presents with neck pain + ipsilateral Horner's syndrome + contralateral focal deficit 4. Bow Hunter's Syndrome : Dynamic VA occlusion with head rotation, usually at C1/2 Risk factors for dissection: - Connective tissue disorders Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan's, fibromuscular dysplasia — strongest risk factors - Hypertension - Recent infection especially URTI — inflammatory arteriopathy - Oral contraceptive use - Migraine with aura - Prior dissection - Recent trauma whiplash, manipulation, trivial neck strain Incidence: - Spontaneous VAD: ~1–1.5 per 100,000/year - ICAD: ~2.6 per 100,000/year - The incidence of a vascular event attributable to cervical manipulation cannot be stated reliably from the cited observational evidence; consultation bias and a possible prodromal dissection are important limitations. - VAD accounts for ~20% of strokes in patients aged This mnemonic is not a diagnostic rule and is not a substitute for the 2020 IFOMPT framework's patient-specific history, risk assessment and neurological examination. Symptom Clinical Significance --------- ----------------------- Dizziness Vertebrobasilar ischaemia; differentiate from cervicogenic positional, brief, associated with neck movement Diplopia Brainstem ischaemia CN III, IV, VI involvement Dysarthria Bulbar ischaemia Dysphagia Medullary involvement Drop attacks Sudden loss of postural tone — vertebrobasilar Nausea Dorsal vagal complex ischaemia Numbness face/body Lateral medullary/trigeminal involvement Nystagmus Vestibulocerebellum ischaemia Ataxia Cerebellar ischaemia Headache new, severe, "thunderclap" Subarachnoid haemorrhage or arterial dissection Horner's Syndrome ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis ICA or VA dissection Neck pain new, severe, ipsilateral occipital Dissection prodrome --- Red Flags Use the International IFOMPT Cervical Framework 2020 to reason about possible vascular pathology. Concerning presentations include new severe or unusual neck pain or headache together with focal neurological features, ataxia, new cranial nerve dysfunction, Horner syndrome or other acute stroke features. - If acute cervical artery dissection or stroke is suspected, stop cervical treatment and arrange emergency medical assessment. - Call 999 for acute focal neurological or stroke features. Do not delay emergency care to complete a musculoskeletal examination. - Do not use symptom provocation in sustained rotation or extension, or the absence of the historical “5Ds/3Ns”, as vascular clearance. - Do not proceed with cervical manipulation when vascular pathology, instability, myelopathy, fracture or another serious contraindication is suspected. The “5Ds/3Ns” may help explain historical teaching but they are not a diagnostic or clearance rule. --- Clinical Frameworks International IFOMPT Cervical Framework 2020 The International Framework for Examination of the Cervical Region for potential of vascular pathologies of the neck prior to Orthopaedic Manual Therapy Intervention , accepted by IFOMPT in October 2020, replaces the earlier CAD terminology and removes provocative positional testing from the framework. Three-stage clinical decision process: 1. Stage 1 — Pre-examination screen: - Comprehensive history of dizziness, headache, neurological symptoms - CVD risk factors, connective tissue disorders, medications anticoagulants - Recent trauma 2. Stage 2 — Physical examination: - Select examination procedures from the history and evolving clinical hypothesis - Perform an appropriate neurological examination and other indicated tests - Do not use provocative positional testing to infer vascular safety; its predictive ability is lacking and the 2020 framework does not recommend it 3. Stage 3 — Decision: - If ANY concern → do NOT perform cervical HVLA; consider alternative techniques - Document reasoning - Share decision-making with patient informed consent including CAD risk AHA/ASA Scientific Statement Biller et al., 2014 - Clinicians should inform patients of the extremely small risk of stroke associated with cervical manipulation - Shared decision-making and informed consent required - Prefer cervical mobilisation over HVLA where risk factors present Differential Vertebrogenic Dizziness Framework Distinguish cervicogenic dizziness from vestibular causes: Feature Cervicogenic Dizziness Vestibular BPPV/Labyrinthitis VBI --------- ---------------------- -------------------------------- ----- Onset With neck movement Head position change Sustained rotation/extension Duration Proportional to neck movement Seconds BPPV or days labyrinthitis Seconds–minutes Associated Neck pain, stiffness Nausea, positional Hallpike positive Diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia Neurological None None Positive CNS signs --- Outcome Measures Primary goal: SAFETY — accurate identification and appropriate management of CAD risk Formal validated outcome measures for the management of CAD are limited — this is primarily a triage/screening condition rather than a primary physiotherapy treatment condition. Tools used in assessment: Dizziness Handicap Inventory DHI - 25 items; 0–100 0=no handicap, 100=maximum - Used for dizziness-related disability differentiate from cervicogenic vs. vestibular - MCID : 11 points Whitney et al., 2004 Neck Disability Index NDI - For associated neck pain disability tracking - MCID : 7.5/50 points NPRS 0–10 - For headache and neck pain severity - MCID : 2.1 points Neurological Examination Documentation - Serial documentation of cranial nerve findings, upper and lower limb neurology - Essential for monitoring improvement or deterioration --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Investigation of Suspected CAD: MRI + MRA Magnetic Resonance Angiography : - May identify arterial-wall and luminal features of dissection; modality choice is an acute medical/radiology decision rather than a universal first-line rule - T1 fat-saturated axial images: intramural haematoma appears as crescentic hyperintensity surrounding lumen - MRA: demonstrates stenosis, occlusion, or "flame sign" of dissection CTA CT Angiography : - Faster than MRI; better availability in ED - Provides rapid high-resolution assessment of the arterial lumen; limitations include ionising radiation, iodinated contrast and possible false-positive or false-negative appearances Doppler Ultrasound: - Limited sensitivity for VA dissection poor vessel visualisation at skull base - Useful for ICA stenosis screening carotid atheromatous disease - Cannot exclude cervical artery dissection Conventional DSA Digital Subtraction Angiography : - Historically used as a reference luminal technique; current use is specialist-led because it is invasive and provides limited arterial-wall information Clinical criteria for diagnosis Brandt criteria for VAD : 1. Local pain neck/occipital/periorbital 2. New neurological deficit 3. Imaging evidence of dissection --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- BPPV Positive Hallpike-Dix, brief <60 sec rotational vertigo, no brainstem signs Vestibular neuritis / Labyrinthitis Sustained vertigo, hearing loss labyrinthitis , no neck pain, normal MRI Cervicogenic dizziness Neck pain + dizziness proportional to cervical ROM, positive FRT, no brainstem signs Subarachnoid haemorrhage Thunderclap headache, worst of life, neck stiffness, photophobia, CT/LP Posterior fossa tumour Progressive headache, ataxia, cranial nerve deficit, MRI Migraine with aura Headache + aura visual, sensory , family history, no focal deficit, recurrent Multiple sclerosis Relapsing-remitting, MRI white matter lesions, young adult Brainstem TIA Transient <24h , multiple deficits, DWI-MRI, cardiac source Mechanical neck pain No neurological signs, ROM limited but symptoms peripheral, predictable Orthostatic hypotension Dizziness with positional change lying → standing , HR/BP response --- Management & Treatment Acute Safety Pathway Suspected acute cervical artery dissection or stroke - Stop cervical treatment and arrange emergency medical assessment. - Call 999 for acute focal neurological or stroke features. - Emergency destination, investigation and treatment are determined by the emergency stroke/vascular pathway. Confirmed dissection Antithrombotic choice, duration, imaging and any endovascular intervention are specialist medical decisions. Physiotherapy may contribute to subsequent neurological rehabilitation. Later cervical treatment requires individual neurovascular review and shared planning; this page does not prescribe a fixed interval or technique. --- Conservative Management For VBI from atherosclerosis stable, not acute dissection : - Medical management antiplatelet, statin, BP management is primary - Physiotherapy: avoid provocative cervical positions; treat associated neck pain with GENTLE Grade I–II mobilisation - Vestibular rehabilitation if chronic vertiginous symptoms with medical clearance For cervicogenic dizziness not VBI : - Manual therapy to C1/2 IFOMPT-compliant, non-HVLA technique - Proprioceptive retraining, gaze stability exercises - Cervical flexion-rotation test FRT to confirm C1/2 involvement Hall et al., 2010; Sens. 91%, Spec. 90% Post-dissection rehabilitation neurology/physio liaison : - Gradual return of cervical mobility pain-free range - Cervical intervention and return to activity require individual neurovascular clearance; no universal imaging or time threshold is asserted here - Core, scapular, and peripheral strengthening safe from early stage - Address psychological impact anxiety, PTSD — dissection can be traumatic event Pharmacological Medical Team-Led - Drug choice, dose and duration are determined by the stroke/neurovascular team using the individual diagnosis, imaging, ischaemic or haemorrhagic risk and comorbidities. This physiotherapy reference intentionally does not prescribe an antiplatelet, anticoagulant, statin, antihypertensive or analgesic regimen. - NICE NG128 Stroke : comprehensive stroke/TIA management guidance Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency: suspected acute dissection or stroke, especially with acute focal neurological features, new cranial nerve dysfunction, ataxia or Horner syndrome with concerning head/neck pain. - Prompt medical assessment: a concerning vascular presentation without acute stroke features, with urgency determined by the clinical presentation. - Specialist follow-up: confirmed dissection, chronic vascular symptoms or post-stroke rehabilitation needs. Do not use positional testing or a negative historical symptom mnemonic to reduce concern when the history or examination suggests possible cervical vascular pathology. --- Key References 1. headings: Modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association Scale mJOA
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Cervical myelopathy CM — more precisely degenerative cervical myelopathy DCM — is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults over 50 years, with an estimated prevalence of 60 per 100,000 in North America/Europe Nouri et al., 2015 . It is the leading cause of acquired spinal cord disability in adults worldwide. Pathophysiology: DCM results from progressive narrowing of the cervical spinal canal leading to spinal cord compression and ischaemia: - Static compression : osteophytes, hypertrophied ligamentum flavum especially in extension , ossification of posterior longitudinal ligament OPLL , degenerative disc bulges, facet joint hypertrophy - Dynamic compression : cord compression exacerbated by flexion/extension movement; cord is stretched over ventral osteophytes in flexion and folded by buckled ligamentum flavum in extension - Vascular compromise : compression of anterior spinal artery and intrinsic cord microvasculature → ischaemia → central grey matter necrosis - Congenital canal narrowing : canal diameter 45, gait deviation - This cluster may raise concern but is not a standalone diagnostic or referral rule; interpret it with the neurological examination and specialist assessment Key examination findings: - Hoffman's Sign : flick middle finger distal phalanx — positive if IP flexion of thumb/index; indicates UMN dysfunction - Finger Escape Sign : patient holds fingers extended, adducted — ulnar 2–3 fingers spontaneously abduct/flex; positive in DCM - 10-Second Step Test : patient taps each foot alternately ≥20 times in 10 seconds — <18 taps considered abnormal Bohlman 1977 - Grip and Release Test : open and close fist as fast as possible for 10 seconds — normal ≥20 cycles; <20 suggests hand dysfunction Yukawa et al., 2012 - Tandem Gait Test : inability to tandem walk heel-to-toe 2–3 steps; sensitive for gait ataxia in early myelopathy - Modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association Scale mJOA : functional severity scoring used to guide surgical timing --- Red Flags Suspected degenerative cervical myelopathy DCM requires prompt medical or spinal assessment. Warning features include worsening hand function, gait disturbance, upper motor neuron findings, progressive limb weakness and new bladder or bowel disturbance. - Arrange emergency medical assessment for acute neurological deterioration, acute cord-compression features or neurological deficit after trauma. - Do not apply cervical manipulation or aggressive mobilisation where DCM or cord compression is suspected. - Do not delay assessment when neurological function is deteriorating. DCM severity and rate of change determine management. Mild DCM is not automatically an emergency and may, following specialist assessment and shared decision-making, be managed with a supervised structured rehabilitation trial. Moderate/severe DCM and deterioration during non-operative care require surgical assessment under the AO Spine guideline. --- Clinical Frameworks Severity Classification mJOA Scale The modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association mJOA scale is the most widely used tool for DCM severity: mJOA Score Severity ------------ ---------- 18 Normal 15–17 Mild 12–14 Moderate <12 Severe mJOA domains: Upper extremity motor function 0–5 , Lower extremity motor function 0–7 , Sensory 0–3 , Sphincter function 0–3 Maitland with significant caveats - Maitland mobilisation is NOT appropriate as primary treatment for confirmed DCM - Grade I–II soft tissue work to peripheral joints shoulder, elbow may be used if confirmed nerve root + cord involvement coexist — only under specialist physiotherapy with neurosurgical knowledge - Post-surgical rehabilitation: Maitland principles applicable once surgical clearance obtained Validated DCM severity measures Use the mJOA severity bands above for the AO Spine/Global Spine Journal guideline. The separate 0–5 scale is the Nurick walking grade , described under Outcome Measures; it must not be labelled as an AO Spine DCM grading system. Physiotherapy Role Post-Operatively ACDF/Laminoplasty/Laminectomy - 80% of patients improve post-decompression surgery Fehlings et al., 2013 - Post-op physiotherapy: gentle ROM, neurological recovery monitoring, functional gait retraining, ADL rehabilitation - Inpatient neuro-physio → community follow-up pathway --- Outcome Measures Modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association Scale mJOA - 18-point scale; MCID : 2.0 points Tetreault et al., 2015 - Most validated for surgical outcome measurement in DCM - Recovery rate = post-op mJOA − pre-op mJOA / 18 − pre-op mJOA × 100 Neck Disability Index NDI - MCID : 7.5/50 points 15% - Useful for tracking functional disability alongside neurological severity Nurick Grade - 0–5 functional walking classification; less sensitive to small changes - Grade 0: No root/cord signs; Grade 5: Chair-bound or bedridden European Myelopathy Score EMS - 5-domain, 5–18 scale; validated European alternative to mJOA - MCID : approximately 2 points Patient-Specific Functional Scale PSFS - MCID : 2.0 points average - Appropriate for post-surgical rehabilitation goal-setting GROC Global Rating of Change - 15-point scale; use at post-op physiotherapy review points --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis MRI principal structural investigation : MRI is the principal imaging modality for suspected DCM because diagnosis requires clinical–radiological correlation. - T2 hyperintensity in spinal cord at level of compression = poor prognostic marker indicates myelomalacia - T1 hypointensity = cavitation/necrosis — even worse prognosis - STIR sequences for inflammatory/infective pathology - Suspected DCM requires prompt medical assessment and appropriate imaging under the relevant specialist pathway Alternative imaging: - If MRI cannot be performed or does not answer the clinical question, alternative imaging such as CT ± myelography may be considered by the specialist/radiology pathway. - The choice depends on the clinical question; it is not an automatic routine second-line step. Electrodiagnostics: - Motor Evoked Potentials MEPs and Somatosensory Evoked Potentials SSEPs may contribute to specialist assessment of cord conduction - EMG/NCS to differentiate coexisting radiculopathy Clinical Diagnosis: - No single pathognomonic test; diagnosis requires combination of: 1. Consistent symptom profile 2. ≥2 UMN signs on examination 3. MRI evidence of cord compression ± signal change - Cook et al.'s multivariable cluster and the individual test-accuracy estimates require human verification against the original study before publication; they do not replace imaging and specialist assessment AO Spine / AOSpine North America Clinical Practice Guidelines Fehlings et al., 2017 : - Recommend surgery for moderate-severe DCM mJOA ≤14 - For mild DCM mJOA 15–17 : structured rehabilitation trial with watchful waiting; surgery if deterioration --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Multiple sclerosis Age <40, relapsing-remitting course, MRI white matter lesions, oligoclonal bands Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ALS/MND UMN + LMN mixed, bulbar involvement, no sensory deficit, EMG fasciculations Subacute combined degeneration B12 deficiency Posterior column signs, B12 low, macrocytic anaemia, no bony compression on MRI Normal pressure hydrocephalus Triad: gait apraxia, cognitive decline, urinary incontinence; no cervical compression Syringomyelia Cape distribution sensory loss, dissociated sensory deficit, often young adults Peripheral neuropathy No UMN signs, glove-stocking distribution, NCS abnormal Cervical radiculopathy Unilateral radicular symptoms, no UMN signs, no gait disturbance Parkinson's disease Tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, pill-rolling tremor; no cord compression Hereditary spastic paraplegia Family history, gradual onset, lower extremity predominant, genetic testing --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway - Suspected DCM: arrange prompt spinal/specialist assessment through the current local pathway. - Acute neurological deterioration or neurological deficit after trauma: use the emergency medical/spinal pathway. - Moderate or severe DCM: the AO Spine guideline recommends surgery. - Mild DCM: specialist-led shared decision-making may include surgery or a supervised structured rehabilitation trial. Deterioration during non-operative care requires operative assessment; lack of improvement prompts reconsideration. Physiotherapy may support function, gait and hand use within the specialist plan. It must not delay escalation or include cervical manipulation where cord compromise is suspected. --- Conservative Management Physiotherapy for mild DCM watchful waiting — Grade C evidence: - Cervical collar : no fixed collar regimen is asserted here; any use requires specialist direction and an individual risk–benefit decision - Balance and proprioceptive retraining : Standing balance, tandem stance, Wii Fit / perturbation training - Upper extremity fine motor retraining : Occupational therapy-led ADL retraining - Strengthening : Gentle scapular/shoulder stabilisation; avoid heavy loading through cervical spine - Gait and mobility: where rehabilitation is appropriate, it should be individualised and may include gait/balance retraining and mobility aids according to functional need; orthotic assessment may be considered when clinically indicated. - Neurological monitoring : Document serial mJOA, grip strength, 10-second step/grip-release test at each visit Post-surgical rehabilitation — Grade B evidence: - Most improvement in first 6 months post-decompression - Targeted: grip/pinch strength, fine motor retraining, gait normalisation, return to ADLs - Core stability and cervical muscle strengthening from 6–8 weeks post-fusion - 80% of patients gain ≥2 mJOA points Fehlings et al., 2013 Pharmacological - Neuropathic pain associated radiculopathy : prescribing is clinician-led; NICE CG173 may apply only after confirming a neuropathic-pain indication - NSAIDs : Short-term for pain; avoid long-term in elderly given GI/CV/renal risk - Corticosteroids : High-dose methylprednisolone for acute traumatic SCI; NOT recommended for degenerative CM Fehlings AANS 2013 - Baclofen/Tizanidine : For spasticity management in confirmed CM; specialist-initiated - Bladder management : Anticholinergics oxybutynin for urgency if confirmed; refer urology Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency medical/spinal assessment: acute deterioration, new bladder or bowel disturbance, or neurological deficit after trauma. - Prompt spinal assessment: suspected DCM, progressive neurological change, worsening hand function, gait disturbance or upper motor neuron findings. - Surgical assessment: moderate/severe DCM, or deterioration during supervised non-operative care. - Shared specialist decision: mild DCM; a supervised structured rehabilitation trial may be considered, with reassessment if the person does not improve. No fixed local route or universal conservative-treatment duration is asserted. --- Key References 1. Nouri A, Tetreault L, Singh A, Karadimas SK, Fehlings MG. Global Spine J . 2017;7 3 Suppl :70S–83S. 4. Fehlings MG, Wilson JR, Kopjar B, et al. title: Cervical Radiculopathy
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Cervical radiculopathy CR is a clinical syndrome characterised by pain, neurological deficits, or both, caused by compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root. Annual incidence is approximately 83 per 100,000 population, with peak onset between 50–54 years of age Rad
headings: McKenzie / MDT Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Cervical radiculopathy CR is a clinical syndrome characterised by pain, neurological deficits, or both, caused by compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root. Annual incidence is approximately 83 per 100,000 population, with peak onset between 50–54 years of age Radhakrishnan et al., 1994 . Aetiology: - Disc herniation ~20–25% : acute onset, more common in younger patients 10° 4. Pain with PA spring testing at C3–5 5. Not performing sedentary work --- Outcome Measures Neck Disability Index NDI - 10 items, 0–5 scale each, total 0–50 or 0–100% - Scoring: 0–8% = no disability; 10–28% = mild; 30–48% = moderate; 50–64% = severe; ≥64% = complete - MCID : 7.5/50 points 15% for CR Young et al., 2009 - Reliability: ICC 0.89–0.93; Strong validity for neck pain populations Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS - 0–10 NRS; MCID : 2.1 points for cervical radiculopathy Cleland et al., 2007 - Use for arm pain AND neck pain separately Patient-Specific Functional Scale PSFS - 3–5 patient-identified activities, scored 0–10 each 0=unable, 10=normal - MCID : 2.0 points per activity average for neck pain Cleland et al., 2006 - Responsive to clinically important change in CR Global Rating of Change GROC - 15-point scale −7 to +7 or 7-point Likert - +5 "quite a bit better" or greater = successful outcome - Use at 4 weeks and discharge Arm Pain NRS - Separate from neck NRS — important to track radicular symptom change - Reduction in arm pain more clinically significant than neck pain in CR --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic investigations: MRI and electrodiagnostic studies answer different questions and neither is a universal standalone gold standard. MRI evaluates structural causes; EMG/NCS may support localisation or identify a peripheral neuropathy when the diagnosis is uncertain. MRI: - Preferred imaging for suspected CR - Imaging is not routine for stable uncomplicated symptoms; request it when the result is expected to change management or when serious/progressive pathology or a specialist procedure is being considered - Do NOT routinely offer imaging in first 6 weeks of uncomplicated CR - MRI has high false positive rate — degenerative changes common in asymptomatic adults >50% over age 40 have disc bulges Electrodiagnostics: - EMG/NCS may support localisation or identify peripheral entrapment when the diagnosis remains uncertain - Findings may lag clinical presentation by 3–4 weeks Wainner test cluster: - May support diagnostic reasoning when the component findings agree; do not use it as a current validated treatment-selection rule IASP Diagnostic Criteria for CR: - Unilateral arm pain in a dermatomal distribution - Corresponding sensory changes hypoaesthesia/paraesthesia - Motor deficit or reflex change at corresponding level - Positive provocative tests Spurling's, distraction - Imaging correlation but not required for clinical diagnosis --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Rotator cuff pathology Local shoulder pain, painful arc, negative Spurling's, positive Hawkins/Neer Thoracic outlet syndrome Provoked by arm elevation, positive Roos test, neurogenic/vascular Carpal tunnel syndrome Nocturnal wrist/hand pain, thenar wasting, positive Phalen/Tinel at wrist Cubital tunnel syndrome Medial elbow + ring/little finger symptoms, positive elbow flexion test Brachial neuritis Parsonage-Turner Acute severe shoulder pain followed by rapid weakness, no spinal correlation Peripheral neuropathy Bilateral, glove distribution, diabetes history Cervical myelopathy Bilateral symptoms, UMN signs, gait disturbance, bladder/bowel dysfunction Shoulder impingement Shoulder-localised pain, arc sign positive, negative neurodynamic tests Complex regional pain syndrome Autonomic changes, disproportionate pain, allodynia --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Stable cervical radiculopathy can usually begin with conservative care. Under NICE NG127, symptoms stable for 6 weeks or more are not routinely referred unless pain is uncontrolled, symptoms are disabling, or specified neurological warning features are present. Progressive motor or neurological deficit requires prompt reassessment and condition-appropriate specialist assessment. Atypical cord, vascular, trauma, infection or malignancy features follow their own pathways. --- Conservative Management Exercise Therapy Grade A evidence : - Specific cervical and scapulothoracic strengthening reduces radicular symptoms - Deep neck flexor strengthening craniocervical flexion test biofeedback — CCFT protocol : Jull et al. 2009 - Neural mobilisation slider vs. tensioner techniques : Moderate evidence for symptom reduction - Median nerve slider: ULNT1-based; gentler, preferred in acute/irritable presentations - Radial nerve mobilisation for C6 root involvement - McKenzie-based exercises: centralisation protocol see Clinical Frameworks - Exercise alone equivalent to combined treatment at 12 months Ylinen et al., 2003 Manual Therapy Grade B evidence : - Cervical manipulation and mobilisation: Short-term pain relief; NCEPOD and NICE caution regarding serious adverse events — shared decision-making essential - Thoracic spine manipulation: Level B evidence for short-term reduction of neck pain and disability in CR Cleland et al., 2005 - HVLA to thoracic spine considered lower risk than cervical HVLA - Soft tissue techniques: Limited evidence as standalone; useful adjunct Education & Self-Management: - Pain neuroscience education PNE : addresses catastrophisation and kinesiophobia - Postural advice: ergonomic assessment desk/screen setup , pillow selection - Activity modification: avoid sustained cervical flexion, repetitive overhead loading - Reassurance regarding favourable natural history Traction: - Mechanical/intermittent cervical traction: Moderate evidence for CR Raney et al., 2009 - CPR for traction Raney et al. : ≥3 of 5 predictors: 1. Age ≥55 2. Positive shoulder abduction test 3. Positive ULNT1 4. Positive neck distraction test 5. Peripheralisation with lower cervical PA spring testing Pharmacological Medical/Prescriber-Led - Analgesia: Any medicine choice is prescriber-led and should follow the established pain mechanism, current prescribing guidance and individual risk assessment - NICE CG173 offers a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin for confirmed neuropathic pain. It does not turn the dose ranges previously shown here into cervical-radiculopathy recommendations. - Drug selection, dosing, oral corticosteroids, benzodiazepines and any injection are prescriber/specialist decisions using current prescribing guidance and patient-specific risks; this learner page does not prescribe them. Onward Referral Criteria Follow NICE NG127 recommendation 1.10.11 for stable cervical radiculopathy of 6 weeks or more. Refer when pain is not controlled, symptoms are disabling, or there is a specified neurological feature such as gait disturbance, clumsy/weak hands or legs, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar responses, or new bladder/bowel disturbance. - Prompt specialist assessment: progressive motor or neurological deficit, atypical presentation or suspected cord involvement. - Emergency assessment: acute neurological deterioration or an applicable trauma/vascular emergency. This Version 1 page does not prescribe generic pain-clinic, injection, epidural, spinal-cord-stimulation or fixed 6–12-week surgical pathways. --- Key References 1. Radhakrishnan K, Litchy WJ, O'Fallon WM, Kurland LT. Epidemiology of cervical radiculopathy: a population-based study from Rochester, Minnesota, 1976 through 1990. Brain . 1994;117 Pt 2 :325–335. 2. Wainner RS, Fritz JM, Irrgang JJ, Boninger ML, Delitto A, Allison S. Reliability and diagnostic accuracy of the clinical examination and patient self-report measures for cervical radiculopathy. Spine . 2003;28 1 :52–62. 3. Rubinstein SM, Pool JJ, van Tulder MW, Riphagen II, de Vet HC. 3. Jull's Assessment Approach Jull, 1997; Jull et al, 2007
Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test as One Component of Assessment

C1-2 SNAG Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glide — Mulligan Concept
content: > Clinical Summary: Cervicogenic headache CGH is a secondary headache attributed to a disorder or lesion of the cervical spine or neck soft tissues. Under ICHD-3, imaging alone is not firm evidence of causation, distinguishing features are not unique, cervical myofascial pain may overlap with tension-type headache, and migrainous features may occur. --- Overview & Pathophysiology Mechanism CGH arises from nociceptive input from the upper cervical spine structures joints, muscles, ligaments, dura mater that converges with trigeminal afferents within the trigeminocervical nucleus TCN in the brainstem. The TCN extends caudally from the trigeminal nucleus caudalis to approximately C3–C4. Afferents from: - C1 suboccipital / atlantoaxial — via the dorsal root of C1 where present and the spino-trigeminal tract - C2 atlantoaxial, C2-3 zygapophyseal joints, C2 dorsal root ganglion - C3 C2-3 and C3-4 zygapophyseal joints, third occipital nerve ...all converge with trigeminal afferents in the TCN. This anatomical convergence creates referred pain to the head and face from cervical structures — central sensitisation at the TCN level underpins the perceived headache. Primary pain generators include: - C1-2 and C2-3 zygapophyseal facet joints - Atlantoaxial and atlanto-occipital joints - Suboccipital muscles rectus capitis posterior minor/major, obliquus capitis inferior - C2-3 intervertebral disc - Upper cervical dura mater - Third occipital nerve branch of C3 dorsal ramus Prevalence - Population prevalence: 0.4–4% general population ; up to 17–20% in chronic headache clinic populations - Post-whiplash: up to 53% of whiplash patients develop CGH Bogduk & Govind, 2009 - Gender: female predominance F:M ≈ 4:1 - Age: peak 30–44 years; increases with age - Third occipital headache C2-3 facet-mediated accounts for ~27% of chronic post-whiplash headache Lord et al, 1994 Typical Clinical Presentation - Unilateral headache without side-shift though bilateral variants exist - Starts in the neck/suboccipital region, radiates to frontotemporal region, orbit, or vertex - Provoked or aggravated by neck movement or sustained neck posture - Reduced cervical range of motion particularly rotation - Ipsilateral shoulder/arm symptoms may coexist - Moderate, non-pulsating quality; not typically severe - Duration: hours to days episodic or continuous with fluctuation chronic --- Special Tests CFRT and upper-cervical examination can contribute to the assessment, but published performance estimates vary with the population and reference standard. Neither is definitive in isolation; apply the ICHD-3 criteria and a full headache and neck assessment. Assessment component Role Limitation --- --- --- Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test CFRT Assesses upper-cervical movement restriction and familiar symptom reproduction Not a standalone diagnosis Upper-cervical segmental assessment Assesses familiar pain reproduction and movement findings Examiner-dependent and not definitive Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test CFRT — Detail Procedure: 1. Patient supine; examiner passively flexes cervix to full end-range locks sub-C2 segments 2. Examiner rotates the head passively left and right whilst maintaining full flexion 3. Normal: ≥44° rotation bilaterally; mean normal ~45° 4. Positive: 33/44, address Relevant in chronic CGH Headache Diary Minimum 4-week prospective diary recommended at baseline: - Record: date, time of onset/offset, pain intensity 0–10 , location, medication taken, possible triggers - Digital options: Migraine Buddy, N1-Headache validated electronic diary - Required to establish baseline frequency and identify patterns before initiating treatment --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test as One Component of Assessment Published studies use different populations and reference standards. Use CFRT findings to inform, not determine, the diagnosis; consider both movement restriction and familiar symptom reproduction alongside the ICHD-3 criteria. Cervical Joint Blocks as Reference Standard Anaesthetic blockade of cervical structures is one specialist method of demonstrating causation under the ICHD-3 criteria: - Third occipital nerve TON block — for C2-3 facet-mediated headache - C1-2 and C2-3 medial branch blocks - The specialist service determines the technique, response threshold and local pathway Clinical reasoning should use the ICHD-3 criteria and a full headache/neck assessment. CFRT and upper-cervical examination may contribute but are not definitive. Diagnostic blockade is one possible ICHD-3 item demonstrating causation and is a specialist procedure, not a routine physiotherapy confirmation test. Differentiation from Migraine and Tension-Type Headache Feature Cervicogenic Headache Migraine without aura Tension-Type Headache --------- ---------------------- ------------------------- ----------------------- Laterality Unilateral consistent side Unilateral variable Bilateral Quality Dull, pressing, non-pulsating Pulsating/throbbing Pressing, tightening Severity Moderate Moderate–severe Mild–moderate Location Starts posterior/occipital → frontotemporal Frontotemporal ± orbital Band-like, vertex Cervical trigger Yes — consistent and reproducible Occasional trigger Occasional CFRT Positive 44° Normal or minimally reduced Nausea/vomiting Rarely Common Rare Photophobia/phonophobia Mild, if present Moderate–severe Mild Aura No Yes in 1/3 of migraineurs No Response to NSAIDs Partial Partial–good Good Response to triptans Poor Good No Response to cervical manual therapy Variable; not diagnostic Variable Variable Duration Hours–days variable 4–72 hours 30 min–7 days Physical activity May worsen Worsens Not worsened Migraine features can coexist and do not automatically exclude a cervical contribution. Apply the diagnostic criteria for each headache disorder and avoid relying on one cervical test. --- Differential Diagnosis Headache Type Key Distinguishing Features CFRT Cervical Signs First-Line Management --------------- ---------------------------- ------ --------------- ----------------------- Cervicogenic Headache Unilateral, consistent side; cervical trigger; restricted CFRT; suboccipital onset Positive Present Cervical physio Migraine Apply the current ICHD criteria; migraine features may coexist Variable Cervical tenderness is non-specific Medical/headache management according to the established diagnosis Tension-Type Headache Apply the current ICHD criteria Variable Pericranial tenderness is non-specific Management according to the established diagnosis Medication Overuse Headache Consider when headache and acute-medicine use are frequent; apply current headache guidance Variable Variable Medical review; no withdrawal regimen is prescribed here Cluster Headache Severe unilateral orbital/temporal headache with autonomic features Variable Cervical findings do not establish the diagnosis Urgent medical/headache assessment where indicated Occipital Neuralgia Paroxysmal pain in an occipital-nerve distribution with possible allodynia Variable Local tenderness is not definitive Specialist assessment where indicated Giant Cell Arteritis >50 years; temporal artery tenderness; jaw claudication; ESR >50; visual symptoms Negative Absent Same-day emergency medical assessment; treatment is medical-team-led TMJ Dysfunction Pain at TMJ; jaw movement provocation; ear pain; clicking Negative Absent Dental/maxillofacial Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Obese female; pulsatile tinnitus; visual obscurations; papilloedema; worse lying Negative Absent Urgent neurology --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway First determine whether the headache presentation is compatible with ICHD-3 cervicogenic headache and whether a secondary-headache warning feature requires medical assessment. Physiotherapy may address a clinically supported cervical contribution after serious pathology has been considered. Manual therapy, exercise and self-management choices should be individualised. Procedural blocks, radiofrequency treatment, preventive medicines and other specialist interventions require separate specialist assessment and evidence; they are not Version 1 physiotherapy referral thresholds. --- Conservative Management Evidence Base Jull et al 2002 — Landmark RCT Spine, 27 17 : 1835–1843 - n=200; 4 groups: manual therapy MT alone, specific exercise alone, combined MT+exercise, control - Key finding: Combined MT + specific cervical exercise produced significantly better outcomes than either alone or control - 10-week intervention; outcomes at 12 months - Combined group: 76% had ≥50% reduction in headache frequency at 12 months - Manual therapy: targeted upper cervical manipulation and mobilisation - Exercise: specific craniocervical flexion training deep cervical flexors C1-2 SNAG Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glide — Mulligan Concept Technique: - Patient seated; therapist applies sustained posteroanterior glide to C1-2 on the symptomatic side using thumb/pisiform contact on the C2 spinous process / articular pillar - Patient performs active cervical rotation in direction of restriction whilst glide is sustained - If pain-free rotation improves → positive response, proceed with treatment - 3 sets × 10 repetitions; can be self-applied with towel home SNAG Evidence: - Hall et al 2007, 2008 : C1-2 SNAG significantly reduces headache frequency and intensity in CGH - Paungmali et al 2003 : SNAG produces hypoalgesic effect — pressure pain threshold increases - Significant improvement in CFRT range of motion following C1-2 SNAG Hall et al, 2007 Upper Cervical Mobilisation - Passive accessory intervertebral movements PAIVMs at C0-C1, C1-C2, C2-C3 - Grades III–IV Maitland grading to restricted, painful segments - May include: atlanto-occipital decompression, C1-2 rotation mobilisation in flexion - Dose: 3–5 sets of 30–60 second sustained holds or oscillatory grades; reassess after each set - Evidence: Jull et al 1997, 2002 ; Zito et al 2006 — upper cervical manual examination and mobilisation reliably identifies and treats CGH Specific Cervical Flexor Retraining Deep Cervical Flexor DCF Training Protocol Jull et al, 2008 : Stage 1 — Activation Weeks 1–2 : - Craniocervical flexion nodding in supine - Pressure biofeedback: target 22 mmHg; 10 × 10-second holds - Avoid SCM/anterior scalene substitution Stage 2 — Endurance Weeks 3–4 : - Progress biofeedback target: 24–26 mmHg - 10 × 10-second holds at each level; 3 levels progressed sequentially Stage 3 — Functional Integration Weeks 5–10 : - DCF activation during functional tasks - Sitting posture training - Progress to 28–30 mmHg as tolerated Stage 4 — Load/Strength Weeks 8–12 : - Resistance exercises: supine neck flexion with gravity resistance - Integration with cervical rotation and lateral flexion Postural Management - Identify and correct forward head posture FHP — increases loading on upper cervical joints and suboccipital muscles - Thoracic mobility: thoracic extension exercises, foam roller mobilisation T4–T8 - Workstation ergonomics assessment — screen height, chair position - Sleep posture: single pillow maintaining neutral cervical alignment; cervical pillow if indicated - Evidence: Ruivo et al 2017 — FHP correction reduces frequency of cervicogenic-type headache; correlation between FHP and CGH prevalence Exercise Prescription Summary Component Exercise Sets × Reps Frequency ----------- ---------- ------------- ----------- DCF activation CCF exercise biofeedback 3 × 10 × 10s holds Daily Cervical mobility CFRT self-mobilisation SNAG in flexion 3 × 10 Daily Suboccipital stretching Self-suboccipital release / chin tuck stretch 3 × 30s 2× daily Thoracic extension Foam roller extension T4-T8 3 × 60s Daily Scapular stabilisation Wall angels / low row 3 × 15 3×/week Postural re-education Chin tuck + retraction in sitting Hourly work breaks Daily --- Pharmacological Management Physiotherapy is the first-line recommended treatment for CGH. Pharmacological management is adjunctive and should be coordinated with the patient's GP. Medicines and diagnostic uncertainty NICE CG150 covers recognised primary headache disorders and must not be presented as a treatment guideline for cervicogenic headache. Analgesic or preventive medication is prescriber-led using the established diagnosis and current guidance. A response or non-response to a triptan does not by itself establish or exclude CGH. Nerve Blocks Occipital or cervical diagnostic/therapeutic blocks are specialist procedures. Indication, agent, dose, anatomical approach and timing require an appropriate pain/neurology service and are not prescribed by this page. Radiofrequency Neurotomy - Third occipital nerve RFN pulsed or conventional - Indication: Confirmed C2-3 facet-mediated CGH positive diagnostic block ; failed conservative management - Evidence: Lord et al 1996 — conventional RFN of TON: median pain-free period 297 days vs 8 days sham - Available via: Belfast City Hospital Pain Management / Neurosurgery Botulinum Toxin Botox - Limited evidence specifically for CGH stronger evidence base in chronic migraine - May be considered for refractory CGH via neurology/pain clinic - NICE TA260 2012 : Botox approved for chronic migraine ≥15 headache days/month ; not specifically for CGH - Use in CGH remains off-label / specialist decision Preventive Pharmacology for refractory/chronic presentations There is no NICE CG150 preventive-drug recommendation for CGH. Any medication requires confirmation of the headache or neuropathic-pain diagnosis and individual GP/neurology prescribing review. --- Onward Referral Criteria - Use NICE CG150 to identify headache features that warrant further investigation or referral. - Arrange emergency assessment for an acute neurological emergency, suspected meningitis, stroke or cervical artery dissection. - Seek medical/specialist review when diagnosis remains uncertain, the headache pattern changes substantially, or symptoms remain disabling despite an appropriate management plan. Version 1 does not use fixed treatment-session percentages, fixed physiotherapy-failure intervals, diagnostic-block thresholds, spinal-cord stimulation or other procedure criteria as referral rules. --- Key References > All references are from peer-reviewed literature. Access via PubMed, CINAHL, or HSC Library NI Athens login via nhs.net credentials . 1. Jull G, Trott P, Potter H, et al. 2002 . A randomized controlled trial of exercise and manipulative therapy for cervicogenic headache. Spine , 27 17 , 1835–1843. PMID: 12195063 — Landmark RCT establishing combined manual therapy + exercise as gold standard treatment. 2. Ogince M, Hall T, Robinson K, Blackmore AM. 2007 . title: Mechanical Neck Pain
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Mechanical neck pain MNP is the most prevalent cervical spine condition, with a point prevalence of ~14–15% globally and lifetime prevalence up to 67% Fejer et al., 2006 . It is the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide Hoy et al., 2014 . Annual incidence in UK prim
headings: Keele STarT MSK / Örebro MSK Questionnaire Short Form
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Mechanical neck pain MNP is the most prevalent cervical spine condition, with a point prevalence of ~14–15% globally and lifetime prevalence up to 67% Fejer et al., 2006 . It is the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide Hoy et al., 2014 . Annual incidence in UK primary care is approximately 15% of adult consultations involving neck-related complaints. Definition: Neck pain of musculoskeletal origin without neurological involvement, arising from cervical structures including intervertebral discs, facet joints, muscles, ligaments, and associated fasciae. Reproduced or modified by cervical movement and mechanical loading. Pathological sources: - Facet joints zygapophyseal joints : Most common identifiable pain source ~54% in chronic neck pain by Bogduk & McGuirk, 2006 ; intra-articular meniscoid inclusions, capsular strain, synovitis - Intervertebral disc discogenic pain : Annular tears, internal disc disruption; C5/6 and C6/7 most common - Muscles and myofascial tissue: Trapezius, levator scapulae, splenius capitis, suboccipitals — trigger points, postural overload - Ligaments: Posterior longitudinal, interspinous ligaments with repetitive strain - Atlantoaxial and atlanto-occipital joints: Particularly relevant in upper cervical pain Classification Guzman et al., 2008 — Bone and Joint Decade 2000–2010 Task Force : - Grade I: No signs of major pathology, does not interfere with daily activities - Grade II: No signs of major pathology, does interfere with daily activities - Grade III: Neck pain with neurological signs radiculopathy - Grade IV: Neck pain with signs of major structural pathology MNP broadly covers Grades I–II. Risk factors: - Sustained postures sedentary work, screen use >6 hours/day - Psychosocial: high job demands, low control, poor support, depression, anxiety - Previous neck pain episode strongest predictor of recurrence - Female sex RR ~1.4 - Age 45–54 years peak - Sleep disturbance Prognosis: Most acute MNP >50% resolves within 6 weeks; however, ~40–50% develop persistent or recurrent symptoms at 1 year Haldeman et al., 2008 . --- Special Tests Mechanical neck pain is primarily a diagnosis of exclusion — the primary role of clinical assessment is to rule out serious pathology and neurological involvement, then classify the mechanical presentation. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR −LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Spurling's negative — rules in MNP over radiculopathy 0.50–0.60 0.86–0.97 — — High ruling out radiculopathy Passive cervical rotation 10° 4. Pain with spring test at C3–5 5. Not performing sedentary work >50% of day Key assessments: - Active ROM goniometry or CROM device : flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation — establish baseline and monitor - PPIVMs : C2–7 intersegmental mobility - PAIVMs : posteroanterior pressure C1–7 — identify comparable sign pain provocation at symptomatic segment - Deep neck flexor endurance : CCFT or cranio-cervical flexion endurance test — assess neuromuscular control - Postural assessment : forward head posture, thoracic kyphosis, scapular position --- Red Flags Screen for serious pathology, including neurological/cord involvement, vascular pathology, significant trauma, fracture, infection, malignancy and inflammatory disease. - Apply the Canadian C-Spine Rule only in an appropriate trauma presentation; it is not a general neck-pain screening rule. - Use IFOMPT 2020 risk-based reasoning for possible vascular pathology. New cranial nerve dysfunction is concerning when it occurs within a vascular or neurological presentation; the historical “5Ds/3Ns” are not a clearance rule. - Suspected meningitis, acute neurological deterioration or another emergency presentation requires emergency assessment. Other concerns require medical assessment with urgency matched to the presentation. Assess psychosocial prognostic factors where useful, but do not use an unsupported fixed STarT MSK threshold to prescribe a treatment package. --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Concept - Identify comparable sign the movement or palpation finding that most reproduces the patient's pain - Symptom/resistance dominance : - Pain-dominant acute, irritable : Grade I–II oscillatory techniques for pain neurophysiology modulation - Resistance-dominant subacute/chronic, stiff : Grade III–IV to increase mobility - Regular reassessment "asterisk sign" : track change in ROM, pain, function after each technique - PAIVMs: C1–7 central PAs, unilateral PAs, transverse pressures - PPIVMs: rotation and lateral flexion intersegmental mobility assessment - Progression: add cervical rotation, extension, lateral flexion McKenzie / MDT - Classify as Derangement most common , Dysfunction , Postural Syndrome , or Other - Repeated movement assessment 10 repetitions each direction - Postural Syndrome : pain only at end range/sustained posture; resolves with posture correction; no structural change - Dysfunction Syndrome : pain at end range due to contracted/adherent tissue; intermittent pain at end range only; treatment: repeated stretching - Derangement : most common; centralisation/peripheralisation determines direction; treat with directional preference exercises - Retraction exercises cervical retractions as first-line for most cervical derangements Norwegian Kaltenborn-Evjenth Approach - Segment-specific mobilisation based on concave-convex rules - Traction grades I–III; glides in plane of facet joint Biopsychosocial / Stratified Care - STarT MSK 3-tier : - Low risk: brief physiotherapy 2–3 sessions , self-management booklet - Medium risk: standard physiotherapy 6–8 sessions - High risk: physiotherapy + targeted psychosocial intervention, consider psychological referral - Pain neuroscience education PNE : Moseley & Butler framework — reduces catastrophisation and fear-avoidance --- Outcome Measures Neck Disability Index NDI - Widely used measure of neck-related disability - 10 items × 0–5 = 0–50 total reported as percentage: score/50 × 100 - MCID : 7.5 points 50-point scale for neck pain; ~5 points for chronic non-specific neck pain Pool et al., 2007 - MDC 95% CI : 10.5 points - High reliability ICC 0.89–0.93 Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS - 0–10; MCID : 1.5–2.5 points for non-specific neck pain Cleland et al., 2008 - Measure at rest, with movement, worst in 24 hours Patient-Specific Functional Scale PSFS - 0–10 per activity 3 patient-identified activities - MCID : 2.0 points average across activities Cleland et al., 2006 - High responsiveness and patient-centredness Global Rating of Change GROC - 15-point scale; use at 4 weeks and discharge - +5 or above = meaningful improvement Keele STarT MSK / Örebro MSK Questionnaire Short Form - Stratification tool , not outcome measure per se - Re-administer at 4–6 weeks to confirm psychosocial risk trajectory Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire FABQ - Work and Physical Activity subscales 0–66 and 0–24 - High scores >29 work subscale predict poor return-to-work; inform targeted management --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis MNP is a clinical diagnosis — imaging rarely changes management in uncomplicated cases. Imaging guidelines: - Imaging decisions require the clinical context, red-flag assessment and applicable local/specialist pathway; no condition-specific NICE neck-imaging recommendation is asserted here. - X-ray: low utility for soft tissue pathology; use if fracture suspected post-trauma, osteoporosis, malignancy - CT: bony anatomy, foraminal stenosis, OPLL when MRI contraindicated - Normal imaging does NOT exclude pain; degenerative changes are ubiquitous and poorly correlate with symptoms Key evidence: - Asymptomatic degenerative changes on MRI present in: 87% at age 70, 50% at age 40 Boden et al., 1990 - Imaging findings should be interpreted within clinical context — avoid iatrogenic nocebo - Systematic review Rubinstein & van Tulder, 2008 : clinical examination sufficient for diagnosis and management in non-complex cases Yellow Flag Screening STarT MSK : - Prognostic stratification improves outcomes vs. one-size-fits-all care Hill et al., 2011 — LBP evidence extrapolated to neck pain; Beneciuk et al., 2013 for cervical --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Cervical radiculopathy Radicular arm pain in dermatomal pattern, positive Spurling's, neurological deficit Cervicogenic headache Headache referral from C1–3, positive FRT, unilateral, occipital to frontotemporal Fibromyalgia Widespread pain, multiple tender points, fatigue, sleep disturbance Rheumatoid arthritis / inflammatory arthritis Morning stiffness, bilateral, systemic features, elevated ESR/CRP, ANA positive Ankylosing spondylitis Young male, sacroiliac involvement, HLA-B27, bamboo spine on X-ray Thoracic outlet syndrome Positional vascular/neurogenic symptoms with arm elevation Temporomandibular joint dysfunction Jaw pain, crepitus, bruxism, ear pain, limited mouth opening Occipital neuralgia Sharp, stabbing occipital pain, positive Tinel over GON, distinct from cervicogenic headache Whiplash associated disorder Mechanism of injury acceleration-deceleration , specific classification WAD grade Muscle tension headache Bilateral, pressure/band-like, no photophobia, not worsened by movement --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Mechanical neck pain without serious-pathology features is generally managed with education, activity, exercise and individualised adjunctive care. Access routes and service capacity vary; use the current local musculoskeletal pathway. Psychosocial assessment may inform shared planning, but Version 1 does not prescribe fixed session allocations or a threshold-based treatment package. --- Conservative Management Exercise Therapy Grade A — highest evidence for neck pain : - Deep neck flexor DNF strengthening : Craniocervical flexion test CCFT protocol — progressive pressure biofeedback 20–26–30 mmHg ; Jull et al. 2002, 2009 - Proven superior to general neck exercise for chronic neck pain - 8–10 week programme; 3–5 × per week - Cervical and scapulothoracic strengthening : Trapezius, rhomboids, serratus anterior — 3 × 10–15 RM, progressive - Aerobic exercise : Walking, swimming; reduces disability and pain catastrophising; NICE recommendation - Proprioceptive/sensorimotor training : Joint position error retraining; laser pointer head exercises; supports neuromuscular control deficits in chronic neck pain Revel et al., 1994 - Stretching : Suboccipital, levator scapulae, scalenes; limited standalone evidence but patient-valued and safe Manual Therapy Grade B–A : - Combined manipulation + exercise superior to either alone Hoving et al., 2002; Hurwitz et al., 2002 - Cervical mobilisation : Safe and effective; Maitland Grade III–IV PAIVMs/PPIVMs - Cervical HVLA manipulation : Any use requires informed consent, exclusion of contraindications and patient-specific reasoning under the IFOMPT 2020 framework; it is not selected by a prediction rule alone - Thoracic manipulation : Level A evidence adjunct for cervical pain Cleland et al., 2005, 2007 - Soft tissue therapy : Trigger point release, myofascial release — adjunct; limited standalone evidence Patient Education Grade A : - PNE: Explain pain as non-threatening; reassure re: natural history; de-medicalize - Postural advice: Ergonomic screen height, chair adjustment, monitor distance, pillow height cervical neutral - Activity modification: vary sustained postures and use tolerable movement breaks according to symptoms and task demands - Return to activity encouraged: "motion is lotion" messaging Dry Needling / Acupuncture: - Trigger point dry needling: Moderate evidence for short-term pain relief in myofascial neck pain Tough et al., 2009 - NICE NG193 permits a limited course of acupuncture or dry needling for chronic primary pain under its specified conditions; applicability to an individual with mechanical neck pain requires confirmation that the chronic-primary-pain scope is met Pharmacological Medical/Prescriber-Led No NICE guideline cited here supplies a mechanical-neck-pain dosing pathway. Medication selection, dose, duration and gastroprotection require an individual prescriber assessment and current prescribing guidance. NG193 recommendations about antidepressants, opioids, gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines, NSAIDs and paracetamol apply specifically to management of chronic primary pain and must not be extrapolated automatically to all mechanical neck pain. Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency or urgent assessment: according to the actual suspected pathology, including acute neurological deterioration, meningitis, significant trauma, fracture or vascular emergency. - Prompt medical/specialist assessment: suspected DCM, progressive neurological change, serious infection or malignancy. - Reassess and consider onward referral: when diagnosis remains uncertain or symptoms remain substantially disabling despite an appropriate conservative plan. Occupational, psychological and pain-service referrals should be based on individual need and the current local pathway, not a fixed treatment duration. --- Key References 1. title: Whiplash Associated Disorders
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Whiplash Associated Disorders WAD is the term describing the constellation of symptoms following an acceleration-deceleration injury to the cervical spine, most commonly from motor vehicle collisions MVCs . The Québec Task Force QTF on Whiplash-Associated Disorders Spitzer
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Whiplash Associated Disorders WAD is the term describing the constellation of symptoms following an acceleration-deceleration injury to the cervical spine, most commonly from motor vehicle collisions MVCs . The Québec Task Force QTF on Whiplash-Associated Disorders Spitzer et al., 1995 provides the foundational classification framework. Epidemiology: - Annual incidence: 235–300 per 100,000 in Western countries - UK: ~250,000–300,000 per year; high rates linked to insurance claims CEGA/ABI data - Most common MVC injury type; estimated annual cost to NHS and insurance >£2 billion - Female:Male ratio ~1.4:1 - Peak incidence: 20–40 years Mechanism of Injury: - Rear-end collision most common: initial extension of lower cervical spine followed by rapid flexion of upper cervical spine S-curve deformation - This S-shaped motion is different from simple extension — it causes: - Stretching of anterior longitudinal ligament - Compression of posterior elements facet joints, nerve roots - Differential motion between segments with relative translation - Strain of zygapophyseal joint capsules most consistent pain source - Side-impact and frontal collisions also produce WAD with different biomechanics - No single lesion visible on standard imaging in most cases hence "soft tissue injury" Pathological pain sources: 1. Zygapophyseal facet joints — most consistently identified pain source; Barnsley et al. 1995 demonstrated by diagnostic nerve blocks that facet joint pain present in ~54% of chronic WAD 2. Intervertebral discs : Annular tears, especially C5/6 and C6/7 3. Musculature : Multifidus, semispinalis, suboccipitals — MRI evidence of fatty infiltration and atrophy in chronic WAD Elliott et al., 2006 4. Neural tissue : Dorsal root ganglia sensitisation; central sensitisation 5. Ligamentous injury : Alar, transverse, C2–3 ligaments rare but important in higher grades 6. Sympathetic nervous system involvement : autonomic dysregulation; links to widespread hypersensitivity Neurobiological Mechanisms: - Peripheral sensitisation: nociceptors in joint capsule, disc sensitised by mechanical and chemical stimuli - Central sensitisation: key driver of chronic WAD — explains widespread hypersensitivity, cold hyperalgesia, psychological distress seen in Grade III WAD - Psychosocial factors amplify and perpetuate sensitisation Québec Task Force Classification: Grade Clinical Presentation ------- ----------------------- WAD 0 No neck complaints, no physical signs WAD I Neck complaint pain, stiffness, tenderness , no physical signs WAD II Neck complaint + musculoskeletal signs reduced ROM, point tenderness WAD III Neck complaint + neurological signs reflex changes, weakness, sensory deficit WAD IV Neck complaint + fracture or dislocation WAD III is analogous to cervical radiculopathy following whiplash mechanism. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR −LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Cold Hyperalgesia cold pain threshold as predictor of chronicity 0.72 0.65 2.1 0.43 Moderate Chien et al., 2008 Widespread Pressure Pain Hyperalgesia PPT 0.68 0.64 1.9 0.50 Moderate Spurling's Test for WAD III/radiculopathy 0.50–0.60 0.86–0.97 3.5–6.1 0.47 High ULNT1 median nerve neurodynamic 0.72–0.97 0.22–0.33 1.1–1.3 0.12 Moderate Neck Distraction Test WAD III 0.44 0.90 4.4 0.62 Moderate Cervical ROM 6 weeks : Progress to Grade III–IV techniques addressing stiffness; PAIVMs/PPIVMs - Comparable sign methodology: identify and track comparable pain response - Avoid techniques that peripheralise neurological symptoms WAD III McKenzie / MDT - Acute WAD: pain frequently multidirectional initially; retraction exercises as starting point - Look for directional preference may be slower to emerge than in disc pathology - If centralisation occurs → directional exercise - Education re: natural history and active recovery integral to MDT approach Graded Activity / Behavioural Approach - Evidence supports active management over passive rest in WAD I–II Rosenfeld et al., 2003 - Graded activity exposure: progressive increase in meaningful activities despite pain - Graded motor imagery GMI and mirror therapy: limited evidence; consider in complex chronic WAD Psychologically Informed Practice PiP - Critical in medium-high risk WAD IES-R ≥26, TSK ≥37 - Address fear-avoidance, catastrophising, catastrophic thinking about injury - CBT-based physiotherapy Linton & Andersson, 2000 principles - Link with psychology services for high-risk presentations Sterling's Risk-Stratified Approach 2010 - Low risk WAD I–II, low distress : Self-management advice, reassurance, brief physiotherapy - Moderate risk WAD II–III, moderate distress : 8–10 sessions physiotherapy + progressive exercise + psychological support - High risk high distress, widespread hyperalgesia : Intensive physiotherapy + psychology liaison + pharmacological management of central sensitisation --- Outcome Measures Neck Disability Index NDI - Primary outcome for WAD disability - MCID : 7.5 points 50-point scale ; chronic WAD: 8.5 points Jull et al., 2014 - Use at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 12 months - NDI ≥30% at 1 month predicts chronic disability Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS - 0–10; MCID : 2.1 points in WAD Sterling et al., 2010 - Measure arm pain if WAD III and neck pain separately Patient-Specific Functional Scale PSFS - Highly responsive to change; MCID : 2.0 points average - Functional activities specific to patient's life/work Impact of Event Scale-Revised IES-R - 22-item PTSD screening tool; score 0–88 - ≥26: moderate impact risk of PTSD ; ≥33: probable PTSD - Not an outcome measure per se but critical prognostic screener in WAD - Re-administer at 4 weeks if initially borderline Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia TSK - 17-item scale; 17–68; ≥37 = high kinesiophobia - MCID : 4 points; use alongside FABQ to guide psychosocial management GROC Global Rating of Change - 15-point scale; meaningful improvement ≥+5 - 6 weeks, 3 months, discharge Whiplash Disability Questionnaire WDQ - 13-item WAD-specific disability questionnaire; 0–130 - MCID : 13.3 points; validated specifically in whiplash populations Pinfold et al., 2004 --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis No imaging required for WAD 0–II without high-risk features Canadian C-Spine Rule . Imaging guidelines: - X-ray: rule out fracture/dislocation; dynamic X-rays flexion/extension for suspected instability — limited sensitivity - CT: preferred for high-energy trauma; superior bony detail; rule out fracture, SCIWORA - MRI: WAD III neurological signs or if neurological deterioration; assess disc, cord, nerve root; also for suspected ligamentous injury - Suspected traumatic cervical artery dissection requires urgent/emergency medical assessment; vascular imaging such as CTA or MRI/MRA should be selected within the acute medical/stroke pathway. Prognostic factors strong evidence — Walton et al., 2013 systematic review : - High initial pain intensity NRS ≥5 : negative prognostic factor - High initial disability NDI ≥30% : negative prognostic factor - Cold hyperalgesia: negative prognostic factor central sensitisation marker - Psychological distress IES-R, anxiety : negative prognostic factor - Low self-efficacy: negative prognostic factor - Compensation claims in some jurisdictions: controversial; complex psychosocial interaction Active management vs. rest: - Rosenfeld et al. 2003 RCT: Active treatment early mobilisation superior to collar/rest at 6 months and 3 years - Söderlund & Lindberg 2001 : early activation combined with education reduces progression to chronicity --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Cervical fracture/dislocation WAD IV High-energy mechanism, midline tenderness, neurological deficit, X-ray/CT confirms Traumatic vertebral artery dissection Severe occipital headache, brainstem signs, Horner's, ataxia — CTA/MRI Traumatic disc herniation WAD III Radicular symptoms, positive Spurling's/distraction, MRI confirmation Concussion / mild TBI Associated head impact, cognitive symptoms, headache, vestibular signs TMJ injury post-MVC Jaw pain, crepitus, limited mouth opening, pain with chewing PTSD Psychological re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal — IES-R ≥33; requires psychology Shoulder injury rotator cuff Mechanism of arm bracing, shoulder-localised pain, arc test Thoracic outlet syndrome Vascular/neurogenic symptoms with arm elevation, positional SCIWORA Spinal cord injury without radiological abnormality — MRI required --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway After serious injury has been excluded, WAD I–II may be managed using education, activity, exercise and individualised physiotherapy. Psychological distress and possible PTSD should be assessed and referred according to clinical need and the current local pathway. Progressive neurological deficit, suspected cord injury or possible cervical artery dissection requires condition-appropriate prompt or emergency assessment. Version 1 does not prescribe fixed pain-clinic, psychology or surgery timelines. --- Conservative Management Active Treatment — Grade A evidence: Exercise: - Early active mobilisation: gentle cervical ROM exercises from day 1 post-injury Rosenfeld et al., 2003 — significantly better outcomes than immobilisation - Progressive cervical and scapulothoracic strengthening — as per mechanical neck pain protocol - Deep neck flexor activation CCFT protocol — impaired in acute and chronic WAD Jull et al., 2008 - Proprioceptive/sensorimotor exercises: laser pointer gaze stability, joint position error retraining Manual Therapy — Grade B: - Cervical mobilisation: Maitland Grade I–II → III–IV as irritability settles - Thoracic manipulation: safer alternative to cervical HVLA; Grade A evidence as adjunct - Cervical HVLA: do not proceed where instability, vascular pathology or another contraindication is suspected; apply the IFOMPT 2020 framework and an individual risk–benefit/consent process Education — Grade A: - Most powerful single intervention for acute WAD with exercise - Reassurance: natural history is favourable in WAD I–II; >70% recover within 3 months - Pain neuroscience education: address sensitisation, avoid catastrophising - Activity continuation messaging: "keep moving, stay active" - Whiplash patient information booklet RACGP/Arthritis Australia evidence-based resources applicable to NI Physical Modalities: - Heat/ice: minimal evidence; low harm; patient-directed short-term use - TENS: limited evidence; may provide short-term pain relief - Ultrasound/laser: insufficient evidence; not recommended as primary treatment - Acupuncture: Moderate evidence for short-term pain relief in chronic neck pain; NICE allows referral Psychological Approaches High-Risk WAD : - CBT-based physiotherapy: fear-avoidance model - Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing EMDR : for confirmed PTSD — psychology-delivered - Acceptance and Commitment Therapy ACT principles incorporated into physiotherapy Pharmacological Medical/Prescriber-Led Acute 6 weeks : - Sensory hypersensitivity alone does not establish a neuropathic-pain indication. NICE CG173 applies to confirmed neuropathic pain, while NG193 drug recommendations apply specifically to chronic primary pain; neither is direct acute-WAD prescribing guidance Injections: - Medial branch blocks / radiofrequency neurotomy for confirmed facet joint pain Barnsley et al., 1995; Lord et al., 1996 : evidence-based for chronic WAD with confirmed facet pain; refer to Pain Clinic/Spinal service Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency: suspected fracture/dislocation, acute spinal cord injury, or suspected cervical artery dissection/stroke with acute neurological features. - Prompt specialist assessment: progressive neurological or motor deficit. - Individual onward referral: consider referral when symptoms remain disabling, significant psychological distress is present, or PTSD is suspected, using the current local pathway. Version 1 does not use fixed 4-week, 12-week, WAD-grade surgery or PiP/CBT timing rules. --- Key References 1. Spitzer WO, Skovron ML, Salmi LR, et al. title: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar Neuropathy at the Elbow)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Cubital tunnel syndrome CuTS is the second most common peripheral nerve entrapment syndrome after carpal tunnel syndrome , accounting for approximately 20% of peripheral nerve compressions. Prevalence estimates range from 25–38 per 100,000 person-years; higher in manual wo
