content: Overview & Pathophysiology Cubital tunnel syndrome CuTS is the second most common peripheral nerve entrapment syndrome after carpal tunnel syndrome , accounting for approximately 20% of peripheral nerve compressions. Prevalence estimates range from 25–38 per 100,000 person-years; higher in manual workers, musicians, and those with habitual elbow flexion. Anatomy of the Cubital Tunnel: The cubital tunnel is a fibroosseous tunnel at the medial elbow through which the ulnar nerve passes. Key anatomical structures: - Floor: Medial collateral ligament ulnar head and posterior capsule - Roof: Osborne's fascia arcuate ligament — the most common site of compression - Walls: Medial epicondyle medial , olecranon lateral - Contents: Ulnar nerve + accompanying vessels Other sites of ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow: 1. Medial intermuscular septum proximal compression 2. Arcade of Struthers fascial band, 8 cm proximal to medial epicondyle 3. Cubital tunnel Osborne's fascia — most common 4. Between heads of flexor carpi ulnaris distal to cubital tunnel Pathophysiology of compression: - During elbow flexion, the cubital tunnel narrows by 55% MacNicol 1979 , increasing intraneural pressure - Normal nerve: 7–8 mmHg at rest; cubital tunnel pressure rises to 100–200 mmHg at 90° flexion - Sustained compression → intraneural oedema → myelin loss → axonal degeneration in severe/chronic cases - Nerve subluxation snapping over medial epicondyle in 20% of population → repetitive traction injury Risk factors: - Habitual elbow flexion sleeping, driving, phone use - Prolonged leaning on medial elbow - Repetitive elbow flexion-extension overhead athletes, musicians - Medial epicondyle fracture/deformity - Cubitus valgus deformity - Medial elbow osteoarthritis, loose bodies - Diabetes mellitus peripheral neuropathy — double crush - Obesity, smoking --- Special Tests Assessment component Role Limitation --- --- --- Elbow-flexion, pressure-provocation and Tinel-type tests May reproduce ulnar-distribution symptoms No single provocation test confirms compression Froment's, Wartenberg's and intrinsic-muscle inspection Explore motor involvement Abnormal findings require localisation and differential assessment Sensory, grip and pinch assessment Establish deficit and monitor function Non-specific in isolation Elbow Flexion Test Wadsworth 1987 : Patient maximally flexes elbow with wrist extended, held for 60 seconds. Positive = tingling/numbness in ring and little finger. Best single test for CuTS. Combined Provocation Test: Elbow flexion + wrist extension + pressure over the cubital tunnel may reproduce familiar ulnar-distribution symptoms. Interpret it with the full neurological examination. Scratch Collapse Test Cheng et al. 2008 : Examiner scratches skin over suspected compression site; patient momentarily loses shoulder resistance. Highly specific for nerve compression location. Froment's Sign: Patient holds paper between thumb and index finger; examiner pulls paper away. Positive = thumb IP joint flexes compensating for adductor pollicis weakness with FPL — indicates ulnar nerve motor involvement. --- Red Flags - Marked or progressive ulnar motor weakness, intrinsic-muscle wasting, clawing or major sensory loss requires prompt neurological/specialist assessment. - Trauma with fracture/dislocation or acute neurovascular compromise requires urgent/emergency assessment. - Atypical systemic, malignancy or mass-lesion features require appropriate medical assessment. Do not infer that two possible compression sites both require treatment. Evaluate each clinically. Do not make neurophysiology, imaging or decompression automatic from the red-flag statement. --- Clinical Frameworks McGowan Classification of CuTS Severity Grade Symptoms Sensory Motor Management ------- ---------- --------- ------- ------------ I Mild Intermittent paraesthesia; minimal Normal or intermittent loss Normal intrinsics Conservative splinting, activity modification II Moderate Persistent paraesthesia; aching Constant sensory deficit Moderate weakness Neurological/specialist assessment according to progression and response III Severe Constant symptoms Marked sensory deficit Significant wasting; clawing Surgical decompression; conservative unlikely to succeed Dellon Classification - Mild: Intermittent paraesthesia; positive elbow flexion test; no muscle weakness - Moderate: Intermittent paraesthesia; positive provocative tests; weak interossei - Severe: Persistent paraesthesia; clawing; intrinsic muscle atrophy Neurodynamic Assessment Upper Limb Neurodynamic Test 3 ULNT3 — ulnar bias : - Position: Shoulder depression, wrist/finger extension, elbow flexion, shoulder abduction, cervical lateral flexion away - Sensitising: Cervical lateral flexion toward; wrist extension/flexion - Positive: Reproduction of concordant symptoms; asymmetrical response vs contralateral - Use for: Screening, differentiating peripheral vs central sensitisation, guiding neural mobilisation --- Outcome Measures Patient-Reported Measures DASH / QuickDASH: - Most widely used for upper limb nerve compression - MCID: DASH 10.2 points; QuickDASH 16 points - Work module available for occupational contexts Boston/Levine CTS Questionnaire: Not validated for CuTS; use DASH instead. Patient-Rated Ulnar Nerve Evaluation PRUNE : Validated specifically for ulnar neuropathy; 17 items; symptom and function subscales. Less widely available but more condition-specific. Objective Measures Grip Strength Jamar : - Compare dominant vs non-dominant; affected vs unaffected - MCID: 6.5 kg; ICC 0.97–0.98 - Serial measurement tracks motor recovery post-decompression Pinch Strength lateral and tip pinch : - Tip pinch directly measures intrinsic function - Lateral pinch tests adductor pollicis ulnar nerve + FPL median nerve Sensory Testing: - Semmes-Weinstein monofilament testing: quantifies sensory threshold in ring/little finger - 2-point discrimination static and moving : >6 mm static 2PD = abnormal; tracks recovery - Vibration threshold 128 Hz tuning fork : reduced in ulnar distribution in moderate/severe CuTS Functional Dexterity: - Purdue Pegboard test manual dexterity; sensitive to intrinsic muscle weakness - Nine-hole peg test: functional fine motor speed assessment --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis based on symptom pattern + provocative tests is appropriate for initial management. NCS confirmation required before surgical intervention. Nerve Conduction Studies NCS : - May support localisation and severity assessment; the neurophysiology service interprets thresholds in clinical context - Compound Motor Action Potential CMAP amplitude: reduced in axonal degeneration - Sensory nerve action potential SNAP : reduced or absent in sensory fibre involvement - Inching technique: localises compression to specific 2 cm segment - Referral pathway: Use the current local neurological/neurophysiology pathway; service locations and waiting times must be confirmed locally EMG: - Detects denervation in FDI, ADM, FCU - Chronic denervation: fibrillations, positive sharp waves, reduced recruitment - Useful for severity stratification and surgical planning Ultrasound: - May demonstrate nerve enlargement or dynamic subluxation; measurements require trained interpretation and are not a standalone diagnosis - Dynamic assessment: nerve subluxation over medial epicondyle - Increasingly used as first-line imaging; lower cost than MRI MRI: - Nerve signal change, perineural fibrosis, intraneural oedema - Identifies compressive lesions ganglion, accessory muscle, post-traumatic fibrosis - Reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or surgical planning --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Investigation ----------- ------------------------ ------------------- Cervical radiculopathy C8 Neck pain; Spurling's positive; triceps weakness; absent triceps reflex Cervical MRI; NCS shows normal forearm ulnar velocity Thoracic outlet syndrome Consider when symptoms are positional and suggest neurovascular compression Diagnosis is primarily clinical; investigations depend on the suspected neurogenic, arterial or venous subtype and specialist pathway Medial epicondylalgia Tendinopathy signs; no sensory deficit; no intrinsic weakness Clinical; NCS normal Guyon's canal syndrome ulnar at wrist Spares FCU wrist flexion intact ; NCS shows distal compression; dorsal ulnar sensory SNAP normal NCS/EMG; wrist ultrasound Double crush syndrome Combined cervical + cubital compression NCS both regions; MRI spine Pancoast tumour Shoulder girdle pain; Horner's; weight loss; smoking history Chest X-ray; CT chest Peripheral neuropathy diabetic, alcoholic Bilateral; length-dependent; other nerves involved NCS bilateral; bloods Ulnar nerve tumour Firm, fixed mass on nerve; Tinel's at mass MRI; ultrasound --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway For clear ulnar compression neuropathy without root-lesion features, NICE NG127 recommendations 1.7.9–1.7.10 support pressure avoidance, orthotic referral and review after 6 weeks, with neurological assessment if there is no improvement. Progressive motor loss, marked wasting or an atypical presentation requires more prompt specialist assessment. Investigation and operative decisions remain specialist-led. --- Conservative Management Activity Modification Grade B - Avoid sustained elbow flexion >90° : phone use speaker/headset , sleeping position - Avoid repetitive elbow flexion-extension under load - Avoid medial elbow pressure : padding on work surfaces, armrests - Workplace ergonomic assessment HSE NI guidance Elbow Extension Splinting at Night Grade A - NICE NG127 recommendation 1.7.9 supports referral to orthotic services for a splint in adults with clear ulnar compression neuropathy and no radiculopathy, followed by review at 6 weeks - The exact splint angle, wear schedule and duration require separate evidence and orthotic/hand-therapy review; NG127 does not prescribe them Nerve Gliding Exercises Grade B The previous detailed neurodynamic prescription is not established by NICE NG127. Any neural mobilisation requires an individual physiotherapy assessment and remains a claim-level evidence review task. Education - Sleep position modification pillow under arm to prevent elbow flexion >90° - Phone/device use modification - Workplace assessment: seated ergonomics, tool use, forearm support --- Pharmacological NG127 does not provide a cubital-tunnel drug or injection regimen. Medication or injection requires confirmation of the indication and an individual prescriber/specialist decision; the previous doses and procedure claims have been removed pending exact evidence review. --- Onward Referral Criteria - Prompt specialist/neurological assessment: marked or progressive motor weakness, wasting, clawing, major sensory loss or diagnostic uncertainty. - NICE NG127 pathway: for clear compression neuropathy without radiculopathy, use pressure avoidance, orthotic referral and 6-week review; refer for neurological assessment if there is no improvement. - Emergency/urgent assessment: trauma with fracture/dislocation or acute neurovascular compromise. Version 1 does not prescribe automatic decompression, electrodiagnostic thresholds or a fixed operative timeline. --- Key References 1. content: Overview Elbow osteoarthritis OA is a degenerative joint disease characterised by progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral bone changes, osteophyte formation, and synovial inflammation within the elbow joint complex humeroulnar, humeroradial, and proximal radioulnar joints . It is relatively uncommon compared to hip and knee OA, accounting for approximately 2% of all OA presentations , but causes significant functional impairment given the elbow's role in positioning the hand in space. Epidemiology - Prevalence: ~2% of the general population; higher in heavy manual workers and throwing athletes - Peak onset: 5th–6th decade; male:female ratio approximately 4:1 in primary OA - Primary idiopathic OA accounts for ~50% of elbow OA; often bilateral - Secondary OA follows prior trauma post-traumatic , inflammatory arthropathy, osteochondral defects, or repetitive occupational loading Pathoanatomy Elbow OA characteristically produces: - Osteophyte formation at the coronoid fossa, olecranon fossa, and radial head - Loose body formation — a cardinal feature; fragments from osteophytes or osteochondral surfaces cause mechanical symptoms - Progressive loss of terminal flexion and extension terminal arc most affected first - Relative preservation of the mid-arc 60°–120° until advanced disease - Capsular contracture contributing to stiffness Typical Clinical Presentation Feature Detail --- --- Pain End-range aching; may be sharp with loose body impingement Stiffness Loss of terminal extension > terminal flexion initially Functional arc Typically 30°–130° preserved in mild–moderate disease Locking/catching Suggests loose body; episodic, position-dependent Crepitus Coarse, palpable; reproducible with passive ROM Swelling Effusion palpable in posterolateral triangle Occupation/sport history Heavy manual work, throwing athletes, combat sports > Normal elbow ROM for reference: Flexion 0°–145°; Pronation 75°; Supination 85°. Functional arc: 30°–130° flexion-extension; 50° pronation–50° supination Morrey et al., 1981 . --- Red Flags Findings atypical for elbow osteoarthritis—such as a hot acutely inflamed joint, systemic illness, progressive neurological deficit, rapidly changing swelling/mass, major trauma or suspected malignancy—require medical or specialist assessment according to urgency. Suspected septic arthritis requires prompt urgent assessment. Do not make aspiration, antibiotics, nerve-conduction testing, imaging or a fixed specialty route automatic in the learner wording. General NICE NG226 osteoarthritis recommendations must be labelled as general OA guidance where elbow-specific evidence is unavailable. --- Special Tests > Sensitivity Sn and specificity Sp data are derived from published validation studies. Most elbow OA-specific test accuracy data are limited; values reflect best available evidence and are presented with appropriate caution. Range of Motion Examination Essential Active and passive ROM measurement with a standard goniometer is the cornerstone of elbow OA assessment. Loss of terminal extension is the earliest and most consistent finding. Provocative & Diagnostic Tests Test Technique Positive Finding Sensitivity Specificity Clinical Use in Elbow OA --- --- --- --- --- --- Terminal arc pain Outerbridge–Kashiwagi sign Passive flexion–extension through full range; note where pain is provoked Pain at end-range extension 120° ~85% expert consensus Moderate Confirms terminal arc impingement — hallmark of elbow OA Loose body provocation test Examiner passively moves elbow through arc while applying axial compression Reproducible locking, catching, or sharp pain Not formally validated — Suggests intra-articular loose body; title: Lateral Epicondylalgia (Tennis Elbow)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Lateral epicondylalgia LE — commonly termed "tennis elbow" — is the most prevalent elbow disorder in primary care, with a population prevalence of 1–3% and peak incidence in the 35–54 age group. It accounts for approximately 5% of all shoulder and arm complaints presenting
headings: Tendinopathy Continuum Model Cook & Purdam 2009; updated Cook et al. 2016
Exercise Therapy Grade A evidence — strongest recommendation
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Lateral epicondylalgia LE — commonly termed "tennis elbow" — is the most prevalent elbow disorder in primary care, with a population prevalence of 1–3% and peak incidence in the 35–54 age group. It accounts for approximately 5% of all shoulder and arm complaints presenting to GPs, with an estimated annual incidence of 4–7 per 1000 patients. Pathophysiology: Contemporary understanding has shifted decisively away from an inflammatory model. Histological studies Nirschl & Pettrone 1979; Khan et al. 2002 consistently demonstrate angiofibroblastic hyperplasia rather than inflammatory infiltrate — absence of inflammatory cells, disordered collagen Type III predominance , neurovascular in-growth, and failed healing response. The condition is therefore better classified as a tendinopathy rather than tendinitis. Primary structure involved: Extensor carpi radialis brevis ECRB origin at the lateral epicondyle — specifically the anterior and superior aspect. ECRB is most vulnerable due to: - Mechanical impingement against the capitellum during elbow extension and forearm pronation - High tensile load during wrist extension under load - Relatively avascular region at the origin contributing to failed healing Contributing structures: Extensor digitorum communis, extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi ulnaris. Risk factors: Manual occupations, repetitive gripping >2 kg, keyboard/mouse use, racquet sports backhand technique errors , age 40–50, smoking, obesity, previous episode. Natural history: Spontaneous resolution expected in 80–90% within 12–18 months without treatment. However, recurrence rates are high up to 72% at 5 years in some cohorts . --- Special Tests Assessment component Role Limitation --- --- --- Resisted wrist extension and gripping Reproduces load-related lateral elbow symptoms Not specific in isolation Passive wrist-flexion stretch May reproduce familiar tendon-related pain Must be interpreted with the history and palpation Middle-finger resistance May provoke lateral elbow pain Also loads structures associated with radial-tunnel symptoms Cozen's Test Protocol: Stabilise the elbow; patient makes fist with wrist in neutral. Examiner resists wrist extension. Positive = pain at lateral epicondyle. Mill's Test Protocol: Elbow extended, forearm pronated. Examiner passively flexes wrist fully. Positive = pain at lateral epicondyle. Maudsley's Test Protocol: Patient resists examiner pressing down on middle finger with elbow extended. Positive = lateral epicondyle pain. Clinical note: No single test is diagnostic in isolation. A cluster of positive tests ≥2 of: lateral epicondyle tenderness, positive Cozen's, positive Mill's increases diagnostic confidence. Exclude radial nerve compression radial tunnel syndrome as concurrent or alternative diagnosis. --- Red Flags - Acute vascular compromise after limb injury—such as an absent pulse, cold/pale limb or acute sensorimotor compromise—requires emergency assessment. Do not use the classic “5 Ps” as a stand-alone diagnostic rule. - Significant trauma with suspected fracture/dislocation requires urgent assessment. - Progressive motor deficit, rapid neurological change, serious infection or malignancy concern requires prompt medical/specialist assessment. Apply current suspected-cancer criteria rather than age plus night pain as an automatic cancer-pathway rule. --- Clinical Frameworks Tendinopathy Continuum Model Cook & Purdam 2009; updated Cook et al. 2016 The continuum model provides a framework for staging tendinopathy and guiding management: Stage Pathology Clinical Features Management Approach ------- ----------- ------------------- --------------------- Reactive tendinopathy Short-term adaptive response; increased proteoglycan, water content Acute onset after sudden load increase; swelling possible; pain with all load Load reduction; relative rest; isometrics may reduce pain Tendon dysrepair Failed healing; early matrix disruption; neurovascular in-growth Sub-acute; pain with higher loads; some thickening on US Moderate load modification; graduated isotonic loading Degenerative tendinopathy Cell death, matrix disruption, failed collagen; angiofibroblastic changes Chronic; pain with daily activities; may have pain-free window mid-activity Graded loading; accept some pain during exercise NRS 0–4 ; longer rehab timeline Pain Monitoring Model - 0–4/10 NRS during loading — acceptable; continue programme - 5–7/10 NRS — monitor closely; modify load - >7/10 NRS or pain lingering >24 hours post-exercise — reduce load; reassess stage Biopsychosocial Considerations Central sensitisation is prevalent in chronic LE >3 months . Assess: - Pain catastrophising PCS >30 → elevated risk of poor outcome - Fear-avoidance FABQ - Work-related psychosocial factors job demands, control, support - Sleep quality --- Outcome Measures Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation PRTEE - Format: 15 items; 0–100 scale 10 pain items + 5 function specific + 10 usual activities - Score interpretation: 0 = no pain/disability; 100 = worst possible - MCID: 11 points Stratford et al. 2001 - MDC: 17 points - Time to complete: 5 minutes DASH / QuickDASH - DASH: 30 items; 0–100 0 = no disability - QuickDASH: 11 items; 0–100 - MCID for LE: DASH 10.2 points; QuickDASH 16 points - Limitation: Less condition-specific; useful for cross-condition comparison Grip Strength Jamar Dynamometer - Protocol: Elbow at 90°, neutral forearm; 3 trials; mean recorded - Normative comparison: Compare to contralateral limb expect 5–10% dominant hand advantage - Pain-free grip strength often more clinically useful than maximum grip - MCID: Approximately 6.5 kg for meaningful change - Reliability: ICC 0.97–0.98 for Jamar at standardised handle position Global Rating of Change GRC - 15-point scale −7 to +7 ; clinically meaningful change = ±3 points --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis is appropriate in typical presentations. Imaging is not routinely required for initial diagnosis. Ultrasound US : - May show tendon changes, but imaging findings do not determine symptom relevance by themselves - Useful to confirm diagnosis in atypical cases, guide injection, rule out partial/full-thickness tear - Power Doppler demonstrates neovascularisation but correlation with symptoms is inconsistent - Indication: Persistent symptoms >6 months despite conservative management, prior to injection, surgical planning MRI: - May characterise tendon or competing pathology when imaging will change management - T2 signal increase at ECRB origin diagnostic of tendinopathy - Reserve for surgical planning or diagnostic uncertainty - Not routinely indicated in primary/community physiotherapy X-ray: - Not required for diagnosis; may show calcification 25–30% of chronic cases or reveal alternative pathology - Indicated with trauma history or red flags NCS/EMG: - Not indicated for lateral epicondylalgia - Consider if radial tunnel syndrome or posterior interosseous nerve palsy suspected Clinical Prediction Rule: No validated CPR exists for LE. Diagnosis is clinical based on: 1. Lateral epicondyle pain 2. Reproduced by resisted wrist extension and/or passive wrist flexion 3. Tenderness on palpation of the lateral epicondyle --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Test ----------- ------------------------ ---------- Radial tunnel syndrome Pain 3–5 cm distal to lateral epicondyle; deep ache; nocturnal pain; weakness; positive resisted supination Resisted supination at 0°; Frohse arcade tenderness Posterior interosseous nerve palsy Finger/wrist drop; weakness of finger extensors; may be painless Neurological examination; NCS/EMG Cervical radiculopathy C6/C7 Neck pain; dermatomal sensory loss; reduced reflexes; Spurling's positive Spurling's test; cervical spine examination Lateral elbow instability PLRI Clicking, locking, giving way; trauma history; positive lateral pivot shift Lateral pivot shift test; MRI Synovial plica irritation Intermittent snapping sensation; pain with full extension Clinical; MRI Elbow OA Age >50; stiffness; crepitus; full ROM loss; X-ray changes X-ray Osteochondral loose body Locking, catching, extension block X-ray; MRI Referred pain from shoulder/neck Absence of local signs; pain not reproduced by local provocation Full UL neurodynamic screen Lateral epicondyle stress fracture Rare; athletes; local bony tenderness; positive imaging X-ray; MRI --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use the current BESS Tennis Elbow/local pathway. In the absence of serious pathology, management is primarily conservative and exercise/load-management based. Progressive neurological change or significant trauma follows a separate specialist pathway. --- Conservative Management Load Management Grade A evidence - Acute phase: Relative rest from provocative activities; avoid sustained gripping >2 kg; modify keyboard/mouse ergonomics - Wrist splinting: Cockup wrist splint 20–30° wrist extension reduces ECRB load; evidence for symptom reduction in acute phase moderate ; not recommended long-term - Counterforce brace epicondyle strap : Moderate evidence for short-term pain reduction with activity; mechanism = force dampening at muscle belly Exercise Therapy Grade A evidence — strongest recommendation Eccentric Exercise Programme Svernlöv & Adolfsson 2001; Tyler et al. 2010 : - Wrist extension eccentrics with forearm pronated over table edge - 3 × 15 repetitions; 2× daily; 12-week programme - Progress via increase in load dumbbell/putty/theraband - Pain up to 5/10 acceptable Isometric Exercise Stasinopoulos et al. 2017; Rio et al. 2015 : - Wrist extension isometric holds: 5 × 45-second holds at 70% MVC - Analgesic effect demonstrated; useful in reactive/irritable tendinopathy - Can precede isotonic loading programme Heavy Slow Resistance HSR Protocol Beyer et al. 2015 — adapted for LE : - Wrist extension with load: 3 sets; 15 reps → 8 reps → 6 reps over 12 weeks - Load progressed to near-maximum effort - Shown superior to eccentric-only in Achilles; extrapolated to upper limb Elbow Manipulation + Exercise Bisset et al. 2006 — landmark RCT : - Mulligan's Mobilisation with Movement MWM : lateral glide of elbow combined with gripping - Combined with exercise showed superior outcomes to corticosteroid injection at 12 months - 8 sessions over 8 weeks; pain-free grip force primary outcome Ergonomic Advice Grade B - Keyboard positioning; mouse size; tool grip modification - Avoiding repetitive wrist extension under load - Occupational therapy assessment if work-related --- Pharmacological and injection care The BESS Tennis Elbow 2023 pathway recommends physiotherapy and recommends against corticosteroid injection for lateral elbow tendinopathy. Other medication decisions remain clinician/prescriber-led; no fixed application schedule or PPI threshold is asserted without an exact source. Platelet-Rich Plasma PRP : - Emerging evidence; some RCTs show benefit over placebo/corticosteroid at 6–12 months - Not currently commissioned within HSC NI patient-funded in private sector - Systematic review Arirachakaran et al. 2016 shows possible superiority over CSI at 6+ months - Insufficient evidence to recommend routinely Autologous Blood Injection: - Similar rationale to PRP; limited high-quality RCT evidence - Not routinely commissioned Nitric Oxide Patches GTN : Evidence and applicability remain under human review; no dose is prescribed by this page. --- Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency/urgent assessment: acute vascular compromise or suspected significant fracture/dislocation. - Prompt medical/specialist assessment: objective progressive motor deficit, serious infection, mass lesion or suspected malignancy under applicable criteria. - Specialist assessment: persistent disabling symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty despite appropriate conservative care. No automatic imaging, injection or operative threshold is asserted. --- Key References 1. Bisset L, Beller E, Jull G, Brooks P, Darnell R, Vicenzino B. 2006 . title: Medial Epicondylalgia (Golfer's Elbow)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Medial epicondylalgia ME — historically termed "golfer's elbow" or medial epicondylitis — is a common cause of medial elbow pain, accounting for approximately 10–20% of elbow tendinopathies presenting in clinical practice. True incidence is lower than lateral epicondylalgi
headings: Valgus Extension Overload Assessment throwing athletes
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Medial epicondylalgia ME — historically termed "golfer's elbow" or medial epicondylitis — is a common cause of medial elbow pain, accounting for approximately 10–20% of elbow tendinopathies presenting in clinical practice. True incidence is lower than lateral epicondylalgia; estimated at 0.4% of the general population per year, with peak onset in the 4th–5th decade. Pathophysiology: As with lateral epicondylalgia, histological evidence confirms angiofibroblastic tendinosis rather than true inflammation. Nirschl 1992 described the same pathological changes: disorganised collagen, fibroblast proliferation, neovascularisation, absence of inflammatory cells. The condition represents failed tendon healing at the common flexor-pronator origin. Primary structures involved: - Pronator teres — most commonly affected originates from medial epicondyle - Flexor carpi radialis — frequently co-involved - Flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis — less commonly The origin is on the anterior aspect of the medial epicondyle; valgus stress during acceleration phases of throwing or golfing creates repetitive tensile overload. Mechanism of injury: - Repetitive wrist flexion and forearm pronation under load - Valgus loading of medial elbow throwing, golf, racquet sports - Occupational exposure: carpentry, plumbing, manual handling Important association — Ulnar collateral ligament UCL : - UCL insufficiency co-exists in up to 60% of throwing athletes with ME - Distinguish clinically as management differs UCL reconstruction vs tendinopathy rehabilitation Concurrent cubital tunnel syndrome: - Ulnar nerve involvement in 20–60% of ME cases - Critical to assess for ulnar neuropathy at every consultation - Failure to identify ulnar nerve involvement leads to suboptimal outcomes --- Special Tests Assessment component Role Limitation --- --- --- Palpation, resisted wrist flexion and pronation Reproduce load-related medial elbow symptoms Not specific in isolation Passive wrist-extension stretch May reproduce familiar tendon-related pain Interpret with load response and function Valgus-stress assessment Explores possible UCL involvement in the appropriate sporting context Requires careful technique and is not a diagnosis alone Ulnar-nerve provocation Explores coexisting neural symptoms Requires a full neurological assessment Resisted Wrist Flexion Protocol: Elbow extended, forearm supinated. Examiner resists wrist flexion. Positive = medial epicondyle pain reproduction. Moving Valgus Stress Test: In an appropriate throwing-athlete assessment, this manoeuvre may reproduce symptoms associated with UCL loading. It does not establish a UCL injury in isolation. Elbow Flexion Test: Maximum elbow flexion with wrist neutral maintained for 60 seconds. Positive = tingling/numbness in ring/little finger distribution. Best test for cubital tunnel syndrome. --- Red Flags - Significant weakness, wasting or progressive neurological change requires prompt reassessment and specialist evaluation; “urgent surgical referral” is not assumed without a defined diagnosis and source. - Suspected physeal/avulsion injury in a young athlete, acute unstable UCL injury, fracture/dislocation or neurovascular compromise requires appropriate imaging/specialist assessment. - A mass lesion, serious infection or malignancy concern requires medical assessment according to urgency. Hypothenar-hammer/ulnar-artery thrombosis is a separate vascular differential and should only be pursued when the presentation supports it. --- Clinical Frameworks Tendinopathy Continuum Model Cook & Purdam 2009 Apply same staging as lateral epicondylalgia: - Reactive: Acute load spike; manage with relative rest, isometrics, provocative load avoidance - Dysrepair: Subacute; graduated isotonic loading; monitor 24-hour pain response - Degenerative: Chronic; accept working pain NRS 0–4 ; long-term loading programme; psychosocial screen Ulnar Nerve Assessment Framework In all ME cases, systematically assess: 1. Subjective: Paraesthesia/numbness in ring/little finger; nocturnal symptoms elbow flexion in sleep ; pain radiating down medial forearm 2. Objective: Froment's sign intrinsic weakness ; first dorsal interosseous wasting; clawing ring/little finger ; sensory testing light touch, 2-point discrimination in ulnar nerve territory 3. Special tests: Elbow flexion test, Tinel's at cubital tunnel 4. Severity classification: - Mild: Intermittent paraesthesia; no motor deficit - Moderate: Persistent paraesthesia; early motor weakness - Severe: Constant symptoms; significant weakness/wasting; consider urgent surgical referral Valgus Extension Overload Assessment throwing athletes - Screen for UCL insufficiency moving valgus stress test - Screen for posterior impingement valgus extension overload test - Screen for radiocapitellar pathology --- Outcome Measures Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation PRTEE - Although named for tennis elbow, validated for use in medial epicondylalgia - Score: 0–100; 0 = no pain/disability - MCID: 11 points DASH / QuickDASH - DASH MCID: 10.2 points LE/ME combined upper limb - QuickDASH MCID: 16 points - Useful for occupational/functional tracking Grip Strength Jamar Dynamometer - Protocol: Elbow at 90°; 3 trials; dominant vs non-dominant comparison - Pain-free grip is more clinically relevant than maximum grip in ME - Expect deficit on affected side; monitor improvement over 6–8 weeks Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS - MCID: 2 points 0–10 scale for musculoskeletal pain - Assess: worst pain last 7 days , average pain, pain during resisted testing --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on: 1. Medial elbow pain ± radiation into proximal forearm 2. Reproduction with resisted wrist flexion and/or forearm pronation 3. Medial epicondyle tenderness on palpation Ultrasound: - May show tendon changes, but imaging findings do not determine symptom relevance by themselves - Power Doppler: neovascularisation correlates with symptom severity - Indicated for diagnostic uncertainty, injection guidance, pre-surgical planning - Can also assess UCL integrity dynamic valgus stress view MRI: - May characterise tendon, ligament or neural pathology when imaging will change management - Indicated if UCL injury suspected, pre-surgical planning, diagnostic uncertainty - MRI arthrogram superior for UCL assessment in throwing athletes NCS/EMG: - Indicated if ulnar neuropathy suspected Elbow flexion test positive, Tinel's positive, motor deficit - Neurophysiology referral via GP or consultant HSC NI: Belfast Trust, Southern Trust, Western Trust - NCS findings: reduced ulnar nerve conduction velocity across elbow 90° at night — particularly important if ulnar neuropathy - Elbow extension orthosis for sleep if cubital tunnel concurrent diagnosis --- Pharmacological and injection care The prior fixed NSAID, injection and GTN regimens were not linked to an exact condition-specific authoritative recommendation and have been removed. Medication or injection is prescriber/specialist-led; extrapolation from lateral elbow or lower-limb tendinopathy must be labelled and human-reviewed. --- Onward Referral Criteria - Prompt specialist assessment: objective motor deficit, significant wasting, suspected UCL/physeal/avulsion injury or a mass lesion. - Urgent assessment: fracture/dislocation, acute neurovascular compromise or serious infection. - Specialist assessment: persistent disabling symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty despite appropriate conservative care. Detailed operative approaches, fixed nerve/surgery timings, return-to-sport thresholds, outcome percentages and recovery timelines are outside Version 1 and remain future evidence expansion. --- Key References 1. title: Olecranon Bursitis
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Olecranon bursitis is inflammation of the olecranon bursa — a superficial synovial-lined sac located between the olecranon process of the ulna and the overlying skin. It is the most common bursitis of the elbow and one of the most frequently encountered superficial bursiti
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Olecranon bursitis is inflammation of the olecranon bursa — a superficial synovial-lined sac located between the olecranon process of the ulna and the overlying skin. It is the most common bursitis of the elbow and one of the most frequently encountered superficial bursitides in clinical practice. Anatomy: The olecranon bursa sits subcutaneously over the posterior olecranon. It does not normally communicate with the elbow joint. Normal bursa contains negligible fluid; in pathological states may enlarge significantly 2–3 cm or greater . Prevalence: Exact epidemiology uncertain; more common in males and in manual occupations involving prolonged elbow contact surfaces. Gout, pseudogout, and rheumatoid arthritis are systemic risk factors. Classification by aetiology: Type Mechanism Features ------ ----------- ---------- Traumatic Direct blow acute or repetitive pressure chronic Most common; clear history Septic Bacterial infection usually Staph. aureus 80% Erythema, warmth, fever, elevated WBC Crystal-induced Gout uric acid or pseudogout CPPD Aspirate shows crystals; may be recurrent Inflammatory Rheumatoid arthritis, other spondyloarthropathies Bilateral; systemic features; rheumatoid nodules Idiopathic No identifiable cause Diagnosis of exclusion Occupational associations: "Student's elbow," "miner's elbow," "plumber's elbow" — prolonged pressure on elbows during work, studying, or sports wrestling, hockey goalies . Pathophysiology: Trauma or sustained pressure causes microhaemorrhage within the bursal walls → inflammatory response → synovial hypertrophy → increased fluid production → bursal enlargement. In septic bursitis, bacteria enter via skin abrasion, puncture wound, or haematogenous spread. Gout deposits urate crystals which trigger intense inflammatory response. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Bursal fluctuance on palpation fluid wave 0.85 0.72 3.04 0.21 Moderate Bursal erythema extending beyond bursa 0.72 0.82 4.00 0.34 Moderate for septic Skin abrasion/puncture wound at olecranon 0.68 0.90 6.80 0.36 Moderate for septic Fever >38°C 0.40 0.97 13.3 0.62 Moderate for septic Tenderness of bursal wall not just fluid 0.78 0.65 2.23 0.34 Low-Moderate Elbow ROM preserved distinguishes from joint pathology 0.88 0.70 2.93 0.17 Moderate Key Distinction — Septic vs Non-Septic: Clinical features alone may not reliably discriminate septic from non-septic olecranon bursitis. Suspected infection requires prompt medical assessment; the medical team determines whether aspiration and analysis are indicated. Aspiration findings: Parameter Non-Septic Septic ----------- ----------- -------- WBC/mm³ 2,000 often >50,000 % Neutrophils 75% Glucose Normal Decreased Gram stain Negative Positive in 50–70% Culture Negative Positive in 80–90% Crystals Absent unless crystal-induced Absent unless concurrent Elbow ROM: Should be full and pain-free in isolated olecranon bursitis. Restricted ROM suggests intra-articular pathology. --- Red Flags - Suspected septic bursitis requires prompt medical assessment. Urgency depends on systemic illness and the clinical presentation; not every suspected case requires emergency aspiration or admission. - A hot joint with concern for septic arthritis requires urgent assessment. - Rapidly changing mass, trauma with neurovascular compromise, or suspected malignancy requires appropriate medical/specialist assessment. Version 1 does not prescribe MRSA-specific antibiotics, diabetes-based intravenous-antibiotic thresholds, mandatory bursal excision or automatic gout testing. Prescribing and infection management follow current medical/local guidance. --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Algorithm for Olecranon Bursitis Septic Bursitis Management Framework - Suspected infection requires prompt medical assessment and appropriate sampling where indicated - The medical team determines antimicrobial choice, route and duration using current antimicrobial guidance, microbiology results and patient-specific factors - A severe or systemically unwell presentation requires urgent assessment; drainage or surgery is a specialist decision --- Outcome Measures Primary Clinical Measures - Bursal size: Measure maximum diameter with tape measure or ultrasound at baseline and follow-up - NPRS Numeric Pain Rating Scale : 0–10; MCID = 2 points; assess posterior elbow pain - Elbow ROM: Flexion/extension/pronation/supination goniometry ; should remain full in isolated bursitis DASH / QuickDASH - Useful for functional impact assessment - MCID for upper limb: DASH 10.2; QuickDASH 16 points - Less specific to olecranon bursitis but useful in occupational contexts Patient Satisfaction - Global Rating of Change GRC scale at 4, 8, and 12 weeks post-intervention - Return to work/sport as functional endpoint --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis is reliable in typical traumatic cases with characteristic swelling over the olecranon and preserved elbow ROM. Aspiration: - Recommended if: septic bursitis suspected, diagnostic uncertainty, crystal arthropathy queried, large painful bursa limiting function - Ultrasound-guided aspiration preferred for complete drainage; reduces recurrence vs landmark aspiration - Send aspirate for: MC&S septic , crystal analysis gout/pseudogout , WBC + differential Ultrasound: - Confirms bursal fluid, size, wall thickening, septation - Doppler: hyperaemia in septic/inflammatory bursitis - Guides aspiration and injection - Identifies concurrent triceps tendon pathology X-ray: - Not required for diagnosis; may show: - Olecranon spur associated with chronic bursitis - Gout tophi soft tissue calcification - Fracture traumatic - Indicated with trauma or concern for bony pathology MRI: - Reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, surgical planning - Distinguishes bursitis from triceps tendon pathology, tumour - Not routine in straightforward cases Bloods if septic bursitis suspected : - FBC, CRP, ESR, urea/electrolytes - Blood cultures if febrile - Serum urate gout screen — note: may be normal during acute flare - Rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP if inflammatory arthropathy suspected --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Investigation ----------- ------------------------ ------------------- Septic arthritis of elbow ROM restricted/painful; fever; systemically unwell; joint effusion Joint aspiration; bloods Gout/crystal arthropathy Very painful; acute onset; hyperuricaemia; crystals on aspiration Serum urate; aspiration Rheumatoid arthritis Bilateral; rheumatoid nodules; systemic features; joint involvement Rheumatoid factor; anti-CCP; X-ray Psoriatic arthritis Psoriasis; dactylitis; enthesopathy; asymmetric joint involvement Clinical; X-ray Triceps tendon tear Posterior elbow pain with resisted extension weakness; palpable defect MRI; ultrasound Posterior elbow impingement Pain at end-range extension; bone spur; athletes X-ray; MRI Lipoma Soft, non-tender, no ROM loss, chronic Ultrasound; MRI Ganglion cyst Tense, translucent, may transilluminate Ultrasound Tumour synovial sarcoma Rare; firm; progressive; systemic features MRI; biopsy --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Differentiate non-septic bursitis, suspected septic bursitis, septic arthritis and other causes. Non-septic presentations may receive appropriate conservative care. Suspected infection or gout requires medical assessment and management under current local prescribing/infection guidance. --- Conservative Management Non-Septic Traumatic/Mechanical Bursitis Grade B Load Modification: - Avoid direct pressure on olecranon; protective elbow padding neoprene sleeve, foam pad - Avoid prolonged elbow weight-bearing - Avoid contact sports until resolved Compression: - Compression bandage or tubigrip reduces re-accumulation of fluid - Evidence: moderate; reduces swelling recurrence vs no compression - Elbow compression sleeve sport-specific for return to activity Ice Therapy: - 15–20 minutes, 3–4× daily; reduces acute inflammatory swelling - No high-quality RCT evidence but widely recommended and safe Aspiration GP/Secondary Care : - If large, painful, or limiting function: aspiration provides symptom relief - Recurrence common 50–70% without compression ; aspiration + compression dressing reduces recurrence - Ultrasound-guided aspiration superior for complete drainage Corticosteroid Injection into bursa — non-septic only : - Reduces recurrence vs aspiration alone in non-septic bursitis Weinstein et al. 1984 - Risk: skin atrophy, depigmentation, bursal sinus, infection → exclude septic bursitis before injecting - Agent, dose and repeat limits are injection-service decisions and remain under source review --- Pharmacological Suspected septic bursitis requires urgent medical assessment, sampling where indicated and antimicrobial selection using the current local microbiology/BNF pathway. This physiotherapy page intentionally does not prescribe antibiotic, analgesic, gout or injection doses. Crystal disease management is likewise diagnosis- and prescriber-led. --- Onward Referral Criteria - Urgent assessment: suspected septic arthritis, systemic illness or rapidly progressive infection. - Prompt medical assessment: suspected septic bursitis or gout, with urgency based on the presentation. - Consider specialist assessment: persistent/recurrent disabling bursitis, a mass lesion, diagnostic uncertainty or malignancy concern under applicable criteria. Investigation, aspiration, antibiotics and operative treatment remain medical/specialist decisions. --- Key References 1. Baumbach SF, Lobo CM, Badyine I, Mutschler W, Kanz KG. 2014 . Bacterial skin infections — management . Available at: https://bnf.nice.org.uk/ 8. Aaron DL, Patel A, Kayiaros S, Calfee R. 2011 . Four common types of bursitis: diagnosis and management. title: Radial Tunnel Syndrome
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Radial tunnel syndrome RTS is a chronic pain condition resulting from compression or irritation of the radial nerve specifically the posterior interosseous nerve — PIN within the radial tunnel. It is arguably the most diagnostically challenging and controversial condition
headings: Differential Framework: RTS vs Lateral Epicondylalgia
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Radial tunnel syndrome RTS is a chronic pain condition resulting from compression or irritation of the radial nerve specifically the posterior interosseous nerve — PIN within the radial tunnel. It is arguably the most diagnostically challenging and controversial condition in elbow pathology, with debate persisting in the literature regarding its existence as a distinct clinical entity separate from lateral epicondylalgia. Prevalence: Poorly defined due to diagnostic difficulty. Often under-diagnosed. Estimated to account for 5% of cases initially presenting as lateral epicondylalgia. More common in manual workers. Anatomy of the Radial Tunnel: The radial tunnel extends from the radiocapitellar joint to the proximal border of the supinator muscle — approximately 5 cm long. The posterior interosseous nerve deep branch of radial nerve traverses this tunnel. Sites of compression within the radial tunnel medial to lateral : 1. Fibrous bands anterior to radiocapitellar joint — most distal compression point 2. Radial recurrent vessels leash of Henry — vascular tether against nerve 3. Tendinous medial border of ECRB — sharp tendinous edge impinges nerve with pronation/wrist extension 4. Arcade of Frohse proximal edge of superficial head of supinator — most common compression site 75% of cases 5. Distal edge of supinator — less common Pathophysiology: Compression at any of the above sites produces: - Intraneural oedema → ischaemia → pain and in severe cases axonal compromise - In pure RTS: pain without significant motor deficit distinguishing from posterior interosseous nerve palsy — PINP - Mechanism: repetitive forearm rotation pronation/supination + elbow extension creates intermittent compression at Arcade of Frohse Important distinction: - Radial Tunnel Syndrome: Primarily painful; minimal or no motor deficit; often confused with lateral epicondylalgia - Posterior Interosseous Nerve Palsy PINP : Motor deficit prominent finger/wrist drop ; may be painless; different management Concurrent lateral epicondylalgia: Co-exists in up to 5% of cases; the two conditions can be concurrent but require independent assessment. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Radial tunnel tenderness 4–5 cm distal to lateral epicondyle 0.84 0.65 2.40 0.25 Low-Moderate Resisted supination elbow extended, forearm pronated 0.76 0.72 2.71 0.33 Low Resisted middle finger extension 0.72 0.58 1.71 0.48 Low Resisted elbow extension with forearm pronation PIN stretch 0.68 0.70 2.27 0.46 Low Passive forearm pronation PIN compression 0.63 0.68 1.97 0.54 Low Lateral epicondyle tenderness absent 0.62 0.85 4.13 0.45 Low-Moderate Radial tunnel Tinel's sign 0.58 0.71 2.00 0.59 Low Diagnostic nerve block radial tunnel ~0.90 ~0.85 ~6.0 ~0.12 Moderate as diagnostic tool Note on evidence quality: RTS diagnostic test evidence is of low quality. No high-quality systematic review of special tests exists. Values above represent best available data primarily from Lister et al. 1979, Portilla Molina et al. 1998, Sotereanos et al. 1999 . Radial Tunnel Palpation: Tenderness localised 3–5 cm distal and anterior to lateral epicondyle over radial tunnel , NOT over the lateral epicondyle itself. This is the key clinical differentiator from lateral epicondylalgia. Resisted Supination Test: Elbow extended, forearm fully pronated. Patient supinates against resistance. Positive = radial tunnel pain. Compresses PIN against Arcade of Frohse. Diagnostic Nerve Block: A specialist may consider a local-anaesthetic block in selected diagnostically uncertain cases. The service determines the medicine, volume, technique and interpretation; response does not replace the full differential assessment. --- Red Flags - True wrist or finger extensor motor deficit is not typical painful radial tunnel syndrome and requires prompt specialist assessment for a motor neuropathy or another neurological cause. - Significant trauma, fracture/dislocation or acute neurovascular compromise requires urgent assessment. - A mass lesion, serious infection, inflammatory systemic presentation or malignancy concern requires medical/specialist assessment according to urgency. Do not make MRI, nerve-conduction studies, EMG or surgical decompression automatic in the red-flag statement. --- Clinical Frameworks Differential Framework: RTS vs Lateral Epicondylalgia Feature Lateral Epicondylalgia Radial Tunnel Syndrome --------- ---------------------- ---------------------- Pain location Over lateral epicondyle 3–5 cm distal/anterior to LE radial tunnel Resisted wrist extension Painful Cozen's positive Usually negative Resisted supination Usually negative Positive Palpation tenderness At lateral epicondyle At radial tunnel over extensor muscle bulk Night pain Uncommon More common forearm ache US/MRI changes Tendon changes at epicondyle Normal tendons; may show nerve changes NCS/EMG Normal Normal or mildly abnormal in severe Diagnostic nerve block response Partial local anaesthetic Complete resolution in true RTS Severity Framework Lister Classification - Type I: Diffuse ache in dorsal forearm; no neurological deficit; tender at Arcade of Frohse - Type II: More localised pain; early motor fatigue; slight grip weakness - Type III PINP : Motor deficit prominent; wrist/finger extension weakness; surgical priority --- Outcome Measures Patient-Reported Outcomes DASH / QuickDASH: - Most commonly used in RTS research and clinical practice - MCID: DASH 10.2; QuickDASH 16 points - Captures functional disability from forearm pain and any motor deficit PRTEE Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation : - Often used in RTS studies due to clinical overlap with LE - 15 items; 0–100; MCID 11 points - Useful for monitoring symptom response to intervention Numeric Pain Rating Scale: - Forearm pain 0–10 ; assess at rest, with resisted supination, with sustained grip - MCID: 2 points Objective Measures Grip Strength: - Reduced in RTS due to pain inhibition and intrinsic weakness - Baseline measurement important; Jamar at 90° elbow flexion - MCID: 6.5 kg Pinch Strength: - Less affected in RTS vs PINP intrinsics partially spared - Baseline assessment useful Forearm Rotation ROM: - Supination may be restricted/painful in active radial tunnel compression - Goniometry at baseline and review --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis RTS is assessed clinically and has no single confirmatory objective test. The evidence base for diagnostic criteria is weak. Approach: Step 1 — Clinical Assessment: - History: occupational repetitive supination, lateral forearm ache often nocturnal , no sensory deficit, no motor weakness - Examination: tenderness at radial tunnel NOT lateral epicondyle ; positive resisted supination; negative Cozen's Step 2 — Exclude Lateral Epicondylalgia: - If Cozen's positive AND radial tunnel tenderness AND lateral epicondyle tenderness → concurrent LE and RTS possible - NCS normal in both conditions; does not differentiate Step 3 — Diagnostic Nerve Block: - If the diagnosis remains unclear, consider specialist assessment; any diagnostic block is a specialist procedure - Complete relief: confirms RTS; partial relief: concurrent LE likely; no relief: alternative diagnosis Nerve Conduction Studies: - Usually NORMAL in RTS motor nerve conduction across tunnel may be mildly reduced: 3 mm² suggests compression limited data MRI: - Detects mass lesions, PINP, post-inflammatory changes - Not routine for RTS; indicated for surgical planning or atypical cases - Can show denervation oedema in extensor muscles in PINP --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Investigation ----------- ------------------------ ------------------- Lateral epicondylalgia Lateral epicondyle tenderness; positive Cozen's; US tendinopathy Clinical; US Posterior interosseous nerve palsy Finger/wrist drop; no sensory deficit; motor deficit on EMG NCS/EMG; MRI Cervical radiculopathy C6/C7 Neck pain; Spurling's positive; dermatomal sensory change; reflex changes Cervical MRI Radial nerve compression at spiral groove Wrist drop; impaired brachioradialis; after prolonged arm compression NCS/EMG Elbow OA Stiffness; crepitus; X-ray changes; older patient X-ray Synovitis of radiocapitellar joint Joint line tenderness; effusion; ROM loss US; MRI Lateral elbow instability PLRI Clicking; apprehension; trauma history Pivot shift test; MRI Radial head fracture Acute trauma; bony tenderness; X-ray fracture X-ray Tendinopathy of ECRB isolated Mid-muscle belly tenderness; not at tunnel US --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Pain without objective motor deficit may begin with individualised conservative care after relevant differentials have been considered. Objective motor deficit, significant trauma or a suspected mass lesion requires prompt specialist assessment. Investigation is determined by the specialist pathway. --- Conservative Management Activity Modification Grade C : - Avoid repetitive forearm pronation-supination - Reduce sustained elbow extension with forearm pronated - Ergonomic review: tool use, keyboard, assembly line tasks Rest and Splinting Grade C : - Cock-up wrist splint + forearm in neutral position during symptomatic phases - Reduces traction on PIN; no RCT evidence but theoretically sound - Avoid unnecessary prolonged immobilisation; maintain tolerable movement according to the clinical presentation Exercise Therapy Grade C — extrapolated from LE evidence : - Supinator stretching: forearm pronation + wrist ulnar deviation gently holds 30 seconds × 5 - Progressive supinator and wrist extensor strengthening - No specific validated exercise protocol for RTS; adapt LE programme Neural Mobilisation Grade C : - Radial nerve neurodynamic technique: - Position: shoulder depression + internal rotation; elbow extension; forearm pronation; wrist/finger flexion; thumb flexion - Gentle sliding technique oscillate neck lateral flexion toward/away - 3 × 10 repetitions; 0–4/10 pain acceptable - Useful for concurrent neural tension component Manual Therapy Grade C : - Radiohumeral joint mobilisation lateral distraction, posterior glide - Limited evidence but may improve symptoms in concurrent LE/RTS presentations --- Pharmacological and injection care There is no condition-specific NICE drug or injection regimen established here. The previous fixed injection composition, response percentage, repeat limit and neuropathic-drug suggestion remain unverified and have been removed. Any diagnostic block, injection or medicine is specialist/prescriber-led. --- Onward Referral Criteria - Prompt specialist assessment: objective wrist/finger extensor weakness, progressive neurological change, suspected mass lesion or diagnostic uncertainty. - Urgent assessment: significant trauma, fracture/dislocation or acute neurovascular compromise. - Specialist assessment: persistent disabling symptoms despite appropriate conservative care. Detailed operative thresholds, fixed timing, surgical approaches, outcome percentages and recovery timelines are outside Version 1 and remain future evidence expansion. --- Key References 1. Roles NC, Maudsley RH. 1972 . Radial tunnel syndrome: resistant tennis elbow as a nerve entrapment. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery , 54 3 , 499–508. 2. Lister GD, Belsole RB, Kleinert HE. 1979 . The radial tunnel syndrome. Journal of Hand Surgery , 4 1 , 52–59. 3. Portilla Molina AE, Bour C, Oberlin C, Nzeusseu A, Vanwijck R. 1998 . The posterior interosseous nerve and the radial tunnel syndrome: an anatomical study. International Orthopaedics , 22 2 , 102–106. 4. Sotereanos DG, Varitimidis SE, Giannakopoulos PN, Westphal RA. 1999 . Results of surgical treatment for radial tunnel syndrome. Journal of Hand Surgery , 24 3 , 566–570. 5. Naam NH, Nemani S. 2012 . Radial tunnel syndrome. Orthopedic Clinics of North America , 43 4 , 529–536. 6. Sarhadi NS, Korday SN, Bainbridge LC. 1998 . Radial tunnel syndrome: diagnosis and management. Journal of Hand Surgery , 23 5 , 617–619. 7. van den Berg PJ, Pompe SM, Beekman R, Visser LH. 2011 . Sonographic incidence of ulnar nerve sub luxation and its associated clinical and electrodiagnostic characteristics. Muscle & Nerve , 43 3 , 347–351. 8. Henry M. 2008 . Radial tunnel syndrome. Journal of the American Society for Surgery of the Hand , 6 2 , 72–78. 9. Dang AC, Rodner CM. 2009 . Unusual compression neuropathies of the forearm, part II: median nerve. Journal of Hand Surgery , 34 10 , 1915–1920. 10. Huisstede BM, Miedema HS, van Opstal T, de Ronde MT, Verhaar JA, Koes BW. 2008 . Interventions for treating the radial tunnel syndrome: a systematic review of observational studies. Journal of Hand Surgery , 33 1 , 72–78.

title: Acromioclavicular Joint Disorders
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology The acromioclavicular joint ACJ is a diarthrodial joint between the distal clavicle and the acromion, stabilised by the acromioclavicular AC and coracoclavicular CC ligaments trapezoid and conoid . It transmits forces between the upper limb and axial skeleton and allows ap
content: Overview & Pathophysiology The acromioclavicular joint ACJ is a diarthrodial joint between the distal clavicle and the acromion, stabilised by the acromioclavicular AC and coracoclavicular CC ligaments trapezoid and conoid . It transmits forces between the upper limb and axial skeleton and allows approximately 20° of rotation during shoulder elevation. Conditions Covered ACJ Sprain / Separation Traumatic disruption of AC and/or CC ligaments, typically from a direct fall onto the point of the shoulder or onto an outstretched hand FOOSH . The distal clavicle rides superiorly relative to the acromion proportional to ligamentous damage. Most common in males aged 20–40 and in contact sports rugby, GAA, cycling . ACJ Osteoarthritis Degenerative joint disease of the ACJ, often presenting in middle-aged to older adults. Associated with repetitive overhead loading, prior trauma, and distal clavicle osteolysis. Cartilaginous narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation reduce the subacromial space and may contribute to secondary impingement. Distal Clavicle Osteolysis Stress-related resorption of the distal clavicle, classically in weight-lifters and overhead athletes. Histology shows microfractures, vascular proliferation, and osteoclastic resorption without infection. X-ray shows tapering and irregular resorption of the distal 2–3 cm of clavicle. --- Rockwood Classification ACJ Separation Grade Structures Damaged Clavicle Displacement Management ------- ------------------- ---------------------- ------------ I AC ligament sprain only None Conservative II AC ligament torn, CC sprain Clinical Note: Rockwood I–II injuries are generally managed non-operatively. Grade III is usually managed non-operatively initially and individualised if symptoms persist. Grades IV–VI warrant orthopaedic assessment; this does not make surgery automatic. --- Special Tests Test Role Limitation --- --- --- O'Brien's Active Compression Test May reproduce pain localised to the AC joint Also provokes other shoulder structures; not diagnostic alone Cross-Body Adduction Test Loads the AC joint and may reproduce familiar pain Interpret with history and local examination Paxinos Test Direct AC-joint provocation Not diagnostic alone Horizontal Adduction Stress Test AC-joint loading Limited discrimination in isolation ACJ Palpation Helps localise symptoms Tenderness alone does not establish the diagnosis > Diagnostic Tip: O'Brien's is most useful when pain is reproduced at the top of the shoulder AND relieved with palm-up position. Pain deep in the shoulder suggests SLAP lesion rather than ACJ pathology. Diagnostic Injection A diagnostic injection may be considered by an appropriate specialist when uncertainty remains. It is not required for routine physiotherapy assessment, and the specialist determines the medicine, technique and interpretation. --- Red Flags - Severe traumatic ACJ injury, open injury, skin compromise, associated fracture/dislocation or neurovascular compromise requires urgent or emergency assessment according to the presentation. - Systemic inflammatory features across multiple joints should prompt appropriate medical/rheumatology assessment; do not use a rigid morning-stiffness threshold in isolation. - Suspected infection or malignancy requires medical assessment under the applicable current pathway and criteria. Distal-clavicle osteolysis, PVNS and metabolic bone disease are differentials, not automatic red-flag pathways. Investigation and referral should follow the clinical presentation and appropriate specialist guidance. --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Algorithm ICF Framework Domain Example -------- --------- Body structure/function ACJ instability, pain, reduced ROM, crepitus Activity limitation Difficulty dressing, reaching overhead, carrying Participation restriction Unable to return to sport, work overhead tasks Contextual factors Sport demands, occupation, psychosocial, activity goals --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID MDC Population Notes --------- ------ ----- ----------- ------- DASH Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder & Hand 10–15 points 12.7 General upper limb 30 items; 0=no disability, 100=most disabled QuickDASH 8–16 points 15.9 General upper limb 11-item version; good for clinical use SPADI Shoulder Pain & Disability Index 8–18 points 18 Shoulder conditions Pain + disability subscales 0–100 Oxford Shoulder Score OSS 5 points — Shoulder surgery/OA 12 items; 0=worst, 48=best; validated for shoulder OA Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS 2 points 1.74 All 0–10; use at every assessment --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Guidelines Modality Indication Findings ---------- ----------- --------- X-ray AP + Zanca 10° cephalic tilt First-line; trauma/OA CC distance normal 11–13 mm , joint space narrowing, osteolysis, stress views for instability Ultrasound Dynamic assessment, guided injection Joint effusion, capsular thickening, distal clavicle changes MRI Soft tissue assessment, planned surgery CC ligament integrity, labral pathology, bone oedema osteolysis CT Complex/comminuted fractures, pre-surgical Clavicle fracture pattern, posterior displacement Grade IV > Zanca View: 10–15° cephalic tilt reduces overlap with spine; reduces beam by 50% for better joint detail. Preferred over standard AP for ACJ assessment. Bilateral Stress Views Weight-bearing X-rays with 10 lb weights hung from wrists: identifies Grade III vs IV by measuring CC distance bilaterally. Now used selectively not routinely . --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Differentiating Features Investigation ----------- ------------------------------ -------------- Subacromial impingement Painful arc 60–120°, positive Neer/Hawkins USS, MRI Rotator cuff tear Weakness on resisted rotation, positive drop arm USS/MRI SLAP lesion O'Brien's positive with deep shoulder pain, biceps involvement MRI arthrogram Sternoclavicular joint pathology Pain medial to ACJ, SCJ tenderness, swelling X-ray, CT Cervical radiculopathy C4–C5 Dermatomal distribution, neck movement reproduces symptoms Cervical assessment, MRI Inflammatory arthropathy Bilateral, morning stiffness, systemic features Blood CRP, RF, anti-CCP , rheumatology Thoracic outlet syndrome Vascular/neurogenic symptoms with provocation EAST test, vascular studies Clavicle stress fracture Localised clavicle tenderness, overhead athletes X-ray, MRI bone oedema --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use the current local shoulder pathway. Urgent escalation is based on neurovascular compromise, open injury, severe traumatic deformity or associated fracture/dislocation. Other ACJ presentations may begin with individualised conservative management when appropriate. --- Conservative Management Grades I–III Acute Phase Week 0–3 : - A sling may be used briefly for comfort after injury; avoid unnecessary prolonged immobilisation and progress according to symptoms and injury stability - Ice 10–15 min, 3–4× daily , activity modification - Analgesia see pharmacological - Patient education: expected recovery timeline, activity modification, return-to-sport guidance Rehabilitation Phase Week 2–12 : - Range of motion : pendular exercises → active-assisted → full active ROM - Rotator cuff strengthening : isometric → isotonic bands → free weights - Periscapular strengthening : lower trapezius, serratus anterior — critical for ACJ load reduction - Proprioception / neuromuscular training : closed-chain progression - Sport-specific rehabilitation : graded return to impact/contact Evidence Base: - Mouhsine et al. 2003 : Grade I–III — 90% satisfaction with conservative management at 2 years - Mazzocca et al. 2011 : No significant difference in outcomes between surgical and conservative Grade III at 5 years ACJ OA / Distal Clavicle Osteolysis - Load modification : reduce overhead pressing, heavy bench press modify grip width — wider grip reduces ACJ stress - Periscapular strengthening as above - Manual therapy : ACJ mobilisation Grade III–IV Maitland ; may reduce pain limited RCT evidence - Distal clavicle osteolysis : relative rest from causative activity for 3–6 months; most resolve Pharmacological Management Analgesia and any AC-joint injection are prescriber/injection-service decisions. No NICE shoulder guideline has been identified that supports the previous fixed doses, duration, PPI logic, injection composition or annual limit; those details have been removed pending exact claim-source review. Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency/urgent assessment: neurovascular compromise, open injury, threatened skin, severe traumatic ACJ injury or associated fracture/dislocation. - Specialist assessment: persistent disabling symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty or a presentation requiring consideration of operative management. - Medical/rheumatology assessment: systemic inflammatory features, infection concern or suspected malignancy under applicable criteria. No fixed “within days”, injection-count, 6–12-week or 3–6-month threshold is asserted. --- Surgical Options for reference - Grade III : ACCR acromioclavicular coracoclavicular reconstruction or Weaver-Dunn procedure - ACJ OA / Osteolysis : Distal clavicle excision Mumford procedure — arthroscopic or open; high satisfaction rates 85–92% --- Key References 1. content: Overview & Pathophysiology Adhesive capsulitis frozen shoulder is a painful, progressive condition characterised by diffuse fibrosis and contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule, resulting in significant restriction of active and passive range of motion in a capsular pattern. It is a distinct clinical entity from other shoulder conditions and follows a broadly predictable natural history. Prevalence: - Lifetime prevalence: 2–5% of the general population - Peak incidence: 40–60 years rare 70 - Female preponderance: approximately 60–70% female - Second shoulder affected in 20–30% of patients usually contralateral; simultaneous bilateral uncommon Associated Conditions: Condition Relative Risk / Prevalence ----------- --------------------------- Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 3–5× increased risk; prevalence 10–20% in frozen shoulder Thyroid disease hypo- and hyperthyroid 2–3× increased risk Dupuytren's contracture Associated fibrotic diathesis Parkinson's disease Increased risk; may be early feature Cardiac disease / post-cardiac surgery Prolonged immobility Post-stroke ipsilateral shoulder Hemiplegia + immobility Cervical disc disease Neurogenic inflammation proposed Post-operative immobilisation Rotator cuff repair; mastectomy Hyperlipidaemia Emerging association Pathophysiology The pathological process involves: 1. Inflammatory phase: Synovial inflammation with fibroblast proliferation; increased vascularity; cytokine release IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6 2. Fibrotic phase: Dense fibrocollagenous tissue formation; capsule thickening normal 2–4 mm → up to 7–10 mm in contracted phase 3. Key site: Rotator cuff interval between supraspinatus and subscapularis — contracture here produces external rotation restriction first 4. Axillary recess obliteration: Normal joint volume 28–30 mL reduced to abduction > IR restriction proportional loss ; distinguishes from other shoulder conditions External Rotation abduction > IR - Exclusion of glenohumeral arthritis X-ray , rotator cuff tear USS , and other causes --- Red Flags Consider alternative or serious pathology when the presentation suggests infection, unreduced dislocation, tumour/malignancy, inflammatory polyarthritis or an acute traumatic rotator-cuff tear. Escalate according to the actual presentation. Progressive focal neurological deficit requires prompt medical/specialist assessment. Age at onset alone does not mandate MRI, and Version 1 does not prescribe Paget-specific testing or a separate CRPS pathway without an appropriate clinical indication and source. --- Clinical Frameworks Hannafin & Chiaia Staging System 2000 Correlates histological findings with clinical stages: - Stage 1: Scattered hypervascular synovium; fibrinous exudate - Stage 2: Hypertrophic synovitis; early fibroplasia - Stage 3: Mild synovitis; dense subsynovial fibrosis; collagen remodelling - Stage 4: Mature collagen; avascular hypocellular tissue; minimal synovitis Treatment Decision Framework Based on Stage: Stage Dominant Problem Priority Intervention Caution ------- ----------------- ---------------------- --------- Stage 1 Painful/irritable Pain; sleep disruption Symptom control; consider glenohumeral corticosteroid injection for short-term improvement; tolerable ROM/exercise Dose exercise to irritability rather than forcing painful end range Stage 2 Frozen Stiffness; functional limitation ROM exercises; joint mobilisation; hydrodilatation Continue pain management Stage 3 Thawing Persistent restriction Progressive strengthening; capsular stretching Normal loading; return to function Biopsychosocial Considerations - Prolonged pain and disability → psychological impact; depression screening PHQ-9 in chronic cases - Impact on work and activities of daily living — occupational advice important - Fear-avoidance behaviours can slow recovery — address early --- Outcome Measures Measure Score Range MCID Clinical Application --------- ------------- ------ --------------------- SPADI 0–100 0 = best 8–13 pts Best validated for shoulder pain and disability; practical OSS Oxford Shoulder Score 0–48 48 = best 5 pts Widely used in NI orthopaedic pathway for frozen shoulder Constant-Murley Score 0–100 100 = best 10–16 pts Objective ROM component useful for frozen shoulder tracking QuickDASH 0–100 0 = best 11–16 pts Upper limb function; practical for serial assessment ASES 0–100 100 = best 12–17 pts Post-procedural assessment injection/hydrodilatation/MUA ROM measurement Degrees ER MCID: ~9°; Flex MCID: ~11° Essential — sequential ROM measurement is primary outcome marker Practical recommendation: SPADI + Constant-Murley ROM components at baseline and follow-up. Serial ROM measurements ER, abduction, flexion, IR essential for monitoring stage progression. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical Diagnosis Frozen shoulder remains a clinical diagnosis based on: 1. Characteristic history gradual onset pain; progressive stiffness 2. Capsular pattern restriction on passive examination 3. Exclusion of other pathology Arthrography: Historically used to assess capsular restriction but now largely replaced; it is not required for routine clinical diagnosis. USS: - Supports diagnosis by excluding structural pathology RC tear, calcific tendinitis - May show thickened rotator cuff interval; increased blood flow power Doppler - Cannot confirm capsular volume reduction directly MRI: - Thickened rotator cuff interval capsule; enhancing synovium on gadolinium - Differentiates from glenohumeral OA; identifies associated pathology - Not routinely required for clinical diagnosis X-ray: Usually normal in primary frozen shoulder — important to exclude glenohumeral OA, calcific tendinitis, malignancy Key Evidence for Management: Corticosteroid injection: - Buchbinder et al. Cochrane 2003; Carette et al. 2003 NEJM: Short-term benefit up to 6 weeks — Level I - Intra-articular corticosteroid superior to physiotherapy alone at 6 weeks; no difference at 12 months - Best in Stage 1 freezing — reduces inflammatory component and provides window for rehabilitation Hydrodilatation arthrographic distension : - Valadie et al. 2000 ; Buchbinder et al. 2004 BMJ: Significant short-term benefit over placebo - Cochrane Maund et al., 2012 : Hydrodilatation + steroid superior to steroid alone at 6 weeks - Hydrodilatation technique, medicines and volume are specialist/injection-service decisions; no fixed protocol is prescribed here - Available via MSK interface services in some HSC NI trusts Manipulation Under Anaesthesia MUA : - Evidence: retrospective series; no high-quality RCTs - Effective for Stage 2/3 — breaks down adhesions; risk of fracture, nerve injury, haemarthrosis - Post-MUA physiotherapy essential — begin same day Arthroscopic capsular release: - For refractory cases >6 months no improvement ; excellent outcomes reported >90% satisfaction - Systematic review Omari & Bunker, 2001 : superior to MUA for recovery speed - Available at NI orthopaedic centres --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Differentiating Features Differentiating Assessment ----------- ------------------------------ --------------------------- Glenohumeral osteoarthritis Older age; crepitus; X-ray changes; gradual onset X-ray — joint space loss, osteophytes Rotator cuff tear with secondary stiffness Lag signs; weakness; USS/MRI confirms tear USS — full-thickness tear Subacromial pain syndrome Painful arc; strength variable; NOT globally restricted ROM testing — not capsular pattern Calcific tendinitis Acute severe pain; X-ray calcification; moves through X-ray — calcification Glenohumeral inflammatory arthritis RA/crystal Bilateral; systemic features; inflammatory bloods Bloods RF, anti-CCP, urate ; X-ray Shoulder impingement + secondary guarding Painful arc; resisted tests positive; ROM pain-limited not structurally restricted Passive ROM under distraction/supine Avascular necrosis AVN History steroids, alcohol, haemoglobinopathy; deep aching MRI — AVN signal Posterior shoulder dislocation missed Trauma; fixed IR; limited ER; BEWARE X-ray axillary view essential ; CT Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Vasomotor; trophic changes; allodynia; disproportionate Specialist assessment Cervical radiculopathy Neck symptoms; referred pain; neurological signs Cervical exam; ULTT; Spurling's --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use the current BESS/local frozen-shoulder pathway. After serious or alternative pathology has been considered, care may include education, exercise and other individually assessed nonsurgical options. Investigation and intervention choices remain clinician/specialist-led. --- Conservative Management Stage 1 Painful/Freezing — Priority: pain management: - Education: condition, stages, natural history, prognosis - Sleep position advice pillow under arm; avoid lying on affected side - Dose stretching and ROM to irritability; do not force painful end range in Stage 1 - Gentle pendulum exercises; active-assisted ROM in pain-free range - Pain-free active exercises isometric, low-load - Early injection referral for pain management Stage 2 Frozen/Stiffening — Priority: ROM restoration: Technique Evidence Dosage ----------- ---------- -------- Passive ROM exercises Moderate 3×10 reps, 3×/day within pain tolerance Hold-relax contract-relax stretching Moderate 5 sec contract; 10 sec passive stretch; 3× each direction Glenohumeral joint mobilisation Grade III–IV Moderate Posterior capsule; inferior glide Physiotherapy-supervised stretching programme High 2–3× per week supervised + home programme Codman's pendulum exercises Low-moderate Daily Stage 3 Thawing/Resolution — Priority: function and strength: - Progressive strengthening: rotator cuff; scapular stabilisers - Return to overhead activities: graded exposure - Occupational/work activities — graded return - Prognosis counselling — complete resolution may take 2+ years Pharmacological and injection care The BESS/BOA Frozen Shoulder pathway supports individualised analgesia/NSAID consideration, intra-articular corticosteroid injection and physiotherapy in appropriate patients, but it does not validate every drug, dose, repeat-injection limit or hydrodilatation protocol previously stated here. Prescribing and injection details remain medical/injection-service decisions pending claim-level review. Onward Referral Criteria - Urgent assessment: infection, unreduced dislocation, acute traumatic cuff-tear presentation, neurovascular compromise or another serious presentation. - Seek medical/rheumatology assessment: when inflammatory polyarthritis or systemic disease is suspected. - Consider specialist shoulder assessment: when diagnosis remains uncertain or disabling restriction persists despite an appropriate conservative plan. Investigation and intervention choices remain clinician/specialist-led; no universal fixed timeframe is asserted. --- Key References 1. Buchbinder R, Green S, Forbes A, Hall S, Lawler G.
