Ann Rheum Dis. 2004;63 3 :302–309. 2. Carette S, Moffet H, Tardif J, et al. Intraarticular corticosteroids, supervised physiotherapy, or a combination of the two in the treatment of adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder. Arthritis Rheum. 2003;48 3 :829–838. 3. Hannafin JA, Chiaia TA. Adhesive capsulitis: a treatment approach. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2000; 372 :95–109. 4. Maund E, Craig D, Suekarran S, et al. Management of frozen shoulder: a systematic review and cost-effectiveness analysis. Health Technol Assess. 2012;16 11 :1–264. 5. Reeves B. The natural history of the frozen shoulder syndrome. Scand J Rheumatol. 1975;4 4 :193–196. 6. BESS/BOA. Frozen Shoulder Patient Care Pathway . BESS patient care pathways. 7. Rangan A, Hanchard N, McDaid C. World J Orthop. 2015;6 2 :263–268. 9. Omari A, Bunker TD. Open surgical release for frozen shoulder: surgical findings and results of the release. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2001;10 4 :353–357. 10. headings: Interventional: ESWT Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Calcific tendinitis CT of the shoulder is characterised by the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals within the rotator cuff tendons, most commonly the supraspinatus 80–90% of cases , followed by infraspinatus ~10% and subscapularis ~5% . It affects 2.7–8% of the adult population, with peak incidence in the 4th–5th decades, and a female predominance F:M ≈ 2:1 . Pathophysiology: Uhthoff Model The most widely accepted pathophysiological model is Uhthoff & Loehr's 1997 cell-mediated theory — a fibrocartilaginous transformation of tendon tissue not a degenerative process , distinct from dystrophic calcification seen in chronic tendinopathy. Uhthoff Stages of Calcific Tendinitis: Stage Phase Histology Clinical Features Duration ------- ------- ----------- ------------------- ---------- Pre-calcific Fibrocartilaginous transformation Chondrocytic metaplasia of tendon fibrocytes; no calcium yet Often asymptomatic; possible mild aching Months Calcific — Formative Crystal deposition Calcium crystals deposited in matrix vesicles; chalk-like, soft consistency Mild–moderate pain; often episodic Weeks–months Calcific — Resting Quiescent Calcium consolidates; vascular ingrowth begins Variable — may be asymptomatic Variable Calcific — Resorptive ⚠️ Most painful Phagocytic resorption; toothpaste-like consistency; highly vascular; intense local inflammation Severe acute pain ; often the presenting crisis Days–weeks Post-calcific Remodelling Fibroblast invasion; collagen remodelling; calcium resolves Pain subsides; function recovers Weeks–months > Key clinical implication: The resorptive phase is the most acutely painful often presenting as apparent 'pseudo-acute' shoulder . Paradoxically, this phase has the best prognosis as calcium is being actively resorbed. Intervention aspiration/barbotage is most effective and technically easiest in this phase fluid/toothpaste consistency . Gärtner Radiographic Classification: Type Appearance Phase Correlation Clinical Note ------ ----------- ------------------- --------------- Type I Dense, homogeneous, well-defined border Formative/resting Harder; less likely to resolve spontaneously Type II Dense/translucent, heterogeneous or poorly defined Transitional Variable behaviour Type III Translucent, heterogeneous, poorly defined 'fluffy' Resorptive Soft; most amenable to barbotage; more likely to resolve spontaneously Why calcium deposits in the critical zone: The supraspinatus is most affected in its "critical zone" — 1 cm proximal to the insertion — an area of relative avascularity and high mechanical stress Rathbun & Macnab, 1970 . Hypoxic conditions may trigger fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and initiate the calcification cascade. Spontaneous resolution rate: 27–50% of deposits resolve within 3 years without intervention. Natural history is generally favourable, but 20–30% of patients develop chronic, recalcitrant symptoms. --- Special Tests > Clinical Note: No shoulder special test is specific for calcific tendinitis. Tests below detect subacromial impingement and rotator cuff pathology — calcific tendinitis should be confirmed by imaging. A positive impingement cluster with acute-onset severe pain warrants X-ray. Impingement & Rotator Cuff Tests Assessment Role Limitation --- --- --- Painful arc, Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy May reproduce subacromial pain Non-specific for calcific tendinopathy Empty/full can and lag/drop-arm tests Explore rotator-cuff function and possible tear features Do not confirm a calcium deposit Cross-body adduction Explores AC-joint contribution Limited discrimination in isolation Use special-test findings as part of the differential examination. Imaging confirms the presence and location of a calcium deposit when that information will change management. > Calcific tendinitis-specific clinical pattern: Sudden onset of exquisite shoulder pain often overnight or following minor activity , severe movement restriction, marked tenderness over supraspinatus insertion, presentation mimicking septic arthritis. X-ray confirms diagnosis. --- Red Flags Escalate genuine systemic/infective features, suspected malignancy, acute neurological deficit, fracture/dislocation or another serious presentation according to clinical urgency. Progressive focal weakness requires prompt medical/specialist assessment. Version 1 does not infer reactive arthritis from recent dental, gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, mandate MRI after a fixed interval, or prescribe a cortical-erosion pathway without separate evidence. --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Framework Treatment Decision Tree HSC NI --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID MDC Score Range Best For Validated? --------- ------ ----- ------------- ---------- ------------ SPADI Shoulder Pain & Disability Index 8–13 points 18 points 0–100 0=best Recommended first-line for CT; pain-heavy presentations; highly responsive to change ✅ Yes DASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder, Hand 10.8 points 12.7 points 0–100 0=best General UE function; good for tracking functional recovery across treatment phases ✅ Yes QuickDASH 14.9–15.9 points — 0–100 0=best Efficient screening at each contact; 11-item version ✅ Yes OSS Oxford Shoulder Score 5 points — 0–48 48=best Pre/post-op comparison; NHS standard for surgical referrals ✅ Yes ASES American Shoulder & Elbow Surgeons 6.4–17 points — 0–100 100=best Research; surgical outcomes ✅ Yes NRS Pain 0–10 1.5–2 points — 0–10 0=no pain Rapid pain monitoring; supplement to functional measure ✅ Yes > HSC NI Practice Recommendation: Use SPADI as primary outcome measure for calcific tendinitis pain-dominant condition; more responsive than DASH in acute presentations . Supplement with NRS pain at each contact. Re-measure SPADI at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and post-intervention. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Comparison Modality Sensitivity Specificity Cost First-Line? Notes ---------- ------------- ------------- ------ ------------- ------- Plain X-ray AP + outlet 66–93% ~99% Low ✅ Yes Mandatory first-line; identifies deposit, size, morphology Gärtner classification Ultrasound USS 79–98% 88–99% Low-Moderate ✅ Yes adjunct Dynamic assessment; guides intervention barbotage ; detects concurrent RC tear; operator-dependent MRI 70–82% 98% High No second-line Best for soft tissue; concurrent pathology RC tear, AC joint ; calcium may appear as signal void CT ~100% ~100% High/Radiation No Rarely needed; useful pre-op planning for large/complex deposits Preferred imaging approach HSC NI : 1. Plain X-ray — confirm diagnosis, classify deposit Gärtner I/II/III , measure size 2. USS — if intervention planned, or if concurrent RC pathology suspected complementary to X-ray 3. MRI — if X-ray/USS inconclusive, suspected full-thickness RC tear, or pre-surgical assessment Deposit characteristics associated with spontaneous resolution: - Gärtner Type III 'fluffy', poorly defined - Smaller deposits 2 cm - Long symptom duration >12 months - Bursal-side deposits --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Differentiating Features Key Tests Imaging ----------- -------------------------- ----------- --------- Subacromial Impingement without calcification Painful arc; similar impingement signs; no sudden onset crisis; gradual onset Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy, Empty Can USS/MRI; X-ray normal or minor degenerative changes Rotator Cuff Tear full-thickness Weakness > pain full thickness ; Drop Arm positive; ER lag sign; older age Drop Arm, ER Lag Sign, Belly Press USS/MRI confirms; X-ray shows superior migration if massive Adhesive Capsulitis Global passive restriction all planes ; ER most restricted; capsular pattern Capsular pattern ROM testing MRI capsular thickening, reduced joint volume ; X-ray normal Septic Arthritis Fever, elevated CRP/ESR/WBC; erythema; systemically unwell; rapid onset FBC/CRP/ESR, joint aspiration USS shows effusion; X-ray may be normal early Acromioclavicular Joint Pathology Pain at AC joint; cross-body adduction positive; no calcium in supraspinatus Cross-body adduction, AC palpation, O'Brien's top pain X-ray AC views; USS Pseudogout CPPD Often older patient; knee/wrist also affected; synovial fluid analysis confirms Joint aspiration — positive birefringent crystals X-ray — chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage Cervical Radiculopathy C5 Dermatomal radiation; neck movement provokes; reduced biceps reflex Spurling's, ULTT, neurological exam Cervical MRI Glenohumeral Osteoarthritis Older patient; global ROM loss; crepitus; stiffness > pain; end-stage Passive ROM, crepitus X-ray joint space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis Reactive Arthritis Preceding infection; other joints affected; systemic features HLA-B27, ESR/CRP, urine culture X-ray; MRI Os Acromiale unfused secondary ossification centre Young adult; anterior acromial tenderness; acromion mobile; X-ray diagnostic X-ray axillary view critical CT for surgical planning --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Begin with clinically appropriate conservative care when serious pathology has been excluded. NICE HTG645 retains extracorporeal shockwave therapy for calcific tendinopathy in research-only governance. Specialist procedures require separate assessment and evidence. --- Conservative Management Physiotherapy Principles: Phase Timeframe Goals Interventions ------- ----------- ------- --------------- Acute Resorptive Weeks 0–4 Pain control; maintain ROM; patient education Pendulum exercises; cryotherapy; gentle passive ROM; avoid provocative overhead loading Subacute Weeks 4–8 Progressive ROM; begin RC strengthening Active ROM; scapular stabilisation; isometric RC; posterior capsule stretching Functional Weeks 8–12+ Full strength; return to function/work Progressive resistance; proprioception; functional tasks; sport-specific if applicable Manual Therapy: - Joint mobilisation GH and thoracic has low-level evidence as adjunct to exercise in subacromial pain — included in multimodal approach - Not recommended as primary or standalone treatment Exercise: - Supervised exercise superior to home exercise alone for subacromial conditions - Scapular stabilisation and rotator cuff strengthening are cornerstones - Avoid provocative overhead loading in acute/resorptive phase Pharmacological Analgesia, corticosteroid injection and any off-label medicine are prescriber/injection-service decisions. The previous fixed doses, durations, annual injection limits and opioid/colchicine suggestions did not have an exact authoritative claim-source relationship and have been removed pending human evidence review. Interventional: ESWT Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy Mechanism: Acoustic pressure waves → mechanical disruption of calcium deposits → stimulate phagocytic resorption + neovascularisation Current NICE HTG645 position: evidence of efficacy is inadequate in quality and quantity. ESWT for calcific tendinopathy in the shoulder should be used only in the context of research. The cited trials may explain why the procedure has been studied, but they do not override this current UK governance position or establish a routine protocol. ESWT contraindications: Coagulation disorders/anticoagulants, local infection, malignancy, pregnancy, pacemaker, bony deposits overlying neurovascular structures Interventional: USS-Guided Barbotage / Needling & Lavage Mechanism: Direct mechanical disruption of calcium deposit via needle; lavage removes calcium debris; induces local inflammatory response to accelerate resorption. Evidence Summary: Parameter Data ----------- ------ Efficacy Significant pain reduction; superior to corticosteroid injection alone de Witte et al., 2012 Best phase Resorptive Gärtner III — calcium has toothpaste-like consistency; easier aspiration Technique The specialist service determines image guidance, equipment, lavage method and medicines; no fixed procedure is prescribed here Combined with corticosteroid Corticosteroid injection after barbotage standard practice for post-procedure flare management Key RCT Randomised trial de Witte et al., 2012 : barbotage + corticosteroid vs corticosteroid alone — ASES score superior in barbotage arm at 12 months Success rate 60–80% significant improvement at 12 months; deposit clearance in 30–70% Local access Use the current local imaging or specialist pathway; do not assume a mandatory imaging step without checking the service criteria Surgical Management Arthroscopic Removal Indication: Specialist assessment after failed conservative management; ESWT cannot be treated as a required routine prerequisite while NICE restricts it to research. Specialist procedure: Operative management may be considered in selected refractory cases. The surgeon determines the procedure after clinical and imaging review. Evidence: - Success rate 85–90% at 2 years - This learner page does not specify an acromioplasty indication or estimate how often surgery is required - Short-stay day-case procedure; physiotherapy essential post-operatively Onward Referral Criteria - Urgent assessment: infection/systemic illness, acute neurological deficit, fracture/dislocation or another serious presentation. - Suspected malignancy: follow the current suspected-cancer pathway only when applicable NICE/local criteria are met. - Consider specialist shoulder assessment: for persistent disabling symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty or when a specialist procedure is being considered. No fixed imaging or procedure timeline is asserted. --- Key References 1. Uhthoff HK, Loehr JW. Calcific tendinopathy of the rotator cuff: pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 1997;5 4 :183–191. Uhthoff model — foundational pathophysiology paper 2. Gärtner J, Heyer A. Calcific tendinitis of the shoulder. Orthopade. 1995;24 3 :284–302. title: Shoulder Labral Tears (SLAP & Bankart Lesions)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the periphery of the glenoid fossa, deepening the socket by approximately 50% and contributing significantly to glenohumeral stability. headings: SLAP Lesions Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior
content: Overview & Pathophysiology The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the periphery of the glenoid fossa, deepening the socket by approximately 50% and contributing significantly to glenohumeral stability. Labral tears fall into two main clinical categories encountered in MSK physiotherapy practice: SLAP Lesions Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior SLAP lesions involve the superior labrum at the biceps anchor long head of biceps tendon inserts at the supraglenoid tubercle and superior labrum . They are common in overhead athletes, throwing sports, and following traction/compression injuries. Snyder Classification 1990 : Type Description Prevalence Management Implication ------ ------------- ----------- ------------------------ Type I Superior labral fraying/degeneration; biceps anchor intact ~11% Conservative Type II Detachment of superior labrum and biceps anchor from glenoid most common ~41% Often surgical if conservative fails Type III Bucket-handle tear of superior labrum; biceps anchor intact ~33% Surgical resection Type IV Bucket-handle tear extending into biceps tendon ~15% Surgical repair/tenotomy Type V–X Extended classifications Morgan/Maffet including combined lesions Variable Specialist-led Pathomechanics: - Repetitive overhead loading : Peel-back mechanism during late cocking phase — posterior biceps vector peels the labrum off the glenoid - GIRD Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit : Posterior capsule tightness shifts humeral head posterosuperiorly, increasing shear on superior labrum - Traction injury : Sudden inferior distraction force e.g., catching a heavy object - Compression : FOOSH fall on outstretched hand with superior shear force Bankart Lesions Anterior Labral Tears Bankart lesions involve detachment of the anteroinferior labrum typically 3–6 o'clock position from the glenoid rim. They are the primary pathological lesion in traumatic anterior glenohumeral instability, present in >85% of first-time anterior dislocations . Subtypes: - Classic Bankart : Labrum and periosteum stripped from glenoid rim - Bony Bankart : Associated anterior glenoid bone loss >15–20% glenoid width indicates critical bone loss and alters surgical planning - ALPSA Anterior Labroligamentous Periosteal Sleeve Avulsion : Periosteum intact; labrum medially displaced — poorer proprioceptive outcome if untreated - HAGL Humeral Avulsion of Glenohumeral Ligament : Less common; IGHL avulses from humeral attachment Associated lesions: Hill-Sachs defect posterolateral humeral head impression fracture in 47–90% of dislocations; engaging Hill-Sachs lesions complicate surgical planning. --- Special Tests > Clinical Note: No single special test confirms labral pathology with sufficient diagnostic certainty. Use the history, mechanism and a coherent examination pattern; specialist imaging may be required when the result will change management. SLAP-Specific Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- O'Brien's, Crank, Biceps Load II and Anterior Slide May reproduce symptoms associated with superior labral/biceps-anchor pathology Performance varies and no single test confirms a SLAP lesion Speed's and Yergason's Explore biceps-related symptoms Limited labral discrimination Compression Rotation May reproduce pain or clicking Do not use in isolation Instability / Bankart Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Apprehension, relocation and anterior release Explore symptomatic anterior instability; apprehension is more relevant than pain alone Interpret as a coherent pattern, not a numeric diagnostic rule Sulcus sign and load-and-shift Explore laxity and direction Laxity is not synonymous with symptomatic instability --- Red Flags - Unreduced dislocation, fracture-dislocation or neurovascular compromise requires urgent/emergency assessment. - Progressive focal neurological deficit requires prompt medical/specialist assessment. - After reduction, early mobilisation should follow the current BESS shoulder pathway; prolonged default immobilisation is not used to reduce recurrence. Glenoid bone loss, Hill-Sachs lesions and procedure selection belong to specialist planning rather than the red-flag list. Version 1 does not prescribe Latarjet, remplissage or another procedure from a fixed threshold. --- Clinical Frameworks SLAP Decision Framework Bankart / Instability Framework HSC NI GIRD Management SLAP prevention/rehab - Sleeper stretch : Side-lying on affected shoulder, horizontal adduction + IR — target ≥5° gain in IR compared to contralateral - Cross-body stretch : Horizontal adduction in standing — posterior capsule release - Goal : Achieve GIRD Outcome-measure note: WOSI may be used for instability-related presentations, with DASH or QuickDASH as a general upper-limb measure. Select measures for the individual purpose and local pathway. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Hierarchy Modality SLAP Sensitivity SLAP Specificity Notes ---------- ----------------- ----------------- ------- MR Arthrography MRA 82–92% 85–98% Gold standard; intra-articular gadolinium required Plain MRI 3T 63–82% 79–94% Adequate for Bankart; misses 18–26% SLAP II Plain MRI 1.5T 44–68% 66–87% Inferior; request MRA if clinical suspicion high Ultrasound Poor for SLAP/Bankart — Not indicated for labral pathology CT Arthrography 78–91% 91% Alternative if MRI contraindicated; better for bone loss quantification Plain X-ray AP/Axillary/Scapular-Y N/A N/A Mandatory first-line to exclude fracture, bone loss, Hill-Sachs Diagnostic Accuracy Summary For suspected SLAP lesions: No standalone test is definitive. Use the history and a coherent examination pattern; specialist imaging may be considered when the result will change management. For Bankart/instability: History of dislocation is the most powerful diagnostic factor. Apprehension + Relocation + Anterior Release triad achieves specificity of 0.99. Plain X-ray to exclude fracture/bone loss is mandatory first-line. --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Differentiating Features Key Tests Imaging ----------- -------------------------- ----------- --------- Subacromial Impingement / RC Tear Pain arc 60–120°, painful resisted abduction/ER; older age group Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy, Empty Can, Lift-Off USS first-line; MRI if full-thickness tear suspected AC Joint Pathology Pain localised to AC joint; positive cross-body adduction; O'Brien's positive with pain at top not deep in shoulder Cross-body adduction, AC joint palpation X-ray AC views, USS Biceps Tendinopathy / Rupture Anterior groove tenderness; "Popeye" deformity rupture ; speed's positive Speed's, Yergason's, palpation USS bicipital groove Adhesive Capsulitis Global passive ROM restriction all planes ; insidious onset; ER most restricted Capsular pattern assessment X-ray to exclude OA; MRI shows capsular thickening SLAC Superior Labral Anterior-posterior Cyst Paralabral cyst on imaging; suprascapular nerve compression; spinati wasting EMG/NCS, suprascapular notch palpation MRI Multidirectional Instability MDI Bilateral laxity; atraumatic onset; sulcus sign; Beighton score Sulcus sign, load-and-shift all directions, Beighton score MRI; often normal Cervical Radiculopathy C5/C6 Dermatomal symptoms; neck movement provokes; reflexes affected Spurling's, Upper limb tension test Cervical MRI Glenohumeral OA Older age; end-stage reduced ROM; crepitus; loss of joint space Crepitus, passive ROM X-ray joint space narrowing, osteophytes --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use the current BESS/local shoulder pathway. Acute dislocation care includes reduction through an appropriate emergency pathway, post-reduction neurovascular examination and individualised rehabilitation. Specialist imaging and operative planning are separate decisions. --- Conservative Management Phase 1 — Acute/Pain Control Weeks 0–4 - Activity modification; avoid aggravating overhead/throwing positions - Pendulum exercises, AROM within comfort - Scapular retraction/depression activation - Heat/ice PRN for symptom management - Patient education: mechanism, prognosis, self-management Phase 2 — Strengthening Weeks 4–12 - Rotator cuff strengthening: ER/IR with resistance band supine → standing progression - Scapular stabiliser strengthening: serratus anterior wall push-up plus , lower trapezius - Posterior capsule stretching if GIRD present sleeper stretch, cross-body stretch - Proprioception: closed-chain upper extremity exercises, unstable surface work Phase 3 — Sport/Function Weeks 12–16+ - Sport-specific progressive loading - Throwing athletes: interval throwing programme ITP — Andrews protocol - Return-to-play criteria: - Full, pain-free ROM - ≥90% strength symmetry isokinetic or HHD - WOSI >85% of maximum score - Negative apprehension/biceps provocation tests - Functional/sport-specific tasks completed without limitation Pharmacological No medicine treats a labral tear itself. Analgesia or injection decisions are prescriber/specialist-led; the previous fixed durations and unsupported treatment hierarchy have been removed pending claim-level evidence review. Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency/urgent assessment: unreduced dislocation, fracture-dislocation or neurovascular compromise. - Prompt specialist assessment: persistent neurological deficit, unreduced or traumatic instability, or other concerning traumatic findings. - Consider routine specialist shoulder assessment: recurrent/persistent instability, diagnostic uncertainty or persistent disabling symptoms despite rehabilitation. Age cut-offs, recurrence counts, ISIS scores, bone-loss thresholds and procedure choice are not universal Version 1 referral rules. --- Key References 1. Snyder SJ, Karzel RP, Del Pizzo W, et al. title: Rotator Cuff Tear
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Rotator cuff tears are among the most clinically significant shoulder conditions encountered in musculoskeletal physiotherapy. They represent a spectrum from partial-thickness tears through full-thickness complete tears to massive rotator cuff tears involving multiple tend
headings: Infraspinatus / Teres Minor Tests ER weakness
Surgical Decision Framework Kuhn et al.
Lewis Framework Applied to RC Tears
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Rotator cuff tears are among the most clinically significant shoulder conditions encountered in musculoskeletal physiotherapy. They represent a spectrum from partial-thickness tears through full-thickness complete tears to massive rotator cuff tears involving multiple tendons. The condition sits at the severe end of the tendinopathy continuum model. Prevalence: - Asymptomatic tears identified in 22% of adults overall; rises to 54% in those >60 years Yamamoto et al., 2010 - Symptomatic full-thickness tears: ~2–3% of the general population - Prevalence doubles each decade after age 50 - Bilateral tears in ~35% of those with symptomatic unilateral tear Classification: Classification Description --------------- ------------- Partial-thickness Bursal-sided, articular-sided PASTA lesion , or intratendinous Full-thickness small 5 cm or involving ≥2 tendons Irreparable massive With muscle atrophy, fatty infiltration Goutallier Grade 3–4 Pathophysiology Degenerative tears >90% of all RC tears : - Culmination of the continuum model — reactive → dysrepair → degenerative tendinopathy → tear - Critical zone of supraspinatus 1 cm from insertion : zone of relative avascularity - Fatty infiltration Goutallier classification correlates with chronicity and repair prognosis - Increasing tear size over time in 40–80% of untreated full-thickness tears Moosmayer et al., 2013 Traumatic tears: - Acute forced abduction/ER against resistance e.g., fall on outstretched arm - More common in younger patients with previously healthy tendons - More likely surgically repairable; better healing rates Relevant Anatomy - Rotator cuff interval: Between supraspinatus and subscapularis; contains biceps tendon and coracohumeral ligament; disruption affects inferior capsule stability - Subscapularis: Largest and strongest cuff muscle; anterior stabiliser; tears often missed clinically - Fatty infiltration Goutallier : Grade 0 normal → Grade 4 fat > muscle ; Grade ≥3 = poor surgical prognosis - Pseudoparalysis: Inability to actively elevate arm despite passive ROM due to massive cuff tear --- Special Tests Supraspinatus Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Empty/full can Explores supraspinatus-related pain and weakness Pain or weakness is not specific for a tear Drop arm and painful arc Explore marked functional deficit and subacromial pain Interpret with trauma history, active/passive movement and strength Infraspinatus / Teres Minor Tests ER weakness Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- External-rotation lag, Hornblower's and external-rotation strength Explore posterosuperior cuff dysfunction A positive finding requires correlation with the whole assessment Subscapularis Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Lift-off, belly-press, bear-hug and internal-rotation lag Explore subscapularis dysfunction No one test establishes a tear in isolation Full-Thickness Tear Pattern The following combination may increase concern for a substantial tear, particularly after trauma, but is not a standalone diagnostic rule: - Age >60 - Positive supraspinatus weakness - Positive impingement sign - Night pain --- Red Flags - Chest, jaw or arm symptoms with dyspnoea or other acute cardiac features require emergency assessment/999. - Marked acute weakness or pseudoparalysis after trauma requires urgent shoulder assessment for possible acute rotator-cuff tear or fracture. - Fracture/dislocation, neurovascular compromise, infection or malignancy concern requires escalation according to the presentation. Do not make ultrasound or MRI automatic in the learner wording; investigation is determined by the assessing clinician and pathway. --- Clinical Frameworks Surgical Decision Framework Kuhn et al. The decision between conservative and surgical management for rotator cuff tears is specialist-led and considers: 1. Tear characteristics: Size, location, fatty infiltration Goutallier , tendon retraction 2. Patient factors: Age, activity level, hand dominance, comorbidities 3. Response to conservative management: 3–6 months' trial first for most tears 4. Chronicity: An acute traumatic presentation with substantial weakness warrants timely specialist assessment Prognosis for conservative management: - Structured rehabilitation can be appropriate for selected tears; the treatment choice depends on the individual clinical and imaging context - Massive tears: poorer conservative outcomes; augmentation strategies superior capsule reconstruction, tendon transfer emerging Lewis Framework Applied to RC Tears - Differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic prevalence of asymptomatic tears is high - Functional deficit is the key clinical driver — not imaging findings alone - Imaging should not drive surgery unless functional deficit correlates --- Outcome Measures Measure Score Range MCID Best Utility --------- ------------- ------ -------------- WORC Western Ontario Rotator Cuff 0–2100 higher = better 275 pts Disease-specific — most responsive for RC pathology ASES American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons 0–100 100 = best 12–17 pts Surgical audit; combines pain VAS + function Constant-Murley Score 0–100 100 = best 10–16 pts Surgical outcomes; requires dynamometer OSS Oxford Shoulder Score 0–48 48 = best 5 pts Post-surgical; simple; patient-completed SPADI 0–100 0 = best 8–13 pts Pain + disability; responsive in conservative management QuickDASH 0–100 0 = best 11–16 pts Upper limb function; useful for work-related cases --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging for RC Tears Ultrasound USS : - Can assess cuff integrity dynamically when imaging is clinically indicated - Advantages: dynamic assessment, bilateral comparison, real-time, no radiation, guided injection - Limitations: operator-dependent; cannot assess labrum; poor visualisation under acromion MRI: - May support specialist assessment and surgical planning when clinically indicated - Advantages: multiplanar; Goutallier grading; fatty infiltration; bone assessment; labrum - MR arthrography may be considered by the specialist for selected partial-thickness or intra-articular questions X-ray: - Plain radiographs may show indirect chronic cuff-related changes but do not establish tear size - Greater tuberosity irregularity/sclerosis - Calcific deposits; glenohumeral arthritis Key Evidence - Moosmayer et al. 2010 JBJS-A: RCT — surgery vs supervised exercise for small-medium full-thickness tears. No significant difference at 1 year; surgery superior at 2 years on Constant-Murley only. - Kukkonen et al. 2015 JBJS-A: RCT — 3 groups physio; physio + acromioplasty; physio + acromioplasty + cuff repair . No significant difference at 2 years for small tears. - Ainsworth et al. 2009 : Structured physiotherapy produces clinically meaningful outcomes in 75% of full-thickness tear patients avoiding surgery. - Re-tear risk varies with tear and patient factors; discuss individual prognosis with the surgical team --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Features Differentiating ----------- ------------- ---------------- Rotator cuff tendinopathy No lag signs; strength preserved pain-limited Strength testing with lag signs Subacromial bursitis Pain without significant weakness USS: isolated bursal pathology Adhesive capsulitis Global ROM restriction; no weakness Capsular pattern; ROM assessment Glenohumeral arthritis Crepitus; age; gradual onset X-ray: joint space narrowing Cervical radiculopathy Neck symptoms; neurological deficit; normal cuff strength Neurological exam; ULTT; Spurling's SLAP tear Young overhead athlete; Popeye sign if associated biceps O'Brien's; MR arthrogram Acromioclavicular pathology Direct AC tenderness; cross-body adduction pain AC joint injection test; X-ray Brachial neuritis Severe acute pain → rapid weakness; no trauma EMG; MRI neurography Suprascapular nerve entrapment Wasting infraspinatus; deep aching; ER weakness EMG; MRI ganglion cyst --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use the current local shoulder pathway. Acute traumatic marked weakness warrants urgent shoulder assessment. Other tears may be considered for individualised conservative care or specialist review according to function, progression, comorbidity and patient goals. --- Conservative Management Structured Rehabilitation Programme: Phase Duration Goals Key Exercises Loading ------- ---------- ------- --------------- --------- Phase 1: Protection Weeks 0–4 Pain control; ROM; protect cuff Pendulum; elbow/wrist AROM; scapular retraction; submaximal isometrics Isometric only Phase 2: Activation Weeks 4–8 Rotator cuff activation; scapular control Side-lying ER; standing ER with band; prone Y/T/W; side-lying IR Light isotonic Phase 3: Strengthening Weeks 8–16 Strength and endurance; functional ROM Progressive band ER/IR; scaption; shoulder press; serratus activation; HSR protocol Progressive load 3×10–15 Phase 4: Function Weeks 16–24 Return to activity/work/sport Functional patterns; overhead mechanics; work simulation Sport/task-specific Evidence base: - Cochrane Page et al., 2016 : Supervised exercise superior to no treatment; comparable to surgery for small-medium tears in 2-year outcomes - Specific exercises ER, IR, scaption preferred over non-specific — Kuhn et al. 2010 - Heavy slow resistance HSR : emerging evidence comparable to surgical outcomes for small-medium tears Pharmacological and injection care Analgesia and any subacromial injection are individual prescriber/injection-service decisions. The cited rotator-cuff literature may inform a specialist discussion, but fixed drug, PPI, image-guidance and annual injection-limit claims require exact source verification before publication. Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency/urgent assessment: cardiac emergency features, fracture/dislocation, neurovascular compromise, or marked acute weakness after trauma. - Prompt specialist assessment: significant or progressive weakness suggesting a substantial tear. - Specialist assessment: persistent disabling symptoms or consideration of operative care after an appropriate shared decision process. Version 1 does not prescribe universal age cut-offs, fixed two-week surgery timing or automatic imaging. --- Key References 1. Yamamoto A, Takagishi K, Osawa T, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2014;96 18 :1504–1514. 3. de Jesus JO, Parker L, Frangos AJ, Nazarian LN. Accuracy of MRI, MR arthrography, and ultrasound in the diagnosis of rotator cuff tears: a meta-analysis. AJR Am J Roentgenol. 2009;192 6 :1701–1707. 4. Kukkonen J, Joukainen A, Lehtinen J, et al. Treatment of non-traumatic rotator cuff tears: A randomised controlled trial with one-year clinical results. Bone Joint J. 2014;96-B 1 :75–81. 5. Page MJ, Green S, McBain B, et al. title: Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Rotator cuff tendinopathy is a broad term encompassing pain and dysfunction arising from the rotator cuff tendons — most commonly the supraspinatus, followed by infraspinatus and subscapularis. It represents one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal conditions in clinical
headings: Continuum Model of Tendinopathy Cook & Purdam, 2009; revised 2016
Cluster Testing Approach Hegedus et al., 2012
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Rotator cuff tendinopathy is a broad term encompassing pain and dysfunction arising from the rotator cuff tendons — most commonly the supraspinatus, followed by infraspinatus and subscapularis. It represents one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal conditions in clinical practice, accounting for 44–65% of shoulder pain presentations in primary care. Prevalence: Point prevalence of shoulder pain is approximately 7–26% in the general population, with rotator cuff pathology implicated in 65–70% of cases. Prevalence increases sharply with age, particularly after 50 years. Continuum Model of Tendinopathy Cook & Purdam, 2009; revised 2016 The continuum model — now the dominant explanatory framework — describes tendinopathy as a spectrum rather than a discrete entity: 1. Reactive tendinopathy: Acute response to compressive or tensile overload. Non-inflammatory cell-mediated matrix changes. Clinically: sudden onset after unaccustomed loading. Potentially reversible. 2. Tendon dysrepair: Failed or incomplete healing response. Disorganised matrix, increased ground substance and vascularity. Clinically: subacute/chronic presentation. 3. Degenerative tendinopathy: Cell death, lipid infiltration, calcification, disorganised collagen. High risk of tear. Clinically: chronic, often in older patients. Key principle: Tendinopathy is a failed healing response, not classic inflammation. This drives management decisions — compressive loading and prolonged rest are counterproductive; progressive tensile loading is the evidence-based intervention. Relevant Anatomy - Supraspinatus: Arises from the supraspinous fossa, inserts on the greater tuberosity superior facet . Primary abductor and force-couple stabiliser. - Infraspinatus: External rotator; inserts on greater tuberosity middle facet . - Subscapularis: Internal rotator; inserts on lesser tuberosity. - Teres minor: External rotator; inserts on greater tuberosity inferior facet . - Critical zone: The avascular zone 1 cm from the supraspinatus insertion — primary site of degenerative change and tears. - Subacromial space: Normal space 7–14 mm; reduction causes impingement on the bursa and rotator cuff. Mechanism Multifactorial — intrinsic and extrinsic factors: - Intrinsic: Age-related tendon degeneration, vascularity compromise, genetic predisposition COL5A1 gene variants , tendon morphology. - Extrinsic: Repetitive overhead activity, heavy lifting, acromion morphology Bigliani Type II/III , scapular dyskinesis, altered glenohumeral kinematics, poor rotator cuff strength/endurance. - Compressive loading at the subacromial space is now recognised as a key perpetuating factor, particularly for supraspinatus tendinopathy. --- Special Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy and painful arc May reproduce subacromial pain Non-specific and not diagnostic alone Empty/full can and resisted external rotation Explore pain and cuff-related weakness Interpret pain inhibition and true weakness separately Lag, drop-arm, lift-off and bear-hug tests Explore features of a substantial cuff tear Positive findings require correlation with history, movement and imaging indications Speed's and other adjacent-structure tests Explore competing sources Limited cuff discrimination Clinical pearl — Cluster testing for rotator cuff tendinopathy: No single test is diagnostic. Use a coherent history and examination pattern, and distinguish pain inhibition from clinically important weakness. --- Red Flags - Chest, jaw or arm symptoms with dyspnoea or other acute cardiac features require emergency assessment/999. - Progressive weakness, rapid muscle wasting or another focal neurological deficit requires prompt medical/neurological assessment. - Infection, malignancy, fracture/dislocation or neurovascular compromise requires escalation according to the presentation. - Possible diaphragmatic referral should be assessed in its clinical context rather than assigned automatic imaging. Do not rely on one provocative or special test in isolation to diagnose rotator-cuff tendinopathy; interpret findings with the history and the rest of the examination. --- Clinical Frameworks Lewis Shoulder Framework 2009, updated 2015 Jeremy Lewis's clinical framework for shoulder assessment emphasises: 1. Symptom behaviour — directional preference, aggravating/relieving factors 2. Movement assessment — active ROM, painful arc, end-range pain 3. Load assessment — rotator cuff strength testing ER, IR, abduction, flexion 4. Differentiation testing — supine positioning to offload subacromial space 5. Treatment-based classification — responds better than diagnosis-based for directing exercise loading Cools Rehabilitation Framework 2016 Ann Cools's evidence-based rehabilitation model for shoulder: 1. Phase 1 — Pain management: Activity modification, posture correction, scapular control 2. Phase 2 — Motor control: Low-load rotator cuff activation, scapular stabilisers 3. Phase 3 — Strength: Progressive loading, ER/IR ratio restoration target ER:IR ≥ 0.66 4. Phase 4 — Function: Sport/work-specific loading, overhead mechanics Cluster Testing Approach Hegedus et al., 2012 - Never rely on a single test - Combine high-sensitivity tests rule out with high-specificity tests rule in - Assess response to load — does isometric contraction reproduce/resolve pain? - Musculoskeletal ultrasound is the recommended first-line imaging in most guidelines --- Outcome Measures Measure Structure Score Range MCID MDC Clinical Utility --------- ----------- ------------- ------ ----- ----------------- DASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder and Hand 30-item PRO; optional work and sport modules 0–100 0=best Use a population-appropriate change threshold — Comprehensive; time-consuming QuickDASH 11-item abbreviated DASH 0–100 0=best 11–16 points 15.9 Excellent for clinical use; highly correlated with DASH SPADI Shoulder Pain and Disability Index 13-item; pain 5 + disability 8 subscales 0–100 0=best 8–13 points 18 Simple; widely validated; best for shoulder-specific pain OSS Oxford Shoulder Score 12-item 0–48 48=best 5 points — Preferred by orthopaedic surgeons; post-surgical monitoring Constant-Murley Score 35-point subjective + 65-point objective 0–100 100=best Use a population-appropriate change threshold — Includes measured abduction strength WORC Western Ontario Rotator Cuff 21-item VAS-based 0–2100 2100=best 275 points — Disease-specific; most responsive for rotator cuff pathology PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 3–5 self-selected activities 0–10/activity 2 points — Excellent for individualised goal tracking; highly responsive Recommendation for routine practice: SPADI + QuickDASH at baseline and discharge. Add Constant-Murley if post-surgical or when objective comparison required. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Guidelines Ultrasound USS : - First-line imaging per BESS British Elbow and Shoulder Society and NICE guidelines - Can assess cuff integrity dynamically when imaging is clinically indicated; accuracy varies with operator, tear type and reference standard - Operator-dependent; limited assessment of labrum and glenohumeral joint MRI: - Preferred for labral pathology, bony assessment, surgical planning - May support specialist assessment of cuff, labral and bony pathology when the result will change management - MR arthrogram for suspected partial-thickness tear, labral tears, instability X-ray: - Limited for soft tissue; useful for: calcific deposits, acromioclavicular joint, glenohumeral arthritis, acromion morphology, greater tuberosity irregularity - AP + axillary views minimum Key Systematic Reviews - Hegedus et al. 2012 — BJSM: Most comprehensive meta-analysis of shoulder special tests. Conclusion: No single test has sufficient diagnostic accuracy; clusters recommended. - Lenza et al. 2013 — Cochrane: USS and MRI comparable for full-thickness tears; MRI superior for partial tears. - Diercks et al. 2014 — BESS: USS first-line before MRI for suspected RC pathology. --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key differentiating features Clinical assessment --- --- --- Subacromial pain syndrome Painful arc and pain with overhead activity Load response and muscle tests interpreted with the history Full-thickness rotator-cuff tear Significant weakness; lag signs may be present Lag/drop-arm findings and traumatic or degenerative context Adhesive capsulitis Global restriction with a capsular pattern Restriction across directions Glenohumeral arthritis Gradual restriction, crepitus and stiffness Joint pattern and clinical context Cervical radiculopathy Arm symptoms, neurological signs and neck-related reproduction Cervical and neurological examination AC-joint pathology Superior pain and direct AC-joint tenderness AC palpation and cross-body loading Biceps or calcific pathology Anterior pain or acute severe presentation Condition-appropriate assessment Instability or thoracic outlet syndrome Apprehension, hyperlaxity or positional neurovascular features Context-specific instability or neurovascular assessment Brachial neuritis Acute severe pain followed by rapid weakness Neurological pattern and medical assessment Investigation choice should follow the clinical context, red-flag assessment and appropriate specialist pathway; no imaging modality is an automatic confirmatory test for every differential. --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use an exercise-led, individualised rotator-cuff tendinopathy plan consistent with the current clinical practice guideline and local pathway. Progressive motor deficit or marked traumatic weakness follows a separate prompt specialist pathway. --- Conservative Management Evidence-based exercise prescription: Phase Timeframe Exercise Focus Dosage Evidence ------- ----------- ---------------- -------- ---------- Acute reactive 0–4 weeks Pain-free isometrics; posture; scapular control 3×10–15 reps, daily Moderate RCT Sub-acute 4–8 weeks Isotonic ER/IR; scapular stabilisers; progressive load 3×12–15 reps, 3×/week High multiple RCTs Rehabilitation 8–16 weeks Functional strengthening; eccentric loading; overhead mechanics 3×8–12 reps progressive High Cochrane Return to activity 16–24 weeks Sport/work-specific; plyometric if relevant Graded exposure Moderate Key exercise principles: - Eccentric loading — most evidence base for patellar tendinopathy; emerging evidence for shoulder Level II - Heavy Slow Resistance HSR — Beyer et al. 2015 AJSM: HSR comparable to eccentric; better adherence - ER:IR strength ratio target ≥ 0.66 at 60°/s isokinetic testing - Scapular stabilisation: Serratus anterior activation; lower/middle trapezius; avoid upper trapezius dominance Manual therapy: - Thoracic manipulation: reduces shoulder pain and improves ROM — moderate evidence Haik et al., 2016 - Glenohumeral joint mobilisation posterior capsule : Grade III–IV for capsular restriction - Soft tissue release: limited high-quality evidence as standalone intervention Education: - Activity modification not rest ; load management principles; graded return - Posture correction; ergonomic advice particularly for occupational factors Nonsurgical medical care The current evidence anchors for this condition are the BESS Subacromial Shoulder Pain pathway and the 2025 rotator-cuff-tendinopathy clinical practice guideline. They do not justify carrying forward unsupported fixed doses, PPI age thresholds, annual injection limits or mandatory post-injection waiting periods. Medicine and injection decisions remain prescriber-led and must be checked against the exact current recommendation and patient context. Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency: acute cardiac features or another emergency presentation. - Prompt medical/specialist assessment: progressive neurological/motor deficit, rapid wasting or marked traumatic weakness. - Specialist shoulder assessment: persistent disabling symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty despite appropriate rehabilitation. Investigation and procedure selection are clinician-led; no automatic MRI or fixed operative timeline is asserted. --- Key References 1. Cook JL, Purdam CR. Is tendon pathology a continuum? content: Overview & Pathophysiology Shoulder instability refers to symptomatic excessive translation of the humeral head relative to the glenoid, ranging from subtle microinstability to recurrent dislocation. It is the most common joint dislocation, accounting for approximately 45% of all dislocations presenting to emergency departments. It represents a significant clinical challenge due to its heterogeneous aetiology, high recurrence rates, and impact on young, active populations. Prevalence / Incidence: - Annual incidence of primary glenohumeral dislocation: 11–27 per 100,000 - Peak incidence: males 20–30 years contact sport ; females 20–50 years atraumatic - Recurrence rate after first dislocation: 55–97% in those 40 years - Recurrence is the dominant clinical concern in young athletes Classification TUBS / AMBRI / AIOS TUBS Traumatic Unilateral Bankart Surgery : - Traumatic onset single event - Unilateral - Bankart lesion anteroinferior labral avulsion - Surgery often required for high recurrence risk AMBRI Atraumatic Multidirectional Bilateral Rehabilitation : - Atraumatic onset no single traumatic event - Multidirectional laxity inferior ± anterior ± posterior - Bilateral often - Rehabilitation primary treatment - Inferior capsular shift if surgery required AIOS Acquired Instability from Overuse in Sport : - Overhead throwing athletes - Acquired internal impingement; microinstability - Direction-specific; sport-related Stanmore Classification Rowe & Zarins / Revised Bayley et al. : Three-point triangle: - Type I: Structural traumatic — Bankart, Hill-Sachs - Type II: Atraumatic structural involuntary; dysplastic glenoid - Type III: Muscle patterning non-structural; habitual; voluntary Relevant Anatomy and Stabilisers Static stabilisers: - Glenoid labrum: Deepens glenoid cavity by ~50%; increases contact area; functions as chock-block for humeral head - Glenohumeral ligaments GHL : - Superior GHL: resists inferior translation in neutral and adduction - Middle GHL: resists anterior translation at 45° abduction - Inferior GHL IGHL : primary restraint at 90° abduction — most important ligament - IGHL anterior band: resists anterior translation with ER - IGHL posterior band: resists posterior translation with IR - Rotator cuff interval: Coracohumeral + superior GHL; resists inferior translation - Bony glenoid: Pear-shaped; inverted glenoid version >15° retroversion = risk for posterior instability Dynamic stabilisers: - Rotator cuff: Compression into glenoid; concavity-compression mechanism - Long head of biceps: Superior glenohumeral stability - Scapular rotators: Position glenoid face; scapular dyskinesis → decreased stability Common Structural Lesions: Lesion Description Direction Imaging -------- ------------- ----------- --------- Bankart lesion Anteroinferior labral avulsion from glenoid Anterior MR arthrogram Bony Bankart Bankart + glenoid bone loss >20–25% = critical Anterior CT glenoid morphology Hill-Sachs defect Posterolateral humeral head impaction fracture Anterior CT; MRI HAGL Humeral Avulsion GHL GHL avulsion from humerus not labrum Anterior MR arthrogram Reverse Bankart Posteroinferior labral tear Posterior MR arthrogram Reverse Hill-Sachs Anteromedial humeral head posterior dislocation Posterior CT; MRI SLAP tear Superior labrum anterior-posterior — MR arthrogram --- Special Tests Anterior Instability Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Apprehension, relocation and anterior release Explore symptomatic anterior instability; apprehension is more relevant than pain alone Interpret as a coherent pattern, not a numeric rule Load-and-shift, anterior drawer and fulcrum Explore translation and symptom reproduction Laxity alone does not establish symptomatic instability Posterior Instability Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Posterior apprehension, jerk, Kim and posterior stress Explore symptomatic posterior instability Performance varies; no single test is definitive Posterior load-and-shift Explores posterior translation Examiner-dependent and must be related to symptoms Multidirectional Instability / Laxity Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Sulcus sign and hyperabduction Explore inferior laxity Laxity is not synonymous with instability Beighton score Screens generalised joint hypermobility Does not diagnose shoulder instability or a connective-tissue disorder Combined/Other Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity Evidence Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ---------- ------- Clunk Test 44% 99% Moderate Full circumduction with axial load; clunk = labral tear O'Brien's Active Compression 47–67% 37–89% Moderate Combined SLAP/ACJ test; limited alone Crank Test 91% 93% Moderate Supine; axial load + rotation; for labral tears --- Red Flags - Unreduced/locked dislocation, fracture-dislocation or vascular compromise requires emergency assessment. - Perform and document a post-reduction neurovascular examination. A persistent neurological deficit requires prompt specialist assessment. - Recurrent or persistent instability requires specialist assessment according to the current BESS/local pathway. Procedure choice, ISIS score, bone-loss thresholds and fixed multidirectional-instability timelines belong to specialist planning, not the Version 1 red-flag criteria. --- Clinical Frameworks Instability Severity Index Score ISIS — Balg & Boileau, 2007 Pre-operative risk tools may inform specialist discussion but do not determine a procedure on their own: Factor Score -------- ------- Age ≤20 2 pts Competitive sport 2 pts Contact/overhead sport 1 pt Hyperlaxity anterior apprehension 2 cm 1 pt Hill-Sachs on AP X-ray 2 pts Loss of sclerotic inferior glenoid contour on AP X-ray 2 pts - Score ≤3: Low recurrence risk — arthroscopic Bankart suitable - Score ≥4: High recurrence risk — Latarjet procedure recommended - Score ≥6: Very high risk — Latarjet mandatory FEDS Classification Functional, Emotion, Direction, Severity Modern classification for MDI — integrates structural, neuromuscular, and psychological components. Rehabilitation Framework for Instability Wilk & Macrina, 2012 Phase 1 — Acute protection 0–4 weeks : - Sling immobilisation IR position — debate ongoing; ER immobilisation: reduced recurrence in young males - Pain management; rotator cuff isometrics; elbow/wrist AROM - Early scapular control: retraction; no provocative positions Phase 2 — Intermediate 4–8 weeks : - Progressive ER; RC strengthening; scapular stabilisers - Proprioception training joint position sense - Activity modification — avoid apprehension position 90°ABD/ER Phase 3 — Advanced strengthening 8–16 weeks : - Progressive loading; functional patterns; perturbation training - Sport-specific preparation Phase 4 — Return to sport 4–6 months : - Graduated sport return; sport-specific exercises - Bracing consideration for contact sports --- Outcome Measures Measure Score Range MCID Application --------- ------------- ------ ------------- WOSI Western Ontario Shoulder Instability Index 0–2100 2100 = best 220–320 pts Disease-specific; most responsive for instability ASES American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons 0–100 100 = best 12–17 pts Surgical audit Rowe Score 0–100 100 = best — Recurrence rate; function; ROM; composite Melbourne Instability Shoulder Score 0–100 — Instability-specific; used in Australia/UK DASH / QuickDASH 0–100 0 = best 11–16 pts Upper limb function; useful for occupational impact PSFS 0–10/activity 2 pts Sport/activity-specific; individualised --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging X-ray first-line — mandatory after acute dislocation : - AP: Hill-Sachs; glenoid erosion; fracture - Axillary lateral: confirms anterior/posterior direction; glenoid morphology - Stryker Notch view: Hill-Sachs optimised - West Point view: anterior glenoid rim Bankart bony lesion CT glenoid bone loss assessment : - Mandated when bony Bankart or significant glenoid loss suspected - Glenoid bone loss, lesion engagement, patient factors and activity demands inform specialist procedure selection; this learner page does not prescribe a numeric operative threshold - CT arthrogram: bone loss + labral assessment combined MRI arthrogram: - May support specialist assessment of Bankart, HAGL and other labral lesions when imaging will change management - Preferred over standard MRI for labral tears gadolinium distension - Identifies: Bankart; HAGL; SLAP; Hill-Sachs; rotator cuff; posterior lesions USS: - Limited for instability; cannot adequately assess labrum - Useful adjunct for associated RC pathology especially in >40 years post-dislocation Key Evidence - Itoi et al. 2007 JBJS: ER immobilisation after primary dislocation reduces recurrence in young males 26% vs 42% at 2 years — but difficult to sustain compliance - Balg & Boileau 2007 : ISIS score — validated prediction of recurrence and surgical decision-making - Burkhart & De Beer 2000 : Glenoid bone loss >25% = "engaging" Hill-Sachs; Bankart repair fails; Latarjet required - Bessière et al. 2014 : Latarjet superior recurrence rate vs arthroscopic Bankart in high-risk patients --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Features Differentiation ----------- ------------- ---------------- Rotator cuff tear post-dislocation Weakness; lag signs; >40 years USS/MRI post-reduction Acromioclavicular dislocation Direct impact; AC step deformity X-ray; AC palpation Multidirectional laxity without instability Asymptomatic hypermobility Beighton score; symptom correlation SLAP tear Overhead athlete; mechanical symptoms MR arthrogram; special tests SAPS/rotator cuff tendinopathy Painful arc; no apprehension Apprehension test negative Cervical radiculopathy Neck; neurological signs; referred Cervical exam; ULTT Brachial neuritis Post-viral; acute severe pain; wasting EMG; MRI Glenohumeral OA Older; crepitus; X-ray changes X-ray Posterior shoulder tightness GIRD Overhead athlete; IR deficit IR ROM measurement --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use the current BESS/local shoulder instability pathway. Acute dislocation care includes appropriate reduction, post-reduction neurovascular assessment and individualised rehabilitation. Vascular compromise is an emergency. Persistent neurological deficit or recurrent/persistent instability requires specialist review. --- Conservative Management Structured Rehabilitation Evidence Grade B–A : Phase Duration Focus Key Exercises ------- ---------- ------- --------------- Acute protection 0–4 weeks Sling; pain control; early activation Pendulum; elbow/wrist AROM; isometrics Activation 4–8 weeks RC activation; scapular control Side-lying ER; scapular retraction; prone Y/T/W Strengthening 8–16 weeks Progressive loading; proprioception Band ER/IR; shoulder press; perturbation Function/sport 16–24 weeks Return to sport/work Sport-specific; dynamic stability MDI specific AMBRI : - Primary treatment is rehabilitation — 80% avoid surgery with structured programme Burkhead & Rockwood, 1992 - Focus: rotator cuff co-contraction; proprioception; scapular control - Minimum 6 months rehabilitation trial before surgical consideration - Avoid provocative positions during initial rehabilitation Pharmacological Acute post-reduction analgesia is determined by the emergency/prescribing team. Recurrent instability management is not a drug pathway; any specific drug duration or injection claim requires its own source and specialist context. Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency: vascular compromise, unreduced/locked dislocation or fracture-dislocation. - Prompt specialist assessment: persistent post-reduction neurological deficit or marked traumatic weakness. - Specialist assessment: recurrent/persistent instability or failure to regain acceptable function with appropriate rehabilitation. Where a persistent nerve deficit is being investigated, test timing and referral route are determined by the specialist pathway. Version 1 does not prescribe fixed age, recurrence-count, ISIS, bone-loss, procedure or multidirectional-instability thresholds. --- Key References 1. Balg F, Boileau P. Radiology. 2005;237 2 :578–583. 3. Burkhead WZ Jr, Rockwood CA Jr. Treatment of instability of the shoulder with an exercise program. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1992;74 6 :890–896. 4. Itoi E, Hatakeyama Y, Sato T, et al. Immobilization in external rotation after shoulder dislocation reduces the risk of recurrence: a randomized controlled trial. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2007;89 10 :2124–2131. 5. Hegedus EJ, Goode AP, Cook CE, et al. Which physical examination tests provide clinicians with the most value when examining the shoulder? Br J Sports Med. 2012;46 14 :964–978. 6. Burkhart SS, De Beer JF. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2014;472 8 :2345–2351. 8. Wilk KE, Macrina LC. Non-operative and post-operative rehabilitation for glenohumeral instability. Clin Sports Med. 2013;32 4 :865–914. 9.
