title: Subacromial Pain Syndrome (SAPS)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Subacromial Pain Syndrome SAPS is the currently preferred umbrella term for pain arising from the subacromial space, replacing the older — and now disputed — term "subacromial impingement syndrome" SIS . SAPS encompasses pathology of the subacromial bursa, the rotator cuff
headings: CSAW Trial Beard et al., 2018 — JAMA
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Subacromial Pain Syndrome SAPS is the currently preferred umbrella term for pain arising from the subacromial space, replacing the older — and now disputed — term "subacromial impingement syndrome" SIS . SAPS encompasses pathology of the subacromial bursa, the rotator cuff tendons particularly supraspinatus , and the coracoacromial arch, without implying a specific structural mechanism. The terminology shift reflects a fundamental change in understanding: the mechanical impingement model Neer, 1972 has been largely replaced by a biopsychosocial and load-based framework. SAPS accounts for 44–65% of all shoulder pain presentations. Historical Concepts vs Current Understanding Model Historical Neer, 1972 Current Lewis, 2009–2016 ------- ------------------------ --------------------------- Mechanism Mechanical pinching of supraspinatus under coracoacromial arch Multifactorial: load, motor control, biopsychosocial Treatment Acromioplasty Exercise; surgical benefit not supported Terminology Subacromial Impingement Syndrome Rotator Cuff Related Shoulder Pain / SAPS Key evidence Cadaveric studies RCT: Beard et al. 2018 CSAW trial CSAW Trial Beard et al., 2018 — JAMA : Landmark RCT demonstrating that arthroscopic acromioplasty + physiotherapy was NOT superior to physiotherapy alone or sham surgery. This fundamentally challenged the impingement model and shifted treatment toward exercise-based management. Pathophysiology Primary contributors: 1. Subacromial bursal inflammation/thickening: The bursa lying between rotator cuff and acromion is highly innervated — a key pain source 2. Rotator cuff tendinopathy: Most commonly supraspinatus — on the continuum from reactive to degenerative 3. Altered shoulder kinematics: Scapular dyskinesis; reduced upward rotation; increased internal rotation during elevation 4. Rotator cuff force couple imbalance: Weakness/fatigue of external rotators and lower trapezius; relative upper trapezius overactivation Extrinsic factors: - Acromion morphology Bigliani Type II — curved; Type III — hooked : associated but not causal - Acromioclavicular joint osteophytes - Coracoacromial ligament thickening - Occupational overhead loading; sport swimming, throwing, racquet sports Intrinsic factors: - Rotator cuff tendon degeneration age-related - Reduced vascularity in supraspinatus critical zone - Tendon morphology and genetic factors Prevalence - Most common shoulder diagnosis in primary care 44–65% - Annual incidence in UK general practice: ~14.7/1000 patients/year Linsell et al., 2006 - Peak incidence: 45–64 years; increasing with overhead occupational exposure --- Special Tests Test group Role Limitation --- --- --- Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer and painful arc May reproduce subacromial pain Non-specific and not diagnostic alone Empty/full can and resisted external rotation Explore pain and cuff-related weakness Interpret pain inhibition and true weakness separately Horizontal adduction and adjacent-structure tests Explore competing pain sources Limited subacromial discrimination in isolation Combining Findings No single test is sufficiently accurate for isolated diagnosis. Interpret a coherent pattern of pain provocation, strength, function and response to load, and consider competing diagnoses. --- Red Flags - Chest, jaw or arm symptoms with dyspnoea or other acute cardiac features require emergency assessment/999. - Progressive weakness, rapid muscle wasting or focal neurological deficit requires prompt medical/neurological assessment. - Infection, malignancy, fracture/dislocation or neurovascular compromise requires escalation according to the presentation. - Possible referred diaphragmatic pain requires medical assessment in context rather than automatic imaging. Do not use disproportionate night pain plus age alone as an automatic suspected-cancer pathway rule; apply current NICE NG12/local criteria. --- Clinical Frameworks Lewis Shoulder Framework 2009, 2016 Jeremy Lewis's pragmatic approach to shoulder assessment challenges the impingement model: 1. Assessment Philosophy: Pain provocation tests have poor diagnostic accuracy; use clusters not single tests 2. Treatment Prioritisation: Shoulder exercise regardless of specific diagnosis; acromioplasty not supported 3. Staging by behaviour: - Stage 1: Pain only at end range/high load — progressive exercise tolerated - Stage 2: Pain through range — modify loading; isometrics may reduce pain - Stage 3: Pain at rest — protect and manage; graded return to load 4. Key principle: The painful arc itself is not diagnostic — assess what provokes, what reduces, and response to load Cools Rehabilitation Model 2016 Scapular focus in SAPS rehabilitation: - Assess scapular kinematics: upward rotation deficit SARD strongly associated with SAPS - Target serratus anterior and lower trapezius activation - Correct upper trapezius dominance - Posterior shoulder stretching for posterior capsule tightness GIRD — Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit GIRD Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit : - IR deficit >25° compared to contralateral = significant - Posterior capsule tightness → anterior-superior humeral head migration → subacromial space reduction - Posterior capsule stretching sleeper stretch, cross-body stretch — evidence from throwing athletes Biopsychosocial Considerations - Central sensitisation contributes to chronic SAPS — screen with PainDETECT - Catastrophising, fear-avoidance, low self-efficacy are predictors of poor outcome - Address from first consultation; avoid overmedicalising with imaging-driven diagnoses --- Outcome Measures Measure Score Range MCID Clinical Application --------- ------------- ------ --------------------- SPADI 0–100 0 = best 8–13 pts Best validated for SAPS specifically; pain 5 items + disability 8 items QuickDASH 0–100 0 = best 11–16 pts Quick screen; upper limb function DASH 0–100 0 = best 10–15 pts Comprehensive; work and sport modules OSS 0–48 48 = best 5 pts 12-item; used in NI orthopaedic pathway Constant-Murley 0–100 100 = best 10–16 pts For pre/post-surgical comparison; requires dynamometer PSFS 0–10 per activity 2 pts Patient-specific; most clinically responsive for individual goals ASES 0–100 100 = best 12–17 pts American standard; pain + function composite NI HSC recommended practice: SPADI at baseline and discharge as minimum; add Constant-Murley for surgical pathway cases. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis CSAW Trial Beard et al., 2018 — JAMA - Multicentre RCT; n=313; 3 arms: 1 arthroscopic acromioplasty + physio; 2 arthroscopic lavage sham + physio; 3 physiotherapy alone - Primary outcome Oxford Shoulder Score at 6 months: No significant difference between groups - Conclusion: Acromioplasty does not add benefit beyond physiotherapy - Impact: Major shift in surgical practice; acromioplasty rates declining significantly in UK/Ireland Imaging Evidence USS Ultrasound : - Identifies bursal thickening, rotator cuff changes, calcific deposits - Dynamic assessment of subacromial space - Not a routine first-line investigation under the BESS primary/community pathway; use when an agreed pathway or a clinical question will change management MRI: - Better for partial-thickness tears, labral pathology, bone marrow changes - MR arthrogram where structural tear or instability suspected X-ray findings in SAPS: - Acromion morphology AP + outlet view - Acromioclavicular joint changes - Calcific deposits - Greater tuberosity sclerosis/cyst Clinical Prediction Rules - No single validated CPR for SAPS diagnosis equivalent to those in lumbar spine - A combination of concordant history and examination findings is more useful than a single manoeuvre - Response to injection can confirm subacromial source functional diagnostic injection --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Features Differentiating assessment --- --- --- Rotator cuff tendinopathy Overlaps significantly with SAPS Load response and muscle tests interpreted with the history Full-thickness rotator-cuff tear Significant weakness; lag signs may be present Lag/drop-arm findings and the overall traumatic or degenerative presentation Adhesive capsulitis Global restriction with a capsular pattern Restriction across directions AC-joint pathology Direct AC tenderness and cross-body pain AC palpation and cross-body loading Calcific tendinopathy Acute severe pain that can mimic infection Clinical context and the presence of a calcium deposit when investigated Glenohumeral OA Gradual restriction, crepitus and stiffness Joint pattern and clinical context Cervical radiculopathy Neck/arm symptoms and neurological signs Cervical and neurological examination Labral pathology or instability Trauma, apprehension, catching or recurrent instability Instability/labral assessment interpreted in context Thoracic outlet syndrome Positional neurovascular symptoms Neurovascular assessment and subtype-specific specialist evaluation Brachial neuritis Severe pain followed by rapid weakness Neurological pattern and medical assessment Investigation choice should follow the suspected diagnosis, red-flag assessment and appropriate specialist pathway; no imaging or electrodiagnostic test in this table is an automatic confirmatory step. --- Management & Treatment Governed Care Pathway Use the current local shoulder pathway and an individualised exercise-led plan when serious pathology has been excluded. Progressive neurological change or marked traumatic weakness follows a separate prompt specialist pathway. --- Conservative Management Exercise Programme Evidence Grade A — multiple RCTs, Cochrane : Exercise Type Example Dosage Rationale --------------- --------- -------- ----------- Scapular stabilisation Prone Y/T/W; band retraction; push-up plus 3×15 reps, daily Lower trap/serratus activation; correct dyskinesis RC activation Side-lying ER; ER at 0°; band ER 3×12–15 reps, daily Restore ER:IR ratio; reduce superior migration Progressive loading Scaption; shoulder press; HSR 3×8–12 reps progressive Tendon adaptation; pain modulation Posterior stretching Sleeper stretch; cross-body stretch 3×30 sec, daily Correct GIRD; improve IR ROM Thoracic mobility Thoracic extension; rotation Daily Improve scapular platform Manual therapy Moderate evidence : - Thoracic spine manipulation: short-term improvement in pain and function Bang & Deyle, 2000; Haik et al., 2016 - Glenohumeral mobilisation posterior capsule : Grade III–IV for internal rotation deficit - NOT recommended as standalone; adjunct to exercise Education Essential : - Explain SAPS framework — avoid impingement/wear-and-tear language negative effects on prognosis - Activity modification: avoid provocative positions initially; graded return - Self-management: posture, sleep position, ergonomics - Prognosis: most SAPS resolves with structured exercise over 3–6 months 80% satisfactory outcome Nonsurgical medical care Use the current BESS Subacromial Shoulder Pain pathway and condition-specific evidence. Analgesia or corticosteroid injection may be discussed by an appropriate clinician, but this page does not specify a drug dose, PPI age threshold, image-guidance superiority figure, annual injection limit or mandatory waiting period because those exact claims have not yet been source-verified. Onward Referral Criteria - Emergency: acute cardiac features or another emergency presentation. - Prompt medical/specialist assessment: progressive neurological deficit, rapid wasting, marked traumatic weakness, infection or other serious pathology concern. - Specialist shoulder assessment: persistent disabling symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty despite appropriate rehabilitation. Version 1 does not mandate MRI or a fixed referral duration from a general red-flag label. --- Key References 1. Beard DJ, Rees JL, Cook JA, et al; CSAW Study Group. Arthroscopic subacromial decompression for subacromial shoulder pain CSAW : a multicentre, pragmatic, parallel group, placebo-controlled, three-group, randomised surgical trial. Lancet. 2018;391 10118 :329–338. 2. Lewis J. Subacromial impingement syndrome: a musculoskeletal condition or a clinical illusion? Phys Ther Rev. 2011;16 5 :388–398. 3. Hegedus EJ, Goode AP, Cook CE, et al. Which physical examination tests provide clinicians with the most value when examining the shoulder? Update of a systematic review with meta-analysis of individual tests. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46 14 :964–978. 4. Michener LA, Walsworth MK, Doukas WC, Murphy KP. Reliability and diagnostic accuracy of 5 physical examination tests and combination of tests for subacromial impingement. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2009;90 11 :1898–1903. 5. BESS. Subacromial Shoulder Pain – 2025 . Patient care pathways and guidelines. 6. Koester MC, Dunn WR, Kuhn JE, Spindler KP. The efficacy of subacromial corticosteroid injection in the treatment of rotator cuff disease: a systematic review. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2007;15 1 :3–11. 7. Cools AM, Johansson FR, Borms D, Maenhout A. Prevention of shoulder injuries in overhead athletes: a science-based approach. Braz J Phys Ther. 2015;19 5 :331–339. 8. Haik MN, Alburquerque-Sendín F, Camargo PR. Short-term effects of thoracic spine manipulation on shoulder impingement syndrome. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2014;95 12 :2229–2236. 9. Neer CS II. Anterior acromioplasty for the chronic impingement syndrome in the shoulder: a preliminary report. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1972;54 1 :41–50. 10. Linsell L, Dawson J, Zondervan K, et al. Prevalence and incidence of adults consulting for shoulder conditions in UK primary care; patterns of diagnosis and referral. Rheumatology Oxford . 2006;45 2 :215–221. 11. NHS England. Subacromial decompression surgery for adults with subacromial pain clinical commissioning policy . 2018. 12. Page MJ, Green S, McBain B, et al. Manual therapy and exercise for rotator cuff disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016; 6 :CD012224. 13. Daniels EW, Cole D, Jacobs B, Phillips SF. Existing Evidence on Ultrasound-Guided Injections in Sports Medicine. Orthop J Sports Med. 2018;6 2 :2325967118756576. 14. Desmeules F, Roy JS, Lafrance S, et al. Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy Diagnosis, Nonsurgical Medical Care, and Rehabilitation: A Clinical Practice Guideline. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2025;55 4 :235–274. doi: 10.2519/jospt.2025.13182.

title: Costochondritis
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Costochondritis is inflammation of the costochondral or costo-sternal junctions causing anterior chest wall pain. It is one of the most common causes of chest pain presenting to both primary care and emergency departments, accounting for approximately 13–36% of chest pain
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Costochondritis is inflammation of the costochondral or costo-sternal junctions causing anterior chest wall pain. It is one of the most common causes of chest pain presenting to both primary care and emergency departments, accounting for approximately 13–36% of chest pain presentations Proulx AM & Zryd TW, 2009 . Distinction from Tietze Syndrome - Costochondritis: Inflammation of the costochondral junctions — no visible or palpable swelling . Multiple levels often affected. More common. - Tietze Syndrome: Localised non-suppurative inflammation with visible/palpable swelling at the costochondral/costo-sternal junction, typically affecting the 2nd or 3rd rib. Rarer; often younger patients. Prevalence & Demographics - Accounts for 13–36% of musculoskeletal chest pain in primary care - Peak age: 20–40 years for Tietze; broader age range for costochondritis - Female:male ratio: approximately 3:1 - Often bilateral involvement; most commonly affects ribs 2–5 at costo-sternal junctions Relevant Anatomy - The costal cartilages connect the osseous ribs to the sternum at costo-sternal junctions - Ribs 1–7 connect directly to the sternum true ribs - Ribs 8–10 connect to costal cartilage of the rib above false ribs - Ribs 11–12 are floating no anterior attachment - The costo-sternal joint is a fibrous rib 1 or synovial ribs 2–7 joint — synovial joints may undergo inflammatory arthritis Mechanism & Aetiology - Often idiopathic ; proposed mechanisms include: - Repetitive microtrauma heavy lifting, coughing, exercise - Viral upper respiratory infection preceding cough - Direct chest trauma - Seronegative spondyloarthropathy e.g., ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis - Post-sternotomy cardiac surgery - Fibromyalgia costochondritis as component - Rarely: septic IV drug use, immunocompromised --- Special Tests > Key point: Costochondritis is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on reproduction of pain with palpation of costochondral junctions. Sensitivity and specificity data specific to costochondritis is limited. The most important role of clinical examination is ruling out serious cardiac, pulmonary, and GI pathology. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Costochondral Palpation reproduction of concordant chest pain ~0.70–0.80 ~0.90 ~7.0–8.0 ~0.22–0.33 Low–Moderate Key diagnostic manoeuvre; press firmly on costal cartilages 2–5 bilaterally Rib Spring Test lateral compression Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Lateral compression of thorax reproducing anterior chest pain; differentiates from rib fracture Sternal Compression Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Compression of sternum reproducing local pain Hooking Manoeuvre Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion For lower rib syndrome ribs 8–10 ; hooking fingers under lower rib margin and pulling anteriorly Key Diagnostic Manoeuvres Expert Consensus 1. Systematic palpation of all costochondral junctions — reproduce concordant pain at ≥1 junction 2. Arm movements: Pain reproduced or worsened with arm elevation, pectoral stretch 3. Deep inspiration/cough: Worsens costochondral pain — important history feature 4. Response to local pressure: Pain reproduced and correlates with patient's presenting complaint References: Proulx AM & Zryd TW 2009 . American Family Physician ; Disla E et al. 1994 . Archives of Internal Medicine . --- Red Flags > This condition requires thorough cardiac, pulmonary, and GI exclusion before confirming a musculoskeletal diagnosis. Chest pain in any patient requires systematic red flag screening. Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Crushing/pressure central chest pain radiating to jaw/left arm Acute coronary syndrome ACS 999 — Emergency Chest pain + diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting ACS / MI 999 — Emergency Pleuritic chest pain + dyspnoea + haemoptysis Pulmonary embolism 999 — Emergency Sudden onset severe chest pain radiating to back Aortic dissection 999 — Emergency Chest pain + fever + productive cough + reduced air entry Pneumonia / pleuritis Same-day GP; chest X-ray Chest pain + weight loss + haemoptysis in smoker Lung malignancy 2WW GP referral Swelling/redness over costochondral junction in IVDU or immunocompromised Septic costochondritis Urgent A&E / bloods Chest pain in patient with known malignancy Metastatic disease to ribs/sternum Urgent oncology review ECG changes ST elevation/depression, new LBBB ACS Emergency Chest pain + haemodynamic instability Tension pneumothorax/PE/dissection 999 Costochondral tenderness + sacroiliitis/uveitis/IBD Seronegative spondyloarthropathy Rheumatology referral --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Costochondritis does not directly fit Maitland's intervertebral movement assessment - However, thoracic spine hypomobility at the costovertebral joints T2–T7 may contribute to anterior chest wall pain - Assess PA central and unilateral pressures at mid-thoracic spine - Rib mobilisation PA on rib angle posteriorly may reduce anterior chest wall pain - Evaluate costo-sternal joint mobility directly cautious anterior pressure on costal cartilage McKenzie/MDT Framework - Thoracic kyphosis correction may reduce sternal/costo-sternal compression anteriorly - Extension exercises thoracic extension over foam roller, doorway pectoral stretches open the anterior chest - Useful when combined with poor posture forward head, protracted shoulder girdle as contributing factor - Patient education: postural correction, activity modification avoid provocative movements during acute phase Pattern Recognition - Mechanical costochondritis: Reproducible with palpation, positional, worse with specific movements/activities; better with rest; no cardiac risk factors - Inflammatory costochondritis spondyloarthropathy : Bilateral, insidious onset, morning stiffness, associated HLA-B27 features, elevated CRP/ESR - Post-infectious: Following viral URTI/cough; diffuse, bilateral, settles over 4–12 weeks - Post-traumatic: Direct blow or sternotomy; localised, appropriate history --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Costochondritis --------- ------------- ------ ---------------------- NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain measure PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Activities limited by anterior chest wall pain Chest Pain Questionnaire Not widely validated for MSK chest pain — Consider GPE/GRC as functional measure Global Rating of Change GRC –7 to +7 Likert +2 to +3 Overall recovery SF-36 / EQ-5D-5L Quality of life EQ-5D MCID 0.037 If chronic/persistent >3 months --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic Criteria There are no validated formal diagnostic criteria for costochondritis. Diagnosis is clinical: 1. Chest pain that is reproducible with palpation of costochondral/costo-sternal junctions 2. No swelling swelling = Tietze syndrome 3. Exclusion of cardiac, pulmonary, and GI causes 4. Pain reproducible with trunk movements or deep inspiration Systematic Review Evidence - Disla E et al. 1994 : Prospective study of 122 patients presenting to ED with chest pain — 30% had reproducible chest wall tenderness; however, 6% of those also had concurrent MI → chest wall tenderness does NOT exclude ACS - Fruergaard P et al. 1996 : 204 patients with acute chest pain — 13% diagnosed with costochondritis/musculoskeletal cause after cardiac exclusion - Levy MJ 2021 : Systematic review of MSK chest pain — costochondritis most common MSK diagnosis; resolution in most cases within 12 months Imaging - Generally not indicated for straightforward presentation - CXR: Required if pulmonary cause not excluded; normal in costochondritis - ECG: Mandatory in any chest pain presentation — to exclude ACS - Cardiac troponin / D-dimer: If clinical presentation raises ACS/PE concern GP/ED decision - Ultrasound: May show costochondral joint hypoechogenicity in Tietze syndrome; limited for costochondritis - Bone scan / MRI: If malignancy or stress fracture suspected; increased uptake in Tietze on bone scan --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Acute Coronary Syndrome Central/crushing, diaphoresis, ECG changes, troponin rise; NOT position-dependent; not reproducible with palpation Pericarditis Pleuritic chest pain, worse lying flat, better leaning forward; pericardial rub; ECG changes saddle ST Pulmonary Embolism Pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, hypoxia, Wells score, D-dimer, CTPA Pneumonia / Pleuritis Fever, productive cough, reduced air entry; CXR consolidation Aortic Dissection Sudden severe tearing pain, BP differential, haemodynamic instability Rib Fracture History of trauma, bony tenderness, X-ray/CT confirmation Tietze Syndrome Visible/palpable swelling at costochondral junction; localised Herpes Zoster Shingles Dermatomal burning pain, vesicular rash may precede rash by 3–7 days Seronegative Spondyloarthropathy Bilateral chest wall pain, morning stiffness, sacroiliitis, enthesopathy, HLA-B27 Fibromyalgia Widespread pain, multiple tender points, fatigue, poor sleep Gastro-oesophageal reflux Burning, retrosternal, relation to meals, improved with antacids Oesophageal spasm Severe, episodic, can mimic cardiac; relieved by GTN problematic for diagnosis Intercostal neuralgia Band-like, dermatomal, often post-herpetic --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community: - GP assessment mandatory to exclude cardiac/pulmonary causes ECG, CXR, clinical assessment - Once excluded → community physiotherapy referral self-referral or GP referral - Typically managed in community MSK physiotherapy across all HSC Trusts - If seronegative spondyloarthropathy suspected → rheumatology referral Secondary Care: - Rarely required for simple costochondritis - Rheumatology if inflammatory arthropathy suspected - Pain management referral if >3 months, severe, and not responding to conservative management - Orthopaedic/surgical referral not typically indicated Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade C limited RCTs; expert consensus : 1. Patient Education Grade A — expert consensus : - Benign, self-limiting condition; most resolve within 12 months - Activity modification during acute phase — avoid provocative heavy lifting, pushing, pulling - Avoid positions that stretch costochondral junctions e.g., reaching overhead during acute phase - Reassurance is a key therapeutic intervention — reduces anxiety-driven symptom amplification 2. Relative Rest then Graded Return to Activity: - Acute phase 0–2 weeks : Avoid provocative activities - Subacute phase 2–6 weeks : Gradual reintroduction of upper limb/thoracic activities - Return to sport/work: Progressive loading programme 3. Manual Therapy: - Thoracic joint mobilisation PA central/unilateral at mid-thoracic levels — may reduce referred anterior chest pain - Rib mobilisation posteroanterior on rib angles - Soft tissue therapy: pectoralis minor, intercostal muscles, sternalis 4. Exercise Therapy: - Thoracic extension exercises foam roller, doorway stretch - Pectoral stretching — cautious in acute phase - Deep breathing exercises diaphragmatic to maintain thoracic cage mobility - Gradual strengthening: scapular stabilisers, thoracic extensors 5. Physical Modalities: - TENS: May provide short-term pain relief Grade C - Ice/Heat: Patient preference; ice for acute inflammation, heat for chronic - Ultrasound: Limited evidence; may consider for Tietze syndrome 6. Acupuncture: Limited evidence; NICE supports acupuncture for chronic primary pain NICE NG193, 2021 Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs first-line : Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD with PPI cover — 2–4 weeks NICE NG59 - Topical NSAIDs: Diclofenac gel 3x/day — NICE preferred for localised musculoskeletal pain NICE NG59 ; fewer systemic side effects - Paracetamol: Limited evidence for musculoskeletal pain NICE NG59 but useful adjunct - Corticosteroid injection: Local corticosteroid methylprednisolone 20–40mg + local anaesthetic injection at costo-sternal junction — under GP/pain clinic guidance; useful for refractory cases. Evidence from case series Waldman SD, 2009 - Avoid long-term opioids for costochondritis — not indicated per NICE NG59 Onward Referral Criteria Back to GP urgent : - Any new cardiac/pulmonary red flag identified during physiotherapy assessment - Features suggesting inflammatory arthropathy bilateral, morning stiffness, sacroiliitis - No improvement after 6–8 weeks conservative management — consider imaging and bloods Rheumatology: - Suspected seronegative spondyloarthropathy - Bilateral costochondritis + elevated inflammatory markers Pain Management: - Persistent costochondritis >3 months unresponsive to conservative management - For consideration of corticosteroid injection or pain management programme Surgical rare : - Septic costochondritis — surgical debridement infectious disease/orthopaedic/thoracic surgery --- Key References 1. Saunders Elsevier. pp. 222–224. 5. Levy MJ, Fayaz A, Freemantle N, Howes N, Langford RM. 2010 . Randomised controlled feasibility trial of acupuncture for chronic pain in the emergency department. title: Scheuermann's Disease
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Scheuermann's disease Scheuermann's kyphosis; juvenile kyphosis is a structural developmental disorder characterised by anterior vertebral body wedging producing a rigid thoracic hyperkyphosis. It is the most common cause of structural kyphosis in adolescents. Diagnostic C
headings: Diagnostic Criteria Sorensen Criteria — 1964, widely accepted
Postural Kyphosis vs Scheuermann's: Key Differentiation
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Scheuermann's disease Scheuermann's kyphosis; juvenile kyphosis is a structural developmental disorder characterised by anterior vertebral body wedging producing a rigid thoracic hyperkyphosis. It is the most common cause of structural kyphosis in adolescents. Diagnostic Criteria Sorensen Criteria — 1964, widely accepted - ≥3 consecutive thoracic vertebrae with ≥5° of anterior wedging each - Associated with irregular vertebral endplates - Presence of Schmorl's nodes nuclear herniations through endplates - Kyphosis typically rigid does not correct fully with hyperextension Prevalence & Demographics - Prevalence: 1–8% of the general population Bradford DS, 1977; Lowe TG, 1990 - Onset: typically 10–15 years of age adolescent growth spurt - Male:female ratio: approximately 2:1 some studies suggest equal distribution - Peak deformity progression during adolescent growth spurt Risser stage 0–3 - Thoracic Scheuermann's most common T7–T9 most frequently involved apex - Lumbar Scheuermann's: Also described; causes low back pain; less common; wedging of lumbar vertebrae Relevant Anatomy - Ring apophysis of vertebral endplate is vulnerable during adolescent growth - During rapid growth, the apophysis is cartilaginous and susceptible to mechanical loading - Proposed mechanism: Disruption of endplate ring apophysis → irregular endplate → asymmetric loading → anterior growth retardation → vertebral wedging - Schmorl's nodes: Herniation of nucleus pulposus through weakened vertebral endplate → reactive sclerosis - Adjacent disc spaces often narrowed Aetiology Multifactorial — exact cause unknown - Genetic predisposition: Autosomal dominant inheritance suggested Halal F et al., 1978 - Mechanical loading: Repetitive flexion loading during growth agricultural work, physical labour — historical association - Collagen/endplate abnormality: Proposed defect in collagen matrix of endplate - Osteoporosis: Some evidence of reduced bone density in affected vertebrae - Tight hamstrings and hip flexors: Common associated finding; may contribute to compensatory thoracic kyphosis Natural History - Adolescents with 75° may cause cardiopulmonary compromise in severe cases - Curve progression after skeletal maturity is generally slow Note: Scheuermann's disease is primarily a clinical + radiological diagnosis . There are no specific orthopaedic special tests with published sensitivity/specificity data for this condition. The following assessments are used clinically. Clinical Assessment Findings Assessment Finding in Scheuermann's Clinical Significance ------------ -------------------------- ---------------------- Adam's Forward Bend Test Kyphosis does not correct rigid ; scoliosis screen simultaneously Differentiates structural from postural kyphosis; postural kyphosis corrects Prone Press-Up / Extension Test Kyphosis partially or fully corrects in postural kyphosis ; remains in Scheuermann's Key differentiating test from postural round back Wall Stand Test Cannot flatten thoracic spine against wall; persistent curve Quantifies rigidity of kyphosis Hamstring Length Assessment SLR Frequently tight 75° FVC/FEV1 if >80° kyphosis Postural Kyphosis vs Scheuermann's: Key Differentiation Feature Postural Kyphosis Scheuermann's Disease --------- ------------------- ---------------------- Corrects with extension Yes — fully No — partially or not at all Vertebral wedging X-ray No Yes ≥5° in ≥3 vertebrae Schmorl's nodes Absent Present Endplate irregularities Absent Present Pain Variable Typically thoracic/lumbar pain Age of onset Any Adolescence 10–15 years --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Rapidly progressive kyphosis in skeletally immature Aggressive structural deformity Urgent orthopaedic/spinal surgery referral Neurological symptoms weakness, paraesthesia, gait change Cord compression from severe kyphosis Urgent MRI + neurosurgical referral Bowel/bladder dysfunction Cord/conus compression Emergency neurosurgical referral Kyphosis with systemic features weight loss, fever Malignancy / infection / inflammatory disease Urgent investigation + specialist referral Kyphosis in a child 80° + exertional dyspnoea Cardiopulmonary compromise Respiratory assessment; refer cardiac/respiratory Kyphosis + skin changes café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas Neurofibromatosis Paediatric genetics/orthopaedic referral Kyphosis + restricted chest expansion + spinal inflammatory markers Ankylosing spondylitis Rheumatology referral Severe thoracic pain at site of kyphosis Acute Schmorl's node, fracture, disc herniation MRI thoracic spine --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Manual therapy has a role in Scheuermann's primarily for pain management and mobility not deformity correction in skeletal maturity - Assess PAIVMs at each thoracic level for localised stiffness and pain - Grade III–IV mobilisations at painful/restricted levels - Rib mobilisation at costovertebral joints often restricted secondary to kyphosis - Extension mobilisations: unilateral and central PA to promote extension - Manipulation Grade V : use with caution; deformity alters biomechanics McKenzie/MDT Framework - Primary approach in adolescent Scheuermann's: - Thoracic extension exercises as cornerstone of conservative management - Prone lying → prone on elbows → prone press-up progression - Seated extension over back of chair, foam roller extension - Active thoracic rotation in flexion/extension to maintain segmental mobility - Postural education and correction - Directional preference: extension consistently beneficial directional preference - McKenzie classification: mostly dysfunction syndrome fixed kyphotic deformity + postural syndrome overlay Bracing Framework Orthopaedic - Milwaukee brace cervico-thoraco-lumbar orthosis : traditional; poor compliance - Boston/TLSO brace : thoraco-lumbar-sacral orthosis; used for apex below T7 - Indication: Cobb angle 45–70° in skeletally immature patient Risser 0–3 - Duration: Full-time wear ~20–23 hours/day until skeletal maturity; then weaning - Evidence: Sachs B et al. 1987 — bracing effective in reducing progression; improvement of 40% in kyphotic angle achieved in some series - Physiotherapy role during bracing: maintain core strength, exercise in and out of brace --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Scheuermann's --------- ------------- ------ ---------------------- Cobb Angle X-ray Radiographic kyphosis measurement 5° change clinically meaningful Primary structural outcome; monitoring progression NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Pain management PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Functional activity limitations SRS-22 Scoliosis Research Society 22-item; 5 domains pain, function, self-image, mental health, satisfaction Domain-specific Best validated for spinal deformity in adolescents/adults ODI Oswestry Disability Index 10% Adult Scheuermann's with chronic pain/disability Chest expansion measurement Tape measure at 4th ICS; normal >5cm >1cm Severe kyphosis; respiratory monitoring Sagittal vertical axis SVA Radiographic global balance assessment — Surgical planning; >5cm positive SVA = surgical concern --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Radiographic Diagnosis Standard lateral thoracic X-ray standing, if possible confirms diagnosis: - Cobb angle of thoracic kyphosis normal 20–40° - Vertebral wedging anterior height 5°/year - Neurological involvement - NI referral: Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children RBHSC paediatric orthopaedics Secondary Care — Adult Orthopaedics/Spinal Surgery: - Refer adult patients with: - Severe kyphosis ≥75° with pain/functional limitation - Neurological compromise - Cardiopulmonary compromise - Surgical teams: Royal Victoria Hospital Belfast spinal surgery Conservative Management Exercise Therapy — Evidence Grade B: 1. Thoracic Extension Exercises Primary intervention : - Prone press-up McKenzie extension - Foam roller thoracic extension - Doorway/corner stretch bilateral shoulder external rotation + extension - Cat-camel mobilisation - Seated extension over chair back - Frequency: daily; 10–15 repetitions, 3 sets 2. Flexibility: - Hamstring stretching: Critical — address tight hamstrings to improve pelvic mechanics. Standing, supine, and neural-flossing techniques. Hold 30–45 seconds, 3–5 times/day - Hip flexor stretching: Thomas position, runner's lunge stretch - Pectoral stretching: Doorway stretch, foam roller bilateral arm extension 3. Strengthening: - Thoracic extensor strengthening: Prone cobras, back extensions hyperextension bench , rows, pull-aparts - Scapular retractors: Rows cable, band, dumbbell , face pulls, reverse flyes - Core stabilisation: Plank, bird-dog, dead bug — avoid excessive thoracic flexion loading - Respiratory training: Incentive spirometry, deep breathing — especially if chest expansion limited 4. Bracing Orthopaedic Prescription — Adolescents Only : - Indicated for Cobb angle 45–70° in skeletally immature Risser 0–3 - Milwaukee or TLSO brace prescribed and monitored by orthopaedics - Physiotherapy to support exercise compliance during bracing 5. Postural Education: - Ergonomics: desk height, monitor position, chair back support - Sleep position: no prone sleeping; supine with thoracic support - Self-monitoring of sitting posture Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD + PPI for pain during acute flares NICE NG59 - Topical NSAIDs: Diclofenac gel for localised thoracic pain NICE NG59 preferred for localised MSK - Paracetamol: Adjunct analgesia; limited evidence but commonly used - Vitamin D + Calcium: If bone density concerns / adolescent with restricted diet NICE NG187 — vitamin D supplementation - Avoid: Long-term NSAIDs in adolescents without gastroprotection; opioids not indicated Onward Referral Criteria Urgent: - Neurological deficit → MRI + neurosurgical referral - Severe cardiopulmonary compromise → respiratory/cardiac referral Elective Orthopaedic/Spinal Surgery: - Cobb angle >75° with pain/functional disability unresponsive to conservative management - Neurological compromise at any angle - Cosmetic deformity with significant psychosocial impact after skeletal maturity - Surgical technique: posterior spinal fusion most common ; occasionally combined anterior-posterior approach for rigid severe curves - Success rate: >85% correction maintained at 10 years Hosman AJF et al., 2002 --- Key References 1. Sorensen KH. 1964 . Scheuermann's Juvenile Kyphosis: Clinical Appearances, Radiology, Aetiology and Prognosis . Munksgaard, Copenhagen. 2. Bradford DS. 1977 . Juvenile kyphosis. Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research , 128, 45–55. 3. Lowe TG. 1990 . Scheuermann disease. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery American , 72 6 , 940–945. 4. Murray PM, Weinstein SL, Spratt KF. 1993 . The natural history and long-term follow-up of Scheuermann kyphosis. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery American , 75 2 , 236–248. 5. Sachs B, Bradford D, Winter R, Lonstein J, Moe J, Willson S. 1987 . Scheuermann kyphosis: follow-up of Milwaukee brace treatment. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery American , 69 1 , 50–57. 6. Halal F, Gledhill RB, Fraser C. 1978 . Dominant inheritance of Scheuermann's juvenile kyphosis. American Journal of Diseases of Children , 132 11 , 1105–1107. 7. Palazzo C, Sailhan F, Revel M. 2014 . Scheuermann's disease: an update. Joint Bone Spine , 81 3 , 209–214. 8. Weiss HR, Turnbull D. 2012 . Physical therapy and bracing in Scheuermann's kyphosis: current evidence and implications. Scoliosis , 7 Suppl 1 , O20. 9. Hosman AJF, Langeloo DD, De Kleuver M, Anderson PG, Veth RPH, Slot GH. 2002 . Analysis of the sagittal plane after surgical management for Scheuermann's disease: a view on overcorrection and the use of an anterior release. Spine , 27 2 , 167–175. 10. title: Thoracic Disc Herniation
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic disc herniation TDH is the displacement of disc material nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus, or both beyond the intervertebral space in the thoracic spine T1–T12 . While less common than cervical or lumbar disc herniation, TDH carries significant clinical importan
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic disc herniation TDH is the displacement of disc material nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus, or both beyond the intervertebral space in the thoracic spine T1–T12 . While less common than cervical or lumbar disc herniation, TDH carries significant clinical importance due to the proximity of the spinal cord and the risk of myelopathy. Prevalence - Symptomatic TDH accounts for approximately 0.25–0.75% of all symptomatic disc herniations Wood KB et al., 1997 - MRI studies report incidental TDH in 11–37% of asymptomatic individuals Wood KB et al., 1995 - Peak age: 40–60 years; slight male predominance - Most common levels: T8–T12 lower thoracic — 75% of symptomatic cases , particularly T11–T12 Mechanism & Pathophysiology - The thoracic spine is relatively immobile rib cage stabilisation , placing lower mechanical stress compared to cervical/lumbar regions - However, the thoracic spinal canal is narrow relative to cord diameter cord:canal ratio ~0.4–0.7 , meaning even small disc protrusions can cause significant myelopathy - Types: - Soft disc herniation: acute, traumatic — nucleus pulposus extrusion - Hard disc/calcified herniation: chronic degeneration, calcification — more common in thoracic region ~70% of symptomatic TDH - Direction: Central and centrolateral protrusions most clinically significant cord compression ; lateral protrusions cause radiculopathy Relevant Anatomy - Spinal cord occupies a larger proportion of the canal than in the lumbar spine - Blood supply: anterior spinal artery single vessel — risk of cord ischaemia with anterior compression - T1–T6: relatively fixed, rib articulations on both superior and inferior costovertebral joints - T10–T12: floating ribs, relatively more mobile, therefore more susceptible to degenerative disc disease --- Special Tests > Critical note: There are no validated specific orthopaedic tests for thoracic disc herniation comparable to lumbar provocative tests. Diagnosis is primarily clinical symptoms + neurological examination confirmed by MRI. The tests below assess for myelopathy or radiculopathy secondary to TDH. Tests for Thoracic Myelopathy Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Babinski Sign 0.50 0.98 25.0 0.51 Moderate Present if UMN lesion; highly specific for cord compression Hoffmann's Sign 0.58 0.98 29.0 0.43 Moderate Cervical/upper thoracic cord compression; flick middle finger DIP Clonus ankle/knee 0.13–0.31 0.97–0.99 4.0–10.3 0.70–0.89 Low–Moderate Sustained clonus >5 beats pathological; indicates UMN lesion Lhermitte's Sign 0.27 0.97 9.0 0.75 Low–Moderate Electric shock sensation down spine/limbs with neck flexion; not thoracic-specific Hyperreflexia lower limb 0.78 0.61 2.0 0.36 Low UMN pattern below level of lesion Loss of Proprioception lower limb Variable Variable — — Expert opinion Posterior column involvement; assess with Romberg's test Romberg's Test 0.75 0.90 7.5 0.28 Low Posterior column dysfunction; positive if sways more with eyes closed For radiculopathy component: Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Kemp's Test thoracic Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion only Thoracic Slump Test Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion; neural tension test for thoracic levels Rib Spring posteroanterior pressure Not validated Not validated — — Clinical utility; pain reproduction at affected level References for myelopathy tests: Cook CE & Hegedus EJ. 2013 . Orthopedic Physical Examination Tests: An Evidence-Based Approach . Pearson; Tong HC et al. 2002 . Spine . --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Bilateral lower limb weakness / paraparesis Cord compression / myelopathy Emergency MRI + neurosurgical referral Bowel or bladder dysfunction retention or incontinence Cord compression / cauda equina-equivalent Emergency neurosurgical referral same day Saddle anaesthesia Conus medullaris compression Emergency referral Progressive gait disturbance / ataxia Myelopathy Urgent MRI within 24–48 hours Night pain, constant pain, systemically unwell Malignancy / metastatic disease Urgent MRI + bloods PSA, CEA, ESR, CRP, calcium, alkaline phosphatase Age >50, history of malignancy Metastatic cord compression MSCC Same-day oncological assessment; refer to MSCC coordinator per NICE NG23 Fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression + back pain Discitis / epidural abscess Urgent MRI + bloods WCC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures ; admit Trauma + thoracic pain Fracture / instability X-ray ± CT; immobilise if instability suspected Thoracic pain + hypotension + pulsatile mass Aortic aneurysm/dissection 999 — Emergency vascular Unexplained weight loss + thoracic pain Malignancy 2-week-wait GP referral --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Passive accessory intervertebral movements PAIVMs at suspected level s : posteroanterior PA central and unilateral pressures - Passive physiological intervertebral movements PPIVMs : flexion, extension, rotation, lateral flexion - Note: with myelopathy, avoid forceful manipulations — Grade I–II mobilisations only pending MRI - Establish comparable sign symptom-reproducing movement then reassess after intervention - Maitland grades III–IV for pain-dominant non-myelopathic TDH McKenzie/MDT Framework - Postural assessment: thoracic kyphosis assessment, correction of slouched sitting - Directional preference: thoracic extension exercises may centralise or reduce symptoms in discogenic pain - Extension bias: thoracic extension in prone press-up , standing extension over foam roller - Contraindicated if extension worsens/peripheralises symptoms — reassess direction - Flexion bias less common in thoracic disc, but assess systematically - Relevant for lower thoracic levels T10–T12 with lumbar-type presentation Pattern Recognition Approach - Myelopathic pattern: UMN signs below lesion level spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski , bilateral involvement, gait disturbance — refer urgently - Radiculopathic pattern: Band-like chest/abdominal pain following dermatomal distribution, unilateral, neurological signs at level - Discogenic/mechanical pattern: Central thoracic pain, worse with flexion/loading, improved with extension — conservative management appropriate --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in TDH --------- ------------- ------ ------------ NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 Primary pain outcome Oswestry Disability Index ODI 10-item back-specific disability 10–12 points 10% Widely used for spinal conditions including thoracic PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Individualised functional limitation Modified JOA Score for myelopathy Japanese Orthopaedic Association score for myelopathy Variable Post-surgical outcome for myelopathy Nurick Classification Myelopathy severity grading 0–5 — Clinical grading for myelopathic presentation EQ-5D-5L Generic health-related quality of life 0.037 NICE/NHS recommended outcome for cost-effectiveness GRC Global Rating of Change –7 to +7 +2 to +3 Patient-perceived recovery --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical Diagnosis - Diagnosis is made by clinical examination + MRI - Physical examination alone is insufficient; MRI is the investigation of choice - High incidence of asymptomatic MRI findings means clinical correlation is essential Imaging Guidelines - MRI thoracic spine: Gold standard — assess disc morphology, cord signal change T2 hyperintensity indicates myelopathy , degree of canal compromise - CT myelography: Alternative when MRI contraindicated; better for calcified disc - Plain X-ray: Limited utility; may show disc space narrowing, calcification, kyphosis — not diagnostic - CT without contrast: Useful for identifying calcified disc important for surgical planning — calcification changes surgical approach risk Key Evidence - Wood KB et al. 1995 demonstrated 37% prevalence of TDH on MRI in 90 asymptomatic volunteers — underscoring need for clinical correlation - Stillerman CB et al. 1998 : Retrospective review of 82 surgically treated TDH — 76% presented with myelopathy or mixed myeloradiculopathy; conservative management successful in mild cases - Bouthors C et al. 2018 : 10-year outcomes study — myelopathic TDH rarely improves without surgical decompression; 75% surgical success rate - No Level 1 RCT evidence exists for conservative vs surgical management of TDH --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Thoracic facet joint pain Localised paraspinal tenderness, no neurological signs, no imaging changes Intercostal neuralgia Band-like pain, dermatomal, often post-herpetic; no cord signs Scheuermann's disease Young patients, kyphotic deformity, wedge vertebrae on X-ray Costochondritis Anterior chest pain, point tenderness on rib/costal cartilage Cardiac ischaemia / angina Mid-sternal chest pain, exertional, ECG changes, troponin elevation Aortic dissection Sudden severe tearing pain, BP differential between arms, haemodynamic instability Oesophageal pathology Pain related to swallowing, GORD symptoms, relieved by antacids Metastatic spinal disease Known malignancy, constant night pain, bone destruction on imaging Multiple sclerosis Relapsing-remitting neurological symptoms, positive Lhermitte's, MRI plaques Spinal cord tumour ependymoma/astrocytoma Progressive myelopathy, MRI intrinsic cord lesion with enhancement Osteoporotic fracture Post-menopausal female, acute onset, deformity, DEXA scan osteoporosis --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community Physiotherapy: - Suitable for non-myelopathic TDH with manageable pain - GP referral to community MSK physiotherapy or direct access where available - Red flag screen mandatory at first assessment - If any UMN signs, bowel/bladder involvement → same-day emergency neurosurgical referral Royal Victoria Hospital Belfast / Altnagelvin Secondary Care: - Orthopaedic/neurosurgical referral for surgical consideration in: - Myelopathy progressive or moderate-severe - Failure of ≥6 weeks conservative management with severe radiculopathy - Significant canal compromise on MRI >50% canal occlusion - Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression MSCC coordinator contact: per NICE NG23; NI MSCC pathway via Belfast City Hospital oncology Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade C limited high-quality RCTs : 1. Education: Natural history majority of non-myelopathic TDH improves with time , activity modification, load management 2. Posture & ergonomics: Thoracic extension exercises, postural correction to reduce disc loading — especially lower thoracic levels 3. Manual therapy: Grade I–II Maitland mobilisations for pain relief; avoid Grade V manipulation without myelopathy exclusion. Soft tissue techniques to thoracic paraspinals, erector spinae 4. Thoracic extension exercises: McKenzie extension exercises, foam roller thoracic extension, seated thoracic rotation — for non-myelopathic cases 5. Neural mobilisation: Thoracic Slump sliders for radiculopathic presentation 6. Core stability: Graduated programme targeting deep thoracic/lumbar stabilisers — avoid high-load flexion exercises 7. Hydrotherapy: Buoyancy-assisted exercise — lower thoracic/mild cases Duration: 6–12 weeks conservative management before surgical re-evaluation in non-myelopathic cases. Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - Analgesia Step 1 : Paracetamol 1g QDS limited evidence for back pain — NICE NG59 - NSAIDs Step 2 : Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD with PPI NICE NG59 ; caution in renal impairment, cardiovascular disease, elderly - Neuropathic agents: Amitriptyline 10–75mg nocte or duloxetine 60–120mg daily for neuropathic/radicular pain NICE NG173 — note: pregabalin/gabapentin NOT first-line per NICE 2021 update without specialist advice - Opioids: Short-term weak opioids codeine ± paracetamol if NSAIDs insufficient — avoid long-term NICE NG59 - Oral corticosteroids: Short course dexamethasone 8mg daily reducing — may be used for acute myelopathic exacerbation pending neurosurgical review off-label; neurosurgery decision - Epidural steroid injection: Thoracic epidural under image guidance — specialist pain management referral; limited evidence Onward Referral Criteria Emergency same day : - Acute myelopathy with progressive paraparesis - Bowel/bladder dysfunction — neurosurgical emergency - Suspected MSCC NICE NG23 — refer within 24 hours to MSCC coordinator Urgent within 2 weeks : - Moderate myelopathy without emergency features - Failure of 4–6 weeks conservative management with significant disability Elective: - Persistent severe radiculopathy unresponsive to ≥12 weeks conservative management - Surgical options: thoracoscopic discectomy video-assisted , posterior laminectomy, transpedicular approach selected by neurosurgeon based on level and calcification --- Key References 1. content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic facet joint pain also termed thoracic zygapophyseal joint pain refers to pain arising from the synovial facet zygapophyseal joints of the thoracic spine. It is a recognised but frequently underdiagnosed cause of mid-back pain in the adult population. Prevalence - Estimated prevalence of thoracic facet joint pain in patients with thoracic back pain: 34–48% based on controlled diagnostic medial branch blocks Manchikanti L et al., 2007 - Cervical facet joint pain is better characterised; thoracic data extrapolated from cervical/lumbar literature - Can occur at any thoracic level; slightly more common at lower thoracic levels - Affects adults of all ages; increased prevalence with degenerative change in middle-older age Relevant Anatomy - Thoracic facet joints zygapophyseal joints are paired synovial joints between the superior and inferior articular processes of adjacent vertebrae - In the thoracic spine, the facet joints are oriented coronally frontal plane — approximately 60° from the horizontal — permitting rotation and lateral flexion, limiting flexion/extension - Each facet joint is innervated by the medial branch of the dorsal ramus from its own level and the level above dual innervation — basis for medial branch block diagnostic technique - Additionally, the thoracic spine has costovertebral joints articulations between rib head and vertebral body and costotransverse joints between rib tubercle and transverse process — these may also contribute to pain syndromes clinically overlapping with facet pain Mechanism & Aetiology - Degenerative: Articular cartilage loss, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis — most common in middle–older age - Postural: Prolonged thoracic flexion kyphotic postures, desk work loads posterior elements; increased facet joint compressive force in hyperkyphosis - Traumatic: Acute hyperextension or rotation injury whiplash-type mechanism , direct trauma - Inflammatory: Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis — facet joint synovitis - Acute locked facet meniscoid entrapment : Sudden onset acute thoracic pain following rotation — proposed entrapment of fibroadipose meniscoid structure within the joint --- Special Tests > Critical note: No single clinical test has been validated for thoracic facet joint pain with adequate sensitivity/specificity data. The gold standard for diagnosis is controlled comparative medial branch blocks two anaesthetics with different durations producing concordant relief . Clinical tests assist in identifying likely facet-mediated pain prior to diagnostic blocks. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Passive Accessory Intervertebral Movement PAIVM — PA Unilateral Not formally validated Not formally validated — — Expert consensus Unilateral PA on articular pillar reproducing concordant pain; primary clinical assessment tool Passive Physiological Intervertebral Movement PPIVM — Rotation Not formally validated Not formally validated — — Expert consensus Restricted painful rotation in direction of affected facet; compare bilaterally Kemp's Test Thoracic Extension-Rotation Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Extension combined with ipsilateral rotation loading facet joint; reproduces back ± referred pain Thoracic Extension Test Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Isolated extension reproducing posterior thoracic pain; suggests posterior element involvement Medial Branch Block diagnostic 0.92–0.96 for concordant ≥80% relief 0.72–0.82 controlled double block 3.3–5.3 0.05–0.10 High reference standard Diagnostic procedure; not a clinical test but the reference standard Maitland Assessment Findings Consistent with Facet Pain - Unilateral paraspinal tenderness at facet joint level - Restricted and painful thoracic rotation ipsilateral side - Positive PA unilateral accessory movement reproducing concordant pain - Often absent neurological signs References: Manchikanti L et al. 2007 . Pain Physician ; Bogduk N. 2011 . Practice Guidelines for Spinal Diagnostic and Treatment Procedures . --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Thoracic pain + fever + elevated inflammatory markers Septic arthritis of facet joint / discitis Urgent MRI + microbiology; admit Constant severe thoracic pain, worse lying Malignancy / metastatic disease Urgent MRI ± bone scan; bloods Age >50 + thoracic pain + history of malignancy Metastatic spinal disease Urgent oncology referral per NICE NG23 Thoracic pain + bilateral neurological signs Cord compression / myelopathy Emergency MRI Thoracic pain + bowel/bladder dysfunction Cord compression Emergency neurosurgical referral Sudden onset thoracic pain + haemodynamic compromise Aortic dissection / aneurysm 999 — Emergency Thoracic pain + weight loss + night sweats Malignancy / lymphoma Urgent GP referral / investigations Thoracic pain in patient with osteoporosis + acute onset Compression fracture X-ray / MRI Thoracic pain + morning stiffness >1 hour + bilateral Ankylosing spondylitis / axial SpA Rheumatology referral; HLAB27, MRI sacroiliac joints --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework Thoracic facet joint pain is highly amenable to the Maitland approach: Assessment: - PAIVMs: Central PA spinous process and unilateral PA articular pillar, 2–3cm lateral to spinous process — assess resistance, end-feel, and pain response. Grade I–IV on quality, resistance, and pain - PPIVMs: Rotation primary thoracic motion , lateral flexion — assess range, end-feel, symmetry - Comparable sign: Identify the movement/pressure that most closely reproduces the patient's concordant pain Treatment Grading: - Grade I–II: Pain dominant; oscillatory movements at start/middle of range acute/irritable presentation - Grade III–IV: Stiffness dominant; end-range mobilisation subacute/chronic presentation - Grade V manipulation : High-velocity low-amplitude thrust — for non-irritable stiff thoracic facet restriction; contraindications: osteoporosis, cord compression, instability, anticoagulation Reassessment: Always reassess comparable sign after each intervention. McKenzie/MDT Framework - Thoracic extension typically the directional preference in posterior element pain - Extension exercises: prone press-up, seated thoracic extension, foam roller extension - Correct flexion postures that load thoracic facets in extension gap - Education on postural modification — sustained flexion perpetuates facet joint stress - May classify as: dysfunction syndrome repeated extension exercises for restricted posterior elements or postural syndrome posture correction Bogduk's Approach Evidence-Based Diagnostic Framework - History-based clinical features alone have poor diagnostic accuracy for facet joint pain Bogduk N, 2011 - Controlled medial branch blocks remain the only validated diagnostic method - Clinical examination used to localise level s for diagnostic block - Identify: unilateral vs bilateral, acute vs chronic, suspected levels --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Facet Joint Pain --------- ------------- ------ ------------------------ NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain outcome PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Individualised functional activities Oswestry Disability Index ODI Validated for spinal pain/disability 10–12 points 10% Widely used; validated for thoracic use Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire RMDQ 24-item back-specific 2.5 points Alternative to ODI; shorter FABQ Fear Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire Physical activity and work subscales 11 pts physical ; 8 pts work Identifies psychosocial barriers to recovery GRC Global Rating of Change +2 to +3 Recovery perception Thoracic range of motion goniometry/inclinometry Objective movement measure Variable Reassessment of mobility gains --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Prevalence Studies - Manchikanti L et al. 2007 : Using controlled double diagnostic medial branch blocks, found 34–48% prevalence of thoracic facet joint pain in patients presenting with chronic thoracic pain. Pain Physician , 10 4 , 521–532. - Atluri S et al. 2011 : Systematic review — thoracic medial branch blocks have good diagnostic accuracy when controlled double-block paradigm used Atluri S et al., Pain Physician , 14 5 , E241–E264 Clinical Prediction Rules - No validated clinical prediction rule exists specifically for thoracic facet joint pain - Cervical and lumbar facet prediction rules exist but have not been validated at thoracic levels - Schwarzer AC et al. 1994 demonstrated that clinical features cannot reliably identify lumbar facet pain — likely applicable to thoracic spine Diagnostic Imaging - Plain X-ray: May show degenerative facet changes, spondylosis, kyphosis — not diagnostic for pain source - CT scan: Better visualisation of facet joint morphology, osteophytes — cannot confirm pain source - MRI: Superior soft tissue assessment; may show facet joint synovitis joint effusion, synovial thickening on T2 — poor correlation with pain in isolation - Bone scan SPECT : Increased uptake at facet joints in active degeneration; moderate diagnostic value — sensitivity ~70%, specificity ~65% Pneumaticos SG et al., 2006 - Diagnostic medial branch blocks: Gold standard; controlled comparative blocks with short-acting lidocaine and long-acting bupivacaine anaesthetic; ≥80% pain relief with concordant duration = positive diagnosis --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Thoracic disc herniation Central or paracentral pain, may have neurological signs; MRI confirms Thoracic radiculopathy Dermatomal band-like pain, neurological deficit; MRI ± NCS Costochondritis Anterior chest pain, costo-sternal junction tenderness Costovertebral joint pain Very lateral paraspinal pain, reproduced by rib mobilisation rather than PA facet pressure Scheuermann's disease Kyphotic deformity, wedge vertebrae on X-ray; younger patients Osteoporotic compression fracture Acute onset, female >60, DEXA confirms osteoporosis; MRI shows fracture Metastatic spinal disease Constant pain, night pain, systemic symptoms, bone destruction on imaging Ankylosing spondylitis Bilateral, morning stiffness, sacroiliitis, elevated CRP/ESR, HLA-B27 Rheumatoid arthritis Symmetrical joint involvement, rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP, systemic features Intercostal neuralgia Band-like dermatomal pain; post-herpetic; no movement reproduction Cardiac/visceral referred pain Not reproducible with spinal palpation/movement; associated systemic symptoms --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Community Physiotherapy First-line : - GP referral or self-referral to community MSK physiotherapy - Appropriate for straightforward mechanical thoracic facet joint pain with no red flags - Adequate trial: 6–8 sessions over 8–12 weeks Secondary Care: - Pain management referral if no improvement after 8–12 weeks conservative management - Medial branch blocks / radiofrequency denervation — referred to pain clinic Belfast City Hospital Pain Management Centre; Causeway/Altnagelvin for western HSC Trusts - Rheumatology if inflammatory arthropathy suspected Occupational Health: Ergonomic assessment for work-related thoracic pain especially sedentary workers with prolonged thoracic flexion Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade B–C: 1. Manual Therapy Grade B — moderate evidence : - Thoracic spine manipulation / high-velocity thrust HVLAT : moderate evidence for short-term pain reduction in thoracic pain Briggs AM et al., 2009 - Maitland Grade III–IV mobilisation at affected levels: well-supported in clinical practice; Grade I–II for irritable presentations - Rib mobilisation for costovertebral component - Contraindications to manipulation: osteoporosis, instability, cord signs, anticoagulation, inflammatory arthritis 2. Exercise Therapy Grade B : - Thoracic extension strengthening: prone cobra, scapular retraction, rowing exercises - Flexibility: thoracic rotation stretches, foam roller extension, lateral flexion stretches - Core stability: deep thoracic/lumbar stabiliser programme - Postural strengthening: lower trapezius, rhomboids, serratus anterior 3. Electrotherapy: - TENS: short-term pain relief, Grade C evidence NICE supports for chronic pain - Therapeutic ultrasound: insufficient evidence for recommendation 4. Education and Self-Management: - Ergonomics: workstation assessment, avoid prolonged thoracic flexion, screen height, chair lumbar support - Activity modification: pace activities, graded return to exercise - Reassurance: often resolves with appropriate management Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - Topical NSAIDs first-line : Diclofenac 1% gel TDS at painful area NICE NG59 — preferred for localised MSK pain - Oral NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD + PPI; 2–4 weeks NICE NG59 - Paracetamol: Adjunct; limited evidence for back pain per NICE - Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants: Amitriptyline 10–25mg nocte for chronic thoracic pain — off-label but supported by NICE NG193 for chronic primary pain - Avoid: Prolonged opioid use, benzodiazepines NICE NG59 Interventional Pain Clinic : - Medial branch blocks: Diagnostic and short-term therapeutic; methylprednisolone 20–40mg + local anaesthetic at thoracic medial branches image-guided - Radiofrequency denervation RFD / thermocoagulation: For confirmed facet joint pain ≥80% relief from dual medial branch blocks — evidence: Manchikanti L et al. 2012 — significant pain/function improvement at 1–2 years vs sham Level II evidence, Pain Physician - Intraarticular steroid injection: Moderate short-term benefit; less evidence than RFD for long-term relief Onward Referral Criteria Urgent: - Any red flag identified see above - Progressive neurological deficit → emergency To Pain Management Elective : - Failure of ≥8–12 weeks physiotherapy - High pain/disability burden suitable for diagnostic medial branch blocks - For consideration of RFD if blocks confirm diagnosis To Rheumatology: - Suspected inflammatory arthropathy bilateral, morning stiffness, elevated inflammatory markers Surgical: - Rarely indicated for isolated facet joint pain - Occasionally: spinal decompression if co-existing stenosis or spondylolisthesis --- Key References 1. Manchikanti L, Singh V, Pampati V, et al. 2007 . Prevalence of thoracic facet joint pain in chronic thoracic pain. Pain Physician , 10 4 , 521–532. 2. Atluri S, Datta S, Falco FJE, Lee M. 2011 . Systematic review of diagnostic utility and therapeutic effectiveness of thoracic facet joint interventions. Pain Physician , 14 5 , E241–E264. 3. Manchikanti L, Kaye AD, Boswell MV, et al. 2012 . A systematic review and best evidence synthesis of effectiveness of therapeutic facet joint interventions in managing chronic spinal pain. Pain Physician , 15 4 , E349–E404. 4. Bogduk N. 2011 . Practice Guidelines for Spinal Diagnostic and Treatment Procedures 2nd ed. . International Spine Intervention Society. 5. Schwarzer AC, Aprill CN, Derby R, Fortin J, Kine G, Bogduk N. 1994 . The false-positive rate of uncontrolled diagnostic blocks of the lumbar zygapophyseal joints. Pain , 58 2 , 195–200. 6. Pneumaticos SG, Chatziioannou SN, Hipp JA, Moore WH, Esses SI. 2006 . Low back pain: prediction of short-term outcome of facet joint injection with bone scintigraphy. Radiology , 238 2 , 693–698. 7. Briggs AM, Smith AJ, Straker LM, Bragge P. 2009 .
