title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic Outlet Syndrome TOS refers to a group of disorders caused by compression of the neurovascular structures brachial plexus, subclavian artery, subclavian vein as they pass through the thoracic outlet — the space between the clavicle, first rib, and scalene muscles.
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic Outlet Syndrome TOS refers to a group of disorders caused by compression of the neurovascular structures brachial plexus, subclavian artery, subclavian vein as they pass through the thoracic outlet — the space between the clavicle, first rib, and scalene muscles. Subtypes - Neurogenic TOS nTOS : ~95% of cases. Compression of the brachial plexus most commonly lower trunk C8–T1 . Presents with pain, paraesthesia, and weakness in the upper limb. - Venous TOS vTOS : ~4%. Subclavian vein compression; Paget-Schroetter syndrome effort thrombosis . Presents with arm swelling, cyanosis, distended veins. - Arterial TOS aTOS : ~1%. Subclavian artery compression; typically associated with a cervical rib. Presents with ischaemic symptoms, pallor, cold limb. Relevant Anatomy - Thoracic outlet consists of three potential compression zones: 1. Interscalene triangle anterior and middle scalene + first rib 2. Costoclavicular space clavicle + first rib + subclavius 3. Subpectoral/retropectoralis minor space Prevalence & Risk Factors - Estimated prevalence: 3–80 per 1,000 in the general population wide range due to diagnostic variability - Female:male ratio approximately 3.5:1 for nTOS - Peak onset: 20–50 years - Risk factors: cervical rib present in ~0.5–1% of population , anomalous first rib, scalene muscle hypertrophy, poor posture, repetitive overhead activity, trauma especially whiplash , and breast hypertrophy Mechanism Compression results in either direct mechanical compression of neural/vascular structures or ischaemic neuropathy. In nTOS, the lower trunk and medial cord of the brachial plexus C8, T1 are most commonly affected, producing ulnar-distribution symptoms. --- Special Tests > Note: Provocative tests for TOS have historically poor diagnostic accuracy. They are best interpreted in combination cluster approach with patient history. No single test is pathognomonic. Many studies are limited by lack of reference standard. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Adson's Test 0.79 0.76 3.29 0.28 Low–Moderate High false-positive rate; tests interscalene triangle; reproduces symptoms or abolishes radial pulse Wright's Hyperabduction Test 0.70 0.53 1.49 0.57 Low Tests subpectoral space; pulse obliteration unreliable as occurs in 60–70% asymptomatic individuals Roos Stress Test EAST – Elevated Arm Stress Test 0.82 0.59 2.00 0.30 Moderate 3-minute arm elevation with repeated hand opening/closing; reproducing symptoms more specific than pulse obliteration Costoclavicular Manoeuvre 0.53 0.68 1.66 0.69 Low Tests costoclavicular space; shoulders drawn back and downward Upper Limb Tension Test ULTT1/ULTT4 0.97 0.22 1.24 0.14 Low–Moderate for nTOS High sensitivity; poor specificity; useful for ruling OUT neurogenic component Spurling's Test 0.50 0.86 3.57 0.58 Moderate Differentiates cervical radiculopathy from TOS References: Hooper TL et al. 2010 . J Man Manip Ther ; Gillard J et al. 2001 . J Hand Surg ; Nord KM et al. 2008 review data. Recommended Test Cluster nTOS A positive diagnosis of nTOS requires ≥3 of the following Consensus criteria — Illig KA et al., 2010 : 1. Symptoms consistent with brachial plexus compression 2. Positive provocative testing EAST or ULTT 3. Response to scalene muscle block 4. Exclusion of other diagnoses --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Sudden severe arm pain + pallor + coldness Arterial TOS / acute limb ischaemia Emergency vascular referral 999/A&E Arm swelling + cyanosis + distended veins after exertion Venous TOS / Paget-Schroetter Urgent same-day vascular referral Horner's syndrome ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis Pancoast tumour / apical lung malignancy Urgent CXR + oncology referral Progressive neurological deficit Space-occupying lesion, cord compression Urgent MRI and neurology/neurosurgery Night sweats, unintentional weight loss, haematoptysis Malignancy Urgent GP referral / 2WW pathway Bilateral symptoms with spasticity Cervical myelopathy Urgent neurosurgical referral Cervical rib with pulsatile mass Subclavian artery aneurysm Emergency vascular review --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Assess accessory and physiological movements of the cervicothoracic junction C7–T1, T1–T4 , first rib mobility, and clavicular movement - Pain mapping: distinguish local thoracic outlet tenderness from peripheral neurological patterns - Grade III–IV mobilisations of the first rib posteroanterior, longitudinal caudad may decompress the interscalene triangle - Reassess neurodynamic sensitisation using ULTT after joint mobilisation McKenzie/MDT Framework - Postural assessment: forward head posture, rounded shoulders, thoracic kyphosis increase scalene tension and reduce outlet volume - McKenzie posture correction and extension exercises may reduce compression in costoclavicular and subpectoral spaces - Classify: postural syndrome vs dysfunction vs derangement though TOS rarely fits classical MDT subgroups - Sustained extension/retraction exercises as home exercise programme Pattern Recognition - Lower trunk brachial plexus pattern C8–T1 : medial forearm, ring/little finger paraesthesia, intrinsic hand weakness especially first dorsal interosseous - Differentiate from ulnar neuropathy at the elbow no neck/shoulder component, positive elbow provocation tests - Vascular pattern: positional symptoms, effort-induced, colour/temperature changes --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in TOS --------- ------------- ------ ------------ NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain outcome DASH / QuickDASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder and Hand 10.2 points DASH / 15.9 QuickDASH Upper limb function — well validated for TOS PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 3–5 activities 2.0 points Individualised functional goals UEFI Upper Extremity Functional Index 20-item self-report 9 points Alternative to DASH Global Rating of Change GRC –7 to +7 Likert scale +2 to +3 Perceived overall recovery Grip Strength dynamometry Hand dynamometry kg Variable Objective functional measure for nTOS --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic Criteria There is no validated gold-standard diagnostic test. The Consensus Statement Illig et al., 2010; endorsed by Society for Vascular Surgery recommends a clinical diagnosis based on: 1. Symptoms consistent with brachial plexus compression 2. Positive provocative test battery 3. Exclusion of other diagnoses cervical radiculopathy, rotator cuff pathology, carpal tunnel syndrome Imaging - CXR/Plain X-ray: First-line to identify cervical rib, elongated C7 transverse process, clavicle/first rib anomalies - MRI brachial plexus: Useful to exclude disc prolapse, Pancoast tumour; poor sensitivity for dynamic compression in TOS - CT angiography / Duplex ultrasound: For arterial/venous TOS with positional manoeuvres - Nerve Conduction Studies NCS / EMG: May show medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve abnormality in nTOS ~77–95% sensitivity in true nTOS per Machanic & Bhatt, 2017 ; however, many nTOS cases have normal NCS - Scalene Muscle Block diagnostic : Considered quasi-gold standard for nTOS; >50% symptom relief supports diagnosis Key Systematic Reviews - Povlsen B et al. 2014 . Cochrane Database : Insufficient RCT evidence to determine superiority of any intervention. - Hooper TL et al. 2010 . J Man Manip Ther 18 2 :74–83: Comprehensive review of diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests. --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Cervical radiculopathy C8/T1 Positive Spurling's, cervical movement provocation, dermatomal pattern; MRI cervical spine Ulnar neuropathy at elbow Positive elbow flexion provocation test, Tinel's at cubital tunnel; NCS localises lesion Carpal tunnel syndrome CTS Positive Phalen's/Tinel's at wrist; median nerve distribution; nocturnal symptoms typical Rotator cuff pathology Localised shoulder pain, positive impingement tests Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer , no neurological symptoms Cervical myelopathy Bilateral, lower limb involvement, Lhermitte's sign, pathological reflexes, Hoffman's sign Pancoast tumour Weight loss, haemoptysis, Horner's syndrome, CXR abnormality; urgent investigation required CRPS Type I Autonomic features sweating, colour change , allodynia; follows injury without nerve lesion Peripheral arterial disease Claudication, ankle-brachial index 15 mmHg between arms --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Community Physiotherapy Primary Care : - First-line management for suspected nTOS - Referral via GP or self-referral where available to community MSK physiotherapy - Initial assessment to exclude red flags and vascular/arterial TOS - Waiting times vary: typically 6–18 weeks community MSK in NI check local BHSCT/SEHSCT/NHSCT/SHSCT/WHSCT directory Secondary Care: - Refer to vascular surgery for arterial/venous TOS urgent if acute vascular compromise - Refer to neurology/orthopaedics/spinal surgery if myelopathy suspected - Consider referral to pain management if conservative management fails at 3–6 months - Scalene block may be arranged via pain clinic or vascular surgery NI — typically at RVH Belfast or Altnagelvin Occupational Health: - Workplace assessment and modification for occupational TOS repetitive overhead work, keyboard posture Conservative Management First-line Physiotherapy Evidence Grade B–C : 1. Postural re-education: Correct forward head posture, rounded shoulders, thoracic kyphosis. Evidence shows postural correction reduces outlet narrowing. Lindgren KA, 1997 2. Stretching: Scalene stretching anterior and middle , pectoralis minor stretching, levator scapulae. Hold 30–45 seconds, 3–5 repetitions, 2–3x/day. 3. Strengthening: Scapular stabiliser strengthening lower trapezius, serratus anterior . Progressive resistance programme over 6–8 weeks. 4. Neural mobilisation ULTT-based : Slider and tensioner techniques for brachial plexus. Evidence from Sanders RJ et al. 2010 . 5. First rib mobilisation/manipulation: PA mobilisations of first rib Grade III–IV Maitland . May improve interscalene space. Lindgren, 1997 6. Breathing retraining: Diaphragmatic breathing to reduce accessory breathing muscle scalene overuse. 7. Education: Activity modification, ergonomic advice, avoidance of provocative postures. Programme Duration: Minimum 6–8 weeks conservative physiotherapy before reassessment for further management. Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs: Short-term up to 4 weeks for pain management — ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD with PPI cover. NICE NG59 musculoskeletal pain - Neuropathic agents: Amitriptyline 10–25mg nocte or gabapentin 300mg TDS titrating for neurogenic symptoms — NICE NG173 neuropathic pain in adults - Muscle relaxants: Diazepam 2–5mg TDS short-term only, maximum 4 weeks for scalene spasm — use with caution - Anticoagulation: For venous TOS / Paget-Schroetter — managed by vascular team typically LMWH → warfarin or DOAC - Thrombolysis/anticoagulation: For acute vTOS — vascular surgery decision Onward Referral Criteria Urgent same-day/within 24 hours : - Acute limb ischaemia arterial TOS — 6 Ps: pallor, pulselessness, pain, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold - Acute axillo-subclavian vein thrombosis with significant swelling Urgent within 2 weeks : - Suspected Pancoast tumour Horner's + shoulder/arm pain + weight loss/haemoptysis - Progressive neurological deficit Elective Referral 6–12 weeks : - Failure of ≥3 months conservative physiotherapy - Confirmed cervical rib with ongoing symptoms — vascular surgery for consideration of rib resection/first rib resection - Diagnostic scalene block — pain clinic/vascular surgery referral Surgical Options vascular surgery decision : - First rib resection transaxillary or supraclavicular approach - Scalenectomy - Cervical rib resection - Venous decompression + thrombolysis for vTOS --- Key References 1. Hooper TL, Denton J, McGalliard MK, Brismée JM, Sizer PS. 2010 . Thoracic outlet syndrome: a controversial clinical condition. Part 1: anatomy, and clinical examination/diagnosis. Journal of Manual & Manipulative Therapy , 18 2 , 74–83. 2. Illig KA, Donahue D, Duncan A, et al. 2010 . Reporting standards of the Society for Vascular Surgery for thoracic outlet syndrome. Journal of Vascular Surgery , 52 6 , 1634–1636. 3. Povlsen B, Belzberg A, Hansson T, Dorsi M. 2014 . Treatment for thoracic outlet syndrome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews , Issue 11. CD007218. 4. Sanders RJ, Hammond SL, Rao NM. 2007 . Diagnosis of thoracic outlet syndrome. Journal of Vascular Surgery , 46 3 , 601–604. 5. Gillard J, Pérez-Cousin M, Hachulla E, et al. 2001 . Diagnosing thoracic outlet syndrome: contribution of provocative tests, ultrasonography, electrophysiology, and helical computed tomography in 48 patients. Joint Bone Spine , 68 5 , 416–424. 6. Machanic BI, Bhatt DL. 2017 . Nerve conduction studies in neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome. Journal of Vascular Surgery , 65 4 , 1060–1065. 7. NICE guideline NG59 2016 . Musculoskeletal conditions . National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. 8. NICE guideline NG173 2020 . Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management in non-specialist settings . NICE. 9. Lindgren KA. 1997 . Conservative treatment of thoracic outlet syndrome: a 2-year follow-up. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation , 78 4 , 373–378. 10. Nord KM, Kapoor P, Fisher J, et al. 2008 . False positive rate of thoracic outlet syndrome diagnostic maneuvers. Electromyography and Clinical Neurophysiology , 48 2 , 67–74.

It is significantly less common than cervical or lumbar radiculopathy,

Diabetic Thoracic Radiculopathy Diabetic Truncal Neuropathy
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic radiculopathy refers to pain and/or neurological dysfunction attributable to irritation or compression of a thoracic nerve root as it exits the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramen. It is significantly less common than cervical or lumbar radiculopathy, partly because the thoracic spine has less mobility and is stabilised by the rib cage, resulting in less disc degeneration and foraminal narrowing. Prevalence - Thoracic radiculopathy is rare in isolation — estimated at Critical note: There are very limited validated clinical tests specifically for thoracic radiculopathy. The thoracic spine lacks equivalent validated provocative tests to the SLR lumbar or Spurling's cervical . Diagnosis is primarily clinical dermatomal distribution + symptom pattern supported by MRI and nerve conduction studies. Available Clinical Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Thoracic Slump Test Limited data one small study Limited data — — Expert opinion Neural tension test for thoracic nerve roots; overpressure in slump + thoracic extension/rotation reproducing dermatomal symptoms Kemp's Test Thoracic Not formally validated Not formally validated — — Expert opinion Extension + ipsilateral rotation + compression at thoracic level; reproduces radicular pain Deep Tendon Reflexes abdominal Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Upper abdominal T7–T9 , lower abdominal T10–T12 reflexes — assessed by skin stimulation; loss suggests root pathology Dermatomal Sensation Testing Not validated as standalone Not validated — — Standard practice Pinprick and light touch in thoracic dermatomal pattern; lateralisation and level identification Intercostal Rib Palpation tender nerve in groove Not validated Not validated — — Expert opinion Palpation along inferior rib border reproducing radicular pain in dermatomal distribution Chest Expansion / Deep Breath Provocation Not validated Not validated — — Expert opinion Exacerbation of band-like pain with deep inspiration suggests intercostal nerve/root irritation Key diagnostic tool: MRI thoracic spine — assesses nerve root compression, foraminal stenosis, disc herniation, cord signal change. Nerve conduction studies / EMG: Limited utility for thoracic radiculopathy intercostal muscles technically difficult to assess ; however, paraspinal EMG may show denervation at affected level. NCS for associated limb pathology useful for differential diagnosis. --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Bilateral band-like thoracic pain + leg weakness + spasticity Myelopathy cord involvement, not purely radiculopathy Emergency MRI + neurosurgical referral Bowel/bladder dysfunction Cord or conus medullaris involvement Emergency neurosurgical referral Thoracic dermatomal pain + known malignancy Metastatic nerve root compression Same-day oncology/MSCC coordinator NICE NG23 Thoracic pain + fever + immunosuppression Herpes zoster, epidural abscess, discitis Urgent: antiviral if vesicular rash; MRI if no rash Vesicular rash in thoracic dermatome Herpes zoster — refer to GP for antiviral within 72 hours GP same-day Thoracic radiculopathy + unexplained weight loss, night sweats Malignancy 2WW GP referral + urgent imaging Thoracic pain + postural hypotension + abdominal pain Aortic aneurysm / dissection 999 Uncontrolled diabetes + thoracic pain + abdominal wall weakness Diabetic thoracic radiculopathy GP referral; exclude other causes first Severe, rapidly progressive neurological deficit Space-occupying lesion; vascular Emergency neurosurgery Thoracic pain in child/adolescent Scheuermann's, tumour, infection Paediatric orthopaedic referral --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Assess thoracic spine segmentally: PAIVMs central and unilateral at suspected root level s and adjacent levels - Identify comparable sign: movement or pressure reproducing concordant radicular symptoms - Rib mobility: assess costovertebral/costotransverse joints — may contribute to foraminal narrowing via rib head position - Neural tension: Thoracic Slump test — assess neural mechanosensitivity; distinguish peripheral sensitisation from local mechanical compression - Treatment: Grade I–II oscillatory mobilisations to reduce pain and neural sensitivity; Grade III–IV for foraminal mobility once irritability assessed - Caution: avoid mobilisations that peripheralise symptoms McKenzie/MDT Framework - Perform systematic assessment of directional preference - Thoracic extension commonly reduces discogenic radiculopathy centralisation - Lateral shift correction if present lateral disc herniation with nerve root displacement - If symptoms centralise with extension: progressive extension programme McKenzie Protocol - If extension worsens/peripheralises: flexion or lateral bias assessment; may indicate foraminal pathology - Education: avoidance of sustained flexion postures increase disc/nerve pressure Neurodynamic Framework Butler/Shacklock - Thoracic radiculopathy produces mechanosensitivity of the thoracic nerve roots and intercostal nerves - Slump Sliders grade I : Gentle rhythmic neural mobilisation — alternating cervical flexion/extension with knee extension to create sliding motion of neural tissue - Tensioners: Held-end-range for more established mechanical adherence use with caution in acute phase - Combined with spinal mobilisation to address the joint component --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Thoracic Radiculopathy --------- ------------- ------ ------------------------------- NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain outcome PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Individualised activities affected by radiculopathy ODI Oswestry Disability Index 10 items 10% Disability measure — validated for spinal pain Neuropathic Pain Scale NPS 10-item scale for neuropathic qualities burning, electric, etc. Variable Characterises neuropathic component DN4 Questionnaire 7-item neuropathic screening tool Score ≥4 suggests neuropathic Identifies neuropathic pain component sensitivity 0.83, specificity 0.90 Global Rating of Change GRC –7 to +7 +2 to +3 Recovery perception EQ-5D-5L Generic HRQoL 0.037 NICE-recommended for cost-effectiveness monitoring --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic Approach 1. History: Band-like, dermatomal chest/abdominal pain; unilateral; aggravated by thoracic movement, deep inspiration, cough; may have history of disc herniation, fracture, herpes zoster, diabetes, or malignancy 2. Neurological Examination: Dermatomal sensory change hypoaesthesia/hyperaesthesia , abdominal reflex loss, focal muscle wasting rare 3. MRI Thoracic Spine: Primary investigation — identifies structural cause disc, osteophyte, fracture, tumour ; cord signal change indicates myelopathy change management 4. EMG/NCS: Limited but paraspinal EMG can show denervation at affected levels; rules out more distal nerve pathology 5. Serological: HbA1c diabetic radiculopathy , ESR/CRP infection/inflammatory , PSA/protein electrophoresis malignancy , VZV serology/PCR herpes zoster Herpes Zoster — Critical Consideration - Herpes zoster shingles reactivation in thoracic ganglia is the most common cause of acute thoracic dermatomal pain in adults - Pain typically precedes the vesicular rash by 3–7 days — during this window, presentation is identical to mechanical thoracic radiculopathy - Always ask: previous chickenpox, immunocompromised state, age >60 - If suspected: Same-day GP referral for antiviral prescription aciclovir 800mg 5x/day or valaciclovir 1g TDS for 7 days — most effective within 72 hours of rash onset NICE CKS Shingles - Post-herpetic neuralgia PHN : Persistent pain >3 months after rash resolution; gabapentin/amitriptyline first-line NICE NG173 Diabetic Thoracic Radiculopathy Diabetic Truncal Neuropathy - Rare; presents as unilateral or bilateral abdominal/thoracic pain and weakness - Associated with abdominal wall bulge muscle atrophy T6–T12 - Often presents in middle-aged males with poorly controlled diabetes - Diagnosis: clinical + EMG; MRI normal - Management: glycaemic control; neuropathic pain agents; physiotherapy --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Herpes zoster shingles Dermatomal burning pain ± vesicular rash; VZV serology; older/immunocompromised Thoracic disc herniation MRI confirms; may present with myelopathy cord signs Intercostal neuralgia post-herpetic Post-rash chronic pain; allodynia in dermatomal distribution Costochondritis Anterior chest wall, costo-sternal tenderness, no neurological signs Cardiac ischaemia Central, crushing; ECG/troponin changes; exertional Pulmonary embolism Pleuritic; dyspnoea; tachycardia; D-dimer/CTPA Aortic dissection Sudden severe tearing pain; BP differential; haemodynamic instability Biliary colic / cholecystitis Right upper quadrant, post-prandial; Murphy's sign; ultrasound Peptic ulcer disease Epigastric, food-related; H. pylori; endoscopy Renal colic Loin-to-groin pain; haematuria; non-positional; CT-KUB Pleuritis / pneumonia Fever, cough, reduced air entry; CXR abnormality Thoracic facet joint pain Paraspinal, localised; no dermatomal neurological signs; not true radiculopathy Diabetic truncal neuropathy Diabetes history; abdominal wall weakness; EMG confirms Metastatic spinal disease Night pain; weight loss; bone destruction; known primary Multiple sclerosis Lhermitte's; relapsing-remitting; MRI brain/spine plaques --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community: - GP assessment to exclude herpes zoster, cardiac, and pulmonary causes — mandatory - Herpes zoster → same-day antiviral prescription from GP - Mechanical thoracic radiculopathy → community physiotherapy referral self-referral or GP referral - Diabetic radiculopathy → GP/diabetology for glycaemic optimisation + physiotherapy - Malignancy/MSCC → NICE NG23 pathway; contact MSCC coordinator NI: Belfast City Hospital oncology Secondary Care: - MRI ordering GP or secondary care : consider for persistent radiculopathy >6 weeks unresponsive to conservative management - Neurosurgical referral: for confirmed compressive pathology on MRI with significant neurological deficit or myelopathy - Pain management: referral for thoracic epidural, nerve root injection, or management programme if conservative management fails at 3 months - NI Pain Management: Belfast City Hospital, Altnagelvin, Daisy Hill Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade C extrapolated from cervical/lumbar radiculopathy evidence : 1. Patient Education: - Natural history: most mechanical radiculopathies improve within 6–12 weeks - Pain neuroscience education PNE : address fear-avoidance, catastrophising - Activity modification: avoid sustained thoracic flexion, heavy lifting during acute phase - Positioning advice: pain-relieving positions, sleep posture 2. Neural Mobilisation: - Thoracic slump sliders — Grade I–II rhythmic neural mobilisation - Intercostal nerve mobilisation: side-lying ipsilateral lateral flexion away + rib spacing - Progress to tensioners when acute irritability settles - Butler DS 2000 — Mobilisation of the Nervous System: neural sliding techniques 3. Manual Therapy: - Grade I–II Maitland mobilisations at affected level pain-dominant/acute phase - Grade III–IV mobilisation for foraminal restriction subacute/chronic phase - Rib mobilisation: costovertebral joints may contribute to foraminal dynamics - Avoid Grade V manipulation in acute radiculopathy with neurological signs 4. Exercise Therapy: - McKenzie extension programme if directional preference confirmed - Thoracic stabiliser strengthening progressive — avoid painful loading - Postural correction: scapular retractors, thoracic extensors 5. TENS / Electrotherapy: - TENS for pain relief in acute neuropathic pain Grade C - Acupuncture: NICE NG193 supports for chronic primary pain Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs: Short-term 2–4 weeks — ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD + PPI NICE NG59 - Neuropathic Pain first-line per NICE NG173 : - Amitriptyline 10mg nocte titrating to 25–75mg — evidence Grade B - Duloxetine 60mg daily titrate from 30mg — evidence Grade B - Gabapentin 300mg TDS titrate — evidence Grade B; note 2019 controlled drug scheduling Schedule 3 - Pregabalin 75–300mg BD — evidence Grade B; also Schedule 3 controlled drug - Antiviral Herpes Zoster : Aciclovir 800mg 5x/day × 7 days OR valaciclovir 1g TDS × 7 days — most effective within 72 hours of rash; reduces PHN risk NICE CKS - Corticosteroids: Oral prednisolone 40mg/day 5-day reducing course — acute severe radiculopathy; limited evidence; off-label - Topical: Lidocaine patches or capsaicin cream 0.025–0.075% for localised neuropathic thoracic pain — NICE NG173 supports as adjunct Interventional Pain Clinic : - Thoracic nerve root injection TNRI / epidural: Methylprednisolone 40–80mg + local anaesthetic — image-guided fluoroscopy or CT ; short-to-medium term pain reduction; limited RCT evidence at thoracic level; risk of cord trauma → high expertise required - Pulsed radiofrequency PRF of dorsal root ganglion: Emerging evidence for refractory radiculopathy NICE IPGS; specialist pain service decision Onward Referral Criteria Emergency: - Myelopathy bilateral signs, cord compression - Bowel/bladder dysfunction - MSCC per NICE NG23 Urgent within 2 weeks : - Progressive neurological deficit - Severe refractory pain with MRI-confirmed compressive lesion - Suspected malignancy Elective 3–6 months : - Failure of conservative management with confirmed compressive pathology - Pain management referral for nerve root injection / PRF consideration - Post-herpetic neuralgia >3 months → pain management NICE NG173 --- Key References 1. The Sensitive Nervous System . NOI Group Publications, Adelaide. 3. Koes BW, van Tulder M, Peul W. 2007 . Diagnosis and treatment of sciatica. BMJ , 334 7607 , 1313–1317. title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Carpal tunnel syndrome CTS is the most common peripheral entrapment neuropathy, affecting 3–6% of the general population and up to 15% of specific occupational groups. It results from compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel — a rigid fibro-os
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Carpal tunnel syndrome CTS is the most common peripheral entrapment neuropathy, affecting 3–6% of the general population and up to 15% of specific occupational groups. It results from compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel — a rigid fibro-osseous canal bounded by the carpal bones posteriorly and the flexor retinaculum anteriorly. Pathophysiological mechanisms: - Elevated intracarpal tunnel pressure normal ~7 mmHg; symptomatic CTS typically >30 mmHg - Ischaemia of the median nerve epineurium → demyelination → axonal degeneration in severe cases - Mechanical deformation of axons with repetitive wrist flexion/extension - Inflammatory oedema of tenosynovium especially in secondary CTS Risk factors: - Female sex 3:1 female:male ratio ; peak incidence 40–60 years - Pregnancy transient, resolves postpartum in ~50% - Obesity BMI >30 doubles risk - Diabetes mellitus metabolic neuropathy compounds compression - Hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly - Repetitive hand/wrist use vibrating tools, keyboard work — moderate evidence - Previous distal radius fracture Colles' fracture - Haemodialysis amyloid deposition Anatomical variants: Bifid median nerve and persistent median artery increase compression risk and complicate surgical release. --- Special Tests > All values referenced against nerve conduction studies NCS as gold standard unless otherwise stated. Test How to Perform Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ --------------- ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Phalen's Test Passive wrist flexion ≥60° for 60 sec; positive = symptom reproduction 0.68 0.73 2.52 0.44 High meta-analysis, Wilder 2010 Tinel's Sign Percussion over carpal tunnel at wrist crease; positive = paraesthesia in median distribution 0.50 0.77 2.17 0.65 High meta-analysis, Wilder 2010 Durkan's Carpal Compression Test Direct thumb pressure over carpal tunnel for 30 sec; positive = symptom reproduction 0.87 0.90 8.70 0.14 High Durkan 1991; replicated Gonzalez 2002 Hand Elevation Test Both hands elevated above head for 2 min; positive = symptom reproduction 0.75 0.98 37.5 0.26 Moderate Ahn 2001 Flick Sign Patient reports relief of nocturnal symptoms by flicking/shaking the hand 0.93 0.96 23.3 0.07 Moderate Pryse-Phillips 1984 Two-Point Discrimination Static 2PD >6 mm on volar fingertip median distribution 0.33 0.99 33.0 0.68 Moderate severe/advanced CTS Thenar Wasting Visual/palpable atrophy of APB 0.19 0.99 19.0 0.82 Low late sign — indicates axonal loss Clinical note: Durkan's compression test has the best combination of sensitivity and specificity among physical examination tests. The Hand Elevation Test has exceptional specificity 0.98 — a positive result is strongly predictive. The Flick Sign, while poorly studied, has high reported accuracy and is highly patient-specific. Sensory distribution to confirm: Thumb, index, middle finger, radial half of ring finger palmar surface . Dorsal surface of distal phalanges. Sparing of thenar eminence palmar cutaneous branch exits proximal to carpal tunnel . --- Red Flags > Immediate escalation required if any present - Thenar muscle wasting — indicates chronic axonal loss; urgent NCS + surgical referral - Complete median nerve motor loss APB weakness, inability to oppose — urgent referral - Bilateral acute onset — consider cervical myelopathy, systemic neuropathy - Night pain with constitutional symptoms weight loss, fever — exclude malignancy - Rapidly progressive neurological deficit — acute compression e.g., post-fracture haematoma ; surgical emergency - Vascular compromise — pallor, pulselessness — exclude thoracic outlet syndrome or vascular pathology - Signs inconsistent with CTS — consider double crush, brachial neuritis, MS --- Clinical Frameworks CTS-6 Clinical Prediction Rule Graham et al., 2006 — validated diagnostic prediction tool Score 1 point for each present: Item Points ------ -------- Nocturnal numbness 1 Shaking relieves symptoms Flick sign 1 Thenar atrophy 1 Positive Phalen's test 1 Loss of 2-point discrimination >6mm 1 Wrist ratio >0.67 AP:ML diameter 1 Interpretation: - ≥4 points: CTS highly likely LR+ = 18.3 — NCS may be deferred; treat clinically - 3 points: Uncertain — NCS recommended - ≤2 points: CTS unlikely LR– = 0.09 — consider alternative diagnosis NCS/EMG Diagnostic Criteria American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine — AANEM Diagnostic threshold for abnormal NCS: - Median sensory distal latency >3.5 ms 14 cm distance - Median motor distal latency >4.2 ms to APB - Median-ulnar sensory latency difference >0.4 ms ring finger comparison - Median-radial sensory latency difference >0.5 ms thumb comparison Severity grading Stevens 1997 : Grade NCS Findings ------- ------------- Mild Sensory latency prolonged only Moderate Both sensory and motor latency prolonged Severe Absent sensory response ± reduced motor amplitude Extreme Absent sensory and motor responses; denervation on EMG HSC NI NCS Referral: NCS arranged via neurology/neurophysiology; await results before surgical referral in non-urgent cases. Urgent track for progressive motor loss. USS Criteria - Cross-sectional area CSA of median nerve at pisiform level ≥10 mm² = abnormal sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.83 - CSA ≥12 mm² has higher specificity 0.94 — useful in equivocal cases - USS preferred in pregnancy avoids NCS ; also useful for anatomical variants pre-surgery --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Administration --------- ------------- ------ ---------------- Boston CTS Questionnaire BCTQ 19 items; Symptom Severity Scale SSS, 11 items + Functional Status Scale FSS, 8 items ; 1–5 scale SSS: 1.14 points; FSS: 0.74 points Self-report; 5–10 min DASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder, Hand 30-item upper limb disability scale; 0–100 10.2 points Self-report; 10–15 min QuickDASH 11-item abbreviated DASH 15.9 points Self-report; 5 min PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 15-item wrist-specific; pain + function subscales; 0–100 14 points Self-report; 5 min Global Rating of Change Single-item; –7 to +7 or similar N/A Clinician/self Recommended for CTS: BCTQ condition-specific, validated for surgical and conservative outcomes + QuickDASH upper limb function . Collect at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, discharge. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic algorithm adapted from NICE NG54 and AANEM guidelines : 1. Clinical diagnosis first — history + physical examination sufficient in classic presentation - Nocturnal paraesthesia, flick sign, median nerve distribution symptoms → high pre-test probability 2. Apply CTS-6 — score ≥4: treat clinically; score 3: NCS; score ≤2: reconsider diagnosis 3. NCS indicated when: - Diagnosis uncertain after clinical assessment - Atypical features e.g., whole-hand numbness, proximal symptoms - Surgical planning baseline severity grading - Medicolegal / occupational health documentation - Failed conservative treatment reassess severity 4. USS as adjunct when: - NCS unavailable or inconclusive - Pregnancy - Anatomical variant suspected - Space-occupying lesion possible lipoma, ganglion, amyloid Diagnostic accuracy of clinical assessment alone: - Experienced clinician with classic history: sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.80 Fowler 2002 - Combined test battery ≥2 positive tests improves specificity substantially --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features Investigation ----------- ---------------------------- --------------- Cervical radiculopathy C6 Neck pain, shoulder/arm radiation, positive Spurling's, symptoms in thumb/index but also dorsal MRI cervical spine; NCS normal distal latencies Pronator teres syndrome Proximal forearm pain, reproduction with resisted pronation, positive Tinel's at pronator, palmar cutaneous branch involved NCS abnormal proximal ; USS forearm Thoracic outlet syndrome Bilateral, positional, Adson's/ROOS test, vascular component Vascular duplex; chest X-ray cervical rib Ulnar neuropathy cubital tunnel Little/ring finger numbness, intrinsic weakness, Froment's sign, Tinel's at elbow NCS ulnar motor/sensory De Quervain's tenosynovitis Radial-sided wrist pain, Finkelstein's positive, no sensory change Clinical; USS Raynaud's phenomenon Colour change white → blue → red , cold trigger, bilateral, no neurological deficit Nailfold capillaroscopy; ANA if secondary suspected Diabetic peripheral neuropathy Stocking-glove distribution, bilateral, distal symmetrical HbA1c; NCS Double crush syndrome CTS + proximal nerve compression C6 radiculopathy ; amplified symptoms Full NCS; MRI spine --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Pathway Conservative Management Splinting strong evidence — Cochrane 2012 : - Wrist splint in neutral position 0° worn nocturnally - 3–6 months trial recommended - Full-time wear more effective than night-only in early stages - Custom thermoplastic vs prefabricated: equivalent outcomes at 1 year Brininger 2007 - NNT for symptom relief: ~3 at 3 months Exercise emerging evidence : - Nerve gliding exercises: equivocal evidence; may reduce need for surgery in mild CTS - Tendon gliding: reduces tendon adhesion, improves flexor tendon excursion - Programme: 5 × daily, 10 repetitions each exercise Activity modification: - Avoid sustained wrist flexion/extension >30° - Vibrating tool exposure reduction - Ergonomic keyboard/mouse assessment HSC OT referral if occupational LLLT/Ultrasound therapy: - Therapeutic ultrasound: some evidence for short-term symptom relief Ebenbichler 1998 ; effect modest - LLLT: insufficient evidence; not routinely recommended Pharmacological Management Corticosteroid injection strong evidence : - Methylprednisolone 20–40 mg + 1% lidocaine, palmar approach at carpal tunnel - NNT for symptom relief at 1 month: 2.0 Armstrong 2004 - Benefit wanes at 3 months; 50% recurrence by 6 months - Maximum 2 injections recommended risk of median nerve damage, tendon rupture - Diagnostic role: short-term response predicts good surgical outcome - Technique: Needle insertion at proximal wrist crease, ulnar to palmaris longus, directed 30° distally; USS-guided preferred to avoid median nerve injury Oral corticosteroids: - Short-term relief prednisone 20 mg/day × 2 weeks : evidence limited - Not recommended for long-term management; significant systemic side effects NSAIDs: No significant evidence for benefit over placebo in CTS; may address coexisting tendinopathy Diuretics in pregnancy : Not recommended; limited evidence Vitamin B6: Insufficient evidence; not recommended Surgical Management Referral Criteria Indications for surgical referral: - Failed ≥6 weeks conservative management splinting ± injection - Moderate–severe NCS findings - Thenar wasting or progressive motor deficit urgent - Patient preference after informed discussion of risks/benefits Surgical options: - Open carpal tunnel release OCTR : gold standard; recurrence <5% at 5 years - Endoscopic carpal tunnel release ECTR : equivalent outcomes; faster return to work; higher risk of transient nerve injury - Mini-open: intermediate approach Post-operative physiotherapy: - Scar desensitisation, grip strengthening, oedema management - Return to light work: 2–4 weeks; heavy manual work: 6–12 weeks NICE Pathway NG54 / CKS - Diagnose clinically; NCS if uncertainty or surgical planning - Offer splinting and/or steroid injection first-line - Refer for surgery if conservative measures fail after 3 months or if motor involvement - Refer urgently if thenar wasting or severe NCS --- Key References 1. Phalen GS. The carpal-tunnel syndrome. Seventeen years' experience in diagnosis and treatment of six hundred fifty-four hands. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1966;48 2 :211–228. 2. Durkan JA. A new diagnostic test for carpal tunnel syndrome. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1991;73 4 :535–538. 3. Wilder-Smith EP, et al. Carpal tunnel syndrome — a clinical review. Eur J Neurol. 2010;17 2 :213–220. Meta-analysis of physical examination test accuracy 4. Graham B, et al. Determining the contents of a predictive model for the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome. Arthritis Rheum. 2006;55 3 :354–358. CTS-6 derivation 5. Fowler JR, et al. The accuracy of the clinical examination in the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2002;84:2278–2282. 6. Marshall S, et al. Local corticosteroid injection for carpal tunnel syndrome. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2007; 2 :CD001554. 7. Page MJ, et al. Splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012; 7 :CD010003. 8. Huisstede BM, et al. Carpal tunnel syndrome: effectiveness of physical therapy, surgery, and steroid injection. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2010;40 1 :2–17. 9. Stevens JC. AAEM minimonograph 26: the electrodiagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome. Muscle Nerve. 1997;20 12 :1477–1486. 10. NICE. Carpal tunnel syndrome. Clinical Knowledge Summary. 2022. Available at: cks.nice.org.uk/topics/carpal-tunnel-syndrome/ 11. Ahn DS. Hand elevation: a new test for carpal tunnel syndrome. Ann Plast Surg. 2001;46 2 :120–124. 12. Brininger TL, et al. Efficacy of a fabricated customized splint vs a prefabricated splint in carpal tunnel syndrome. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2007;88 11 :1429–1435. 13. Ebenbichler GR, et al. Ultrasound treatment for treating the carpal tunnel syndrome: randomised 'sham' controlled trial. title: De Quervain's Tenosynovitis
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology De Quervain's tenosynovitis is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, affecting the tendons of abductor pollicis longus APL and extensor pollicis brevis EPB . The fibro-osseous tunnel at the radial styloid becomes thickened and constrictive
content: Overview & Pathophysiology De Quervain's tenosynovitis is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, affecting the tendons of abductor pollicis longus APL and extensor pollicis brevis EPB . The fibro-osseous tunnel at the radial styloid becomes thickened and constrictive, producing friction, pain, and swelling with thumb and wrist movement. Pathological mechanism: - Repetitive radial/ulnar deviation with thumb use → mechanical irritation of the tendon sheath - Fibrosis and thickening of the extensor retinaculum - Oedema and mucoid degeneration within the tendon sheath - Anatomical variant: EPB subcompartment present in ~33–50% of patients — missed subcompartment is the most common cause of treatment failure Epidemiology: - Incidence: ~0.5 per 1,000 person-years - Female:male ratio approximately 6–10:1 - Peak age: 30–50 years - Strong association with new mothers infant lifting , repetitive manual work, and racket sports - Prevalence in postpartum women estimated at 17–30% --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Finkelstein's test original: ulnar deviation with thumb adducted in fist 0.89 0.14 1.03 0.79 Moderate Kutsumi et al., 2005 Eichhoff's test patient makes fist around thumb, examiner deviates ulnarly ~0.89 ~0.14 — — Low-moderate commonly conflated with Finkelstein Modified Finkelstein / Wrist Stretch Test WST examiner-administered: passive thumb flexion + ulnar deviation Higher specificity reported — — — Limited Goubau et al., 2014 Tenderness over radial styloid ~0.85 0.55 1.89 0.27 Low Palpable crepitus 0.40 0.90 4.0 0.67 Low > Clinical note: Finkelstein's and Eichhoff's tests are frequently conflated in the literature. The true Finkelstein 1930 involves the examiner grasping the thumb and sharply deviating the wrist ulnarly — this is the higher-sensitivity version. The Eichhoff patient-performed has similar sensitivity but poorer specificity. Both are positive if pain is reproduced over the first dorsal compartment. A positive test in isolation has poor specificity; clinical context is essential. > Modified Finkelstein/WST Goubau et al., 2014 : Passive thumb CMC and MCP joint flexion combined with wrist ulnar deviation — may improve specificity compared to standard Eichhoff. Useful when standard tests produce equivocal results or when differentiating from intersection syndrome. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent onward referral if any of the following are present: - Rapidly progressive swelling with systemic features fever, erythema tracking, rigors → Septic tenosynovitis — surgical emergency - Inability to straighten/bend fingers + fever → septic flexor tenosynovitis Kanavel's signs - Traumatic mechanism with bony tenderness → scaphoid fracture / radial styloid fracture - Suspected inflammatory arthropathy bilateral, symmetrical, morning stiffness >1 hour, raised ESR/CRP - Rapidly enlarging mass at radial wrist → consider ganglion, lipoma, or rarely tumour - Neurovascular compromise paraesthesia, colour change, absent pulse --- Clinical Frameworks Anatomical Variants — Surgical Relevance - EPB subcompartment 33–50% : failure to release this separate compartment = most common surgical failure - Multiple APL slips up to 6 reported : associated with higher recurrence - Ultrasound can identify subcompartmentalisation pre-procedure Intersection Syndrome Differential - Pain 4–6 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle at crossover of APL/EPB and ECRB/ECRL - Palpable/audible crepitus at crossover point - Often seen in rowers, weightlifters Diagnostic Framework 1. Clinical diagnosis history + special tests sufficient for initial management 2. USS confirms if clinical uncertainty or prior to corticosteroid injection 3. MRI reserved for complex/refractory cases or suspected concurrent pathology --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- QuickDASH 16 points Preferred for upper limb function; 11 items; validated in hand/wrist conditions DASH 10–15 points Full 30-item version; higher ceiling for complex cases PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 14 points Wrist-specific; pain + function subscales; highly responsive to change in wrist conditions NRS Pain 0–10 2 points Simple, rapid; use alongside functional measure Grip strength Jamar dynamometer 6–7 kg Compare with contralateral; use at baseline and discharge --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Ultrasound USS Findings - First-line imaging when diagnosis uncertain - Findings: thickened tendon sheath >3 mm , hyperaemia on Doppler, peritendinous fluid, EPB subcompartment identification - Sensitivity ~0.87, specificity ~0.89 for confirming de Quervain's Klauser et al., 2002 - USS-guided injection significantly improves corticosteroid placement accuracy vs anatomical landmark injection MRI - Not routinely indicated - Demonstrates tendon sheath thickening, fluid, and tendon changes - Useful if concurrent intra-articular pathology suspected SLAC, STT OA --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Intersection syndrome Pain 4–6 cm proximal; crepitus at crossover point; common in rowers Thumb CMC osteoarthritis Grind test positive; bony enlargement at base of thumb; Eaton-Littler staging Scaphoid fracture Trauma history; anatomical snuffbox tenderness; X-ray ± MRI Wartenberg's syndrome Radial sensory nerve entrapment; burning/paraesthesia dorsal thumb; Tinel's over radial forearm FCR tendinopathy Pain at volar wrist; tenderness over FCR tendon Trigger thumb A1 pulley Triggering/locking; palmar MCP tenderness Extensor tendon tear/subluxation Sudden deformity; localised swelling; positive subluxation test --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care → Physiotherapy/Hand Therapy → Surgical/Injection if required Step 1 — Initial assessment physiotherapy/hand therapy : - Confirm diagnosis; screen red flags - Baseline QuickDASH/PRWE + grip strength - Advise activity modification; avoid provocative loading Step 2 — Conservative management first-line; 4–6 weeks : - Thumb spica splint see below - Activity modification and ergonomic advice - Hand therapy graded loading programme when acute phase resolves Step 3 — Corticosteroid injection if inadequate response at 4–6 weeks, or severe at presentation : - USS-guided injection strongly preferred - Refer to physiotherapist with injection qualification or GP/MSK interface clinic - Document EPB subcompartment injection if USS confirms separate compartment Step 4 — Surgical referral if 2 injections fail, or persistent >6 months : - HSC NI Trauma & Orthopaedics / Hand Surgery waiting list - Include EPB subcompartment status in referral --- Conservative Management Thumb Spica Splinting: - Cochrane Peters-Veluthamaningal et al., 2009 : Low-quality evidence; splinting reduces symptoms in short-term but no RCT demonstrates superiority over other conservative treatments - Thermoplastic thumb spica immobilising wrist in slight extension and CMC in palmar abduction; IP joint free - Wear: 24 hours for acute phase; wean to activity-only as symptoms improve - Duration: 4–6 weeks; reassess at 2–4 weekly intervals Exercise therapy: - Limited high-quality evidence; tendon-gliding exercises, graded loading - Eccentric loading of APL/EPB not well-studied; clinical consensus supports gentle tendon mobilisation post-acute phase Acupuncture/dry needling: Insufficient evidence; not routinely recommended in HSC NI pathway --- Pharmacological Corticosteroid Injection CSI : - Cochrane Peters-Veluthamaningal et al., 2009 : One small RCT 20 participants — CSI superior to splinting alone; combination of CSI + splint may not be superior to CSI alone - Evidence base non-Cochrane : Pooled data suggests ~62–83% success rate with single CSI; second injection adds limited additional benefit - Methylprednisolone acetate 20–40 mg with 1 mL lidocaine; USS-guided - Complication awareness: Skin depigmentation, fat atrophy, and tendon rupture risk rare ; counsel patient NSAIDs: Topical diclofenac gel or oral for acute symptom management; short-course only; follow NICE/HSC NI prescribing guidance --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- Diagnosis unclear / USS required MSK USS radiology Failed conservative 4–6 weeks Injection service qualified physiotherapist / GP-with-SI / MSK interface clinic Failed 2 corticosteroid injections HSC NI Hand Surgery / T&O Red flags septic tenosynovitis Emergency Department — same day Inflammatory arthropathy suspected Rheumatology --- Key References 1. Finkelstein H. Stenosing tendovaginitis at the radial styloid process. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1930;12:509–540. 2. Kutsumi K, Amadio PC, Zhao C, et al. Finkelstein's test: a biomechanical analysis. J Hand Surg Am. 2005;30 1 :130–135. 3. Goubau JF, Goubau L, Van Tongel A, et al. The wrist hyperflexion and abduction of the thumb WHAT test: a more specific and sensitive test to diagnose de Quervain tenosynovitis than the Eichhoff's Test. J Hand Surg Eur. 2014;39 3 :286–292. 4. Peters-Veluthamaningal C, van der Windt DA, Winters JC, et al. Corticosteroid injection for de Quervain's tenosynovitis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2009; 3 :CD005616. 5. Klauser A, Frauscher F, Bodner G, et al. Finger pulley injuries in extreme rock climbers: depiction with dynamic US. Radiology. 2002 — See also: Klauser AS et al. Ultrasound findings of de Quervain's tenosynovitis. Eur Radiol. 2002;12 8 :1940–1945. 6. Ilyas AM. Nonsurgical treatment for de Quervain's tenosynovitis. J Hand Surg Am. 2009;34 5 :928–929. 7. Stahl S, Vida D, Meisner C, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis on the work-relatedness of de Quervain's tenosynovitis. Occup Environ Med. 2013;70 6 :374–381. 8. Goel R, Abzug JM. de Quervain's tenosynovitis: a review of the rehabilitative options. Hand NY . 2015;10 1 :1–5.

title: Dupuytren's Contracture
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Dupuytren's contracture is a benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar and digital fascia, characterised by progressive thickening and shortening of the palmar aponeurosis, resulting in fixed flexion contractures of the MCP and PIP joints. Named after Baron Guillaum
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Dupuytren's contracture is a benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar and digital fascia, characterised by progressive thickening and shortening of the palmar aponeurosis, resulting in fixed flexion contractures of the MCP and PIP joints. Named after Baron Guillaume Dupuytren 1831 , though Plater described it earlier in 1614. Pathological mechanism: - Myofibroblast proliferation within palmar fascia Skoog's pretendinous bands, spiral bands, natatory ligaments, Grayson's ligaments - Three histological phases: proliferative → involutional → residual - Pretendinous cord → MCP contracture; spiral cord Cleland's, Grayson's, pretendinous, lateral digital sheet → PIP contracture + neurovascular bundle displacement - Spiral cord displaces NVB medially, superficially, and proximally — critical surgical consideration Epidemiology: - Prevalence: ~2–30% in Western European populations; highest in Northern Europe Scandinavia, Scotland, Ireland, Northern England - Northern Ireland prevalence estimated 10–15% in those >65 years — clinically significant for HSC NI - Male:female ratio 6–10:1 young ; equalises with age - Peak presentation: 50–60 years males ; 60–70 years females - Ring finger most commonly affected 70–80% , followed by little finger Risk Factors Established : Risk Factor Evidence Notes ------------- ---------- ------- Northern European ancestry Strong genetic Autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance Age >50 years Strong Risk increases linearly with age Male sex Strong — Diabetes mellitus Moderate OR ~3–4 Bilateral; radial digits; more aggressive Epilepsy / anticonvulsant use Moderate phenobarbitone historically Possibly drug-mediated Alcohol use disorder Moderate Liver fibrosis association Smoking Moderate Microvascular ischaemia proposed Manual labour / vibration Weak-moderate Contested; some evidence for repetitive hand trauma HIV infection Emerging — Diathesis Hueston : Aggressive phenotype — bilateral disease, ectopic involvement Peyronie's, Ledderhose/plantar , radial digit involvement, strong family history, early onset. Higher recurrence post-treatment. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Hueston tabletop test patient cannot lay palm flat on table ~0.95 ~0.90 ~9.5 ~0.06 Low-moderate widely used; limited formal validation Passive joint angle assessment goniometry Reference standard — — — Moderate Palpable cord in palm/digit ~0.90 ~0.85 6.0 0.12 Low Skin pitting/tethering ~0.70 ~0.90 7.0 0.33 Low > Diagnosis is clinical — history of progressive painless contracture + palpable cord + skin changes. Imaging not required for diagnosis. > Hueston tabletop test: Positive when patient cannot simultaneously lay palm and fingers flat on a table surface. Indicates ≥30° combined MCP/PIP contracture and is commonly used as the surgical referral threshold . --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Expedited onward referral if: - Rapidly progressive contracture weeks, not months/years → consider rare desmoplastic fibroma or sarcoma; request USS ± MRI - Painful, inflamed cord with systemic features → exclude infection or acute inflammatory condition - Neurovascular compromise digital paraesthesia, colour change, absent pulse → urgent surgical assessment - Locked digit in acute flexion with trauma history → exclude fracture/dislocation - Child/adolescent with progressive hand contracture → consider knuckle pads alone vs juvenile Dupuytren; rare — paediatric orthopaedic referral --- Clinical Frameworks Tubiana Staging System Stage Total Passive Extension Deficit TPED Description ------- --------------------------------------- ------------- N 0° Palmar nodule/cord only; no contracture Stage I 0–45° Mild; MCP predominantly Stage II 45–90° Moderate; MCP + PIP involvement Stage III 90–135° Severe; significant PIP contracture Stage IV >135° Very severe; fixed contracture; DIP may be involved > TPED = sum of extension deficit at MCP + PIP + DIP for the affected ray. Guides surgical planning and outcome benchmarking. Surgical Referral Threshold HSC NI - MCP contracture ≥30° or PIP contracture ≥15° any degree of PIP contracture is functionally significant - Positive tabletop test - Progressive disease documented over 3–6 months Anatomorphological Types - Nodular: Early; may be painful; proliferative phase - Cord: Band-like; main driver of contracture - Diffuse: Skin involvement; poor prognosis; higher recurrence --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- QuickDASH 16 points Primary functional outcome measure DASH 10–15 points Full version for complex presentations URAM scale Unité Rhumatologique des Affections de la Main 5 points Dupuytren-specific PRO; validated; 9 items Goniometry passive extension deficit 10° Primary objective measure; document per joint, per digit Hueston tabletop test Pass/fail Binary; document at each review PRWE 14 points Less Dupuytren-specific; use QuickDASH/URAM preferentially --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging - USS: Not required for diagnosis; useful to identify cord anatomy, NVB position pre-procedure needle aponeurotomy - MRI: Reserved for atypical cases or suspected malignancy aggressive/rapidly progressive - No routine imaging indicated for established Dupuytren's Histopathology - Rarely required; if diagnosis uncertain e.g., excludes fibrosarcoma - Alpha-smooth muscle actin α-SMA positive myofibroblasts — hallmark --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Palmar ganglion Fluctuant; transilluminates; no contracture; USS confirms Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath Firm, lobulated nodule; USS — vascular; no cord Fibroma/fibrosarcoma Rapidly progressive; painful; USS ± MRI Trigger finger Active triggering/locking; A1 pulley tenderness; no palmar cord Ulnar nerve palsy Intrinsic minus hand; clawing 4th/5th digits; motor/sensory deficit Camptodactyly Congenital; painless PIP flexion; no palmar cord; young onset Knuckle pads Thickening over PIP/MCP dorsum; no contracture; Dupuytren diathesis association Ledderhose disease plantar fibromatosis Ectopic manifestation; plantar nodules; part of Dupuytren diathesis --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Monitoring → Hand therapy conservative → Procedural/Surgical intervention when threshold met Step 1 — Baseline Assessment: - Tubiana staging + goniometry per joint/digit - Hueston tabletop test document pass/fail - QuickDASH + URAM scale - Risk factor screening; document diathesis features Step 2 — Watchful waiting Stage N–I; not functionally limiting : - Reassure re: benign nature; lifestyle advice alcohol, smoking - Review at 6–12 months or if progression - Educate: "not cured by treatment; recurrence is expected" Step 3 — Hand therapy pre- and post-procedural : - Pre-procedural: Serial static night extension splinting NOT evidence-based as standalone; do not delay referral - Post-procedural: Extension splinting + hand therapy exercise programme is essential for all interventions - Post-collagenase/NA: Immediate hand therapy; night splinting 3–6 months Step 4 — Procedural Intervention MCP ≥30° or PIP ≥15°, or functionally significant : - Discuss all options; patient choice and comorbidities guide selection - Refer HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery --- Conservative Management Splinting alone, non-post-procedural : - No high-quality RCT evidence that splinting alone alters disease progression or prevents contracture recurrence - Night extension splinting is appropriate post-procedure; not as primary disease-modifying treatment - Radiotherapy low-dose, <30 Gy : May slow progression at nodular stage Stage N–I ; limited UK availability; experimental in HSC NI --- Interventional Options — Comparative Evidence Intervention Procedure Initial Correction Recurrence at 5 years Notes --- --- --- --- --- Needle fasciotomy NA/PNA Percutaneous needle division of cord; outpatient; LA 75–80% MCP; 50–60% PIP ~50–65% MCP ; higher PIP Rapid recovery; lowest cost; office procedure; suitable elderly/comorbid Collagenase injection Xiapex / CCH Clostridium histolyticum collagenase; 2-visit: inject Day 1, manipulate Day 2 ~75–90% MCP; ~40–60% PIP ~47–66% at 5 years CORDLESS study NICE-approved; withdrawn UK market 2020 commercial ; may return; discuss if available Limited fasciectomy LF Surgical excision of diseased fascia; regional/GA; day case ~85–95% MCP; ~70–80% PIP ~20–40% at 5–10 years Gold standard; higher complication rate 10–15% ; nerve/vessel risk; longer recovery Dermofasciectomy Fasciectomy + skin graft Z-plasties ; recurrent/diathesis cases Similar to LF ~8–10% at 5 years Lowest recurrence; highest morbidity; reserved for recurrence or severe diathesis Key comparative evidence: - CORD-I & CORD-II RCTs Hurst et al., 2009; Gilpin et al., 2011 : Collagenase CCH vs placebo — CCH significantly superior; 64% achieved full correction MCP - CORDLESS study Peimer et al., 2013 : Long-term follow-up — 47% recurrence ≥20° contracture at 5 years post-CCH - Cochrane Zhao et al., 2022 : Needle fasciotomy vs limited fasciectomy — LF achieves superior correction; NA has shorter recovery and fewer complications; recurrence higher with NA - van Rijssen et al. 2012 : RCT — NA vs LF; at 5 years, recurrence 85% NA vs 21% LF for MCP joints --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- MCP ≥30° contracture HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Any PIP contracture affecting function HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Positive tabletop test HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Diathesis features + progressive disease HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery early discussion Rapidly progressive / atypical mass MSK Radiology USS ± MRI → Orthopaedics --- Key References 1. Surg Clin North Am. 1968;48 5 :979–984. 3. Hueston JT. The table top test. Hand. 1982;14 1 :100–103. 4. Hurst LC, Badalamente MA, Hentz VR, et al. headings: Ottawa Wrist Rules Derived Criteria — Scaphoid Application
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fractures, accounting for approximately 60–70% of all carpal fractures and 2–7% of all fractures. They typically result from a fall on an outstretched hand FOOSH with the wrist in dorsiflexion and radial deviation, transmitting compressive force through the thenar eminence to the scaphoid waist. Anatomical Vulnerability The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply predominantly from the radial artery entering distally through the dorsal ridge. The proximal pole receives no direct blood supply, making proximal pole fractures particularly vulnerable to avascular necrosis AVN . AVN occurs in up to 30–40% of untreated or delayed-diagnosis fractures of the proximal pole. Fracture Classification Herbert & Fisher - Type A: Stable acute fractures A1: tubercle fracture; A2: incomplete waist fracture - Type B: Unstable acute fractures B1: distal oblique; B2: complete waist; B3: proximal pole; B4: trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation - Type C: Delayed union - Type D: Established non-union D1: fibrous; D2: pseudarthrosis Epidemiology - Peak incidence: males aged 20–30 years - Annual incidence: ~5 per 10,000 population UK - Up to 20% of scaphoid fractures are occult on initial plain X-ray - Delayed diagnosis is associated with non-union up to 12% waist fractures if missed and AVN --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Anatomical snuffbox tenderness 0.90 0.40 1.50 0.25 Moderate Parvizi et al. 1998; Duckworth et al. 2012 Scaphoid compression test longitudinal compression of thumb 0.80 0.48 1.54 0.42 Moderate Parvizi et al. 1998 Scaphoid tubercle tenderness 0.82 0.57 1.91 0.32 Moderate Grover 1996 Pain on supination against resistance 0.74 0.76 3.08 0.34 Low–Moderate Freeland 1989 Combined 3-test rule snuffbox + compression + tubercle 0.98 0.40 1.63 0.05 Moderate Unsworth et al. 2020 Clinical Notes on Tests Anatomical Snuffbox Tenderness: High sensitivity 0.90 makes it an excellent screening test — a negative test is clinically useful −LR 0.25 . However, poor specificity 0.40 means many false positives; should not be used in isolation to confirm fracture. Scaphoid Compression Test: Apply longitudinal compression along the axis of the thumb toward the scaphoid. Positive = pain at the anatomical snuffbox or radial wrist. Lower sensitivity than snuffbox tenderness; adds specificity when combined. Combined 3-Test Rule: If all three tests are negative, fracture is unlikely −LR 0.05, post-test probability ⚠️ Urgent / Do Not Miss - Perilunate dislocation / trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation — Carpal malalignment on X-ray; median nerve compromise; requires emergency orthopaedic referral - Open fracture — Requires same-day surgical review - Median nerve symptoms acute carpal tunnel syndrome post-injury — Sensory loss in median nerve distribution, thenar weakness; urgent decompression may be required - Vascular compromise — Skin changes, absence of digital pulses post-injury - Pathological fracture — Low-energy mechanism; consider bone metastasis, primary bone tumour, or metabolic bone disease osteoporosis workup in older patients - Child/adolescent — Growth plate involvement; paediatric orthopaedic referral Non-union risk factors refer urgently : - Proximal pole fracture - Displaced fracture >1 mm gap or >10° humpback deformity - Delayed presentation >4 weeks - Previous non-union --- Clinical Frameworks Ottawa Wrist Rules Derived Criteria — Scaphoid Application The original Ottawa Wrist Rules were developed for wrist fracture detection post-FOOSH. Validated sensitivity for any wrist fracture: ~98%. For scaphoid specifically: Image if ANY of the following: 1. Point tenderness over anatomical snuffbox 2. Point tenderness over scaphoid tubercle 3. Painful supination against resistance 4. Age 65 years with mechanism of FOOSH 5. Neurovascular deficit Clinical Prediction Rule Duckworth et al. 2012 — BSSH guidance : - Negative snuffbox + negative compression + negative tubercle → fracture extremely unlikely NPV ~98–100% - Any positive → proceed to imaging regardless of plain X-ray result Injury Grading — DISI Deformity A scapholunate angle >60° on lateral wrist X-ray suggests DISI Dorsal Intercalated Segment Instability associated with ligamentous instability — requires specialist review. --- Outcome Measures Measure Full Name MCID Notes --------- ----------- ------ ------- DASH Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand 10.2 points 30-item PRO; validated for wrist fractures QuickDASH Quick DASH 11 items 15.9 points Strong correlation with DASH; preferred in busy clinical settings PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 11.5 points Wrist-specific; highly responsive to change post-fracture; recommended for monitoring scaphoid outcomes VAS Pain Visual Analogue Scale 1.5–2.0 cm Use alongside functional measures Grip strength Dynamometry Jamar ≥10% deficit vs contralateral Functional endpoint; target ≥80% contralateral at discharge PRWE is recommended as the primary outcome measure for scaphoid fractures in research and clinical audit settings MacDermid et al. 1998 . --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Pathway MRI: - Gold standard for occult scaphoid fracture detection - Sensitivity 0.88–1.00; Specificity 0.97–1.00 Yin et al. 2010 — systematic review - Recommended within 72 hours if X-ray negative but clinical suspicion high - NICE guidance NG38, 2016 : Offer MRI within 72 hours; if unavailable, CT acceptable; bone scintigraphy third-line CT: - Sensitivity 0.72–0.93; Specificity 0.99 Brydie & Raby 2003 - Superior to MRI for cortical detail and surgical planning - Preferred for fracture characterisation once diagnosed displacement, comminution, union monitoring Bone Scintigraphy: - High sensitivity ~1.00 but low specificity ~0.60 — significant false-positive rate - Reserved for when MRI and CT are both unavailable NICE NG38 Plain X-ray Limitations: - Sensitivity for scaphoid fracture: 0.54–0.70 on initial films Yin et al. 2010 - Up to 20% missed on day 1; repeat X-ray at 10–14 days improves but does not replace MRI --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features Investigation ----------- ---------------------------- --------------- Distal radius fracture Tenderness over distal radius not snuffbox ; visible on X-ray Plain X-ray Scapholunate ligament injury Scapholunate gap >3 mm on PA X-ray "Terry Thomas sign" ; stress views X-ray stress views; MR arthrography De Quervain's tenosynovitis Positive Finkelstein's test; tenderness over 1st extensor compartment Clinical; USS Radial styloid fracture Tenderness at radial styloid; fracture on X-ray Plain X-ray Trapezium fracture Tenderness at CMC joint; rare CT Carpal tunnel syndrome acute Median nerve symptoms; Tinel/Phalen positive Clinical + nerve conduction TFCC injury Ulnar-sided pain; fovea sign positive; piano key test MRI / MR arthrography Wrist sprain Diffuse tenderness; no specific bony point tenderness; normal imaging Diagnosis of exclusion --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Pathway Emergency Department ED : 1. Clinical assessment + Ottawa Wrist Rules application 2. Plain X-ray scaphoid series: PA, lateral, oblique, scaphoid view 3. If fracture confirmed: immobilise in thumb spica plaster/splint; refer to fracture clinic next available, within 5 working days 4. If X-ray negative but clinical suspicion high: - Immobilise in thumb spica backslab - Refer urgently for MRI within 72 hours via fracture clinic or radiology direct access - Written safety-netting advice return if symptoms worsen 5. If perilunate dislocation suspected: same-day orthopaedic review Fracture Clinic HSC NI Trust : - Review with MRI/CT results - Classify fracture Herbert & Fisher - Decision: conservative vs surgical management - Physiotherapy referral: post-immobilisation rehabilitation Conservative Management Evidence-Based Indications: Non-displaced 1 mm step-off or >10° humpback deformity on CT - Proximal pole fracture high AVN risk - Non-union at 12 weeks - Athlete/manual worker preference for earlier return to activity - Perilunate fracture-dislocation emergency Procedure: Percutaneous or open cannulated headless compression screw fixation e.g., Herbert screw, Acutrak Post-surgical physio: As conservative Phase 1–3, typically commencing 2 weeks post-op Onward Referral Criteria Physiotherapy → Orthopaedics - Failure to progress with conservative management at 12 weeks - Development of AVN pain, restricted ROM, X-ray/MRI changes - Non-union on imaging - Complex regional pain syndrome CRPS signs --- Key References 1. Clinical and radiological outcome of cast immobilisation versus surgical treatment of acute scaphoid fractures at a mean follow-up of 93 months. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 2008;90 7 :899–905. 4.
