title: TFCC Injury (Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology The Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex TFCC is the primary stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint DRUJ and the ulnocarpal joint , and acts as a load-transmitter distributing approximately 20% of axial load across the ulnar side of the wrist Palmer & Werner, 1984 . Injury
content: Overview & Pathophysiology The Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex TFCC is the primary stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint DRUJ and the ulnocarpal joint , and acts as a load-transmitter distributing approximately 20% of axial load across the ulnar side of the wrist Palmer & Werner, 1984 . Injury is a common cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain. Anatomical components: - Articular disc fibrocartilage : Central avascular zone; periphery is vascular - Dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments: Deep fibres insert at fovea primary DRUJ stabilisers ; superficial fibres insert at ulnar styloid - Ulnotriquetral UT ligament - Ulnolunate UL ligament - Extensor carpi ulnaris ECU subsheath - Meniscus homologue Vascular anatomy surgical relevance : - Central disc = avascular; poor healing potential; debridement is treatment of choice - Peripheral 1–2 mm = vascular; repair is feasible - Deep fibres at fovea = critical stabilisers; foveal detachment = DRUJ instability Mechanism of injury: - Traumatic Palmer Type I : Fall on outstretched hand; forceful forearm rotation; axial loading with ulnar deviation; DRUJ dislocation; distal radius fracture associated - Degenerative Palmer Type II : Repetitive loading; ulnar impaction syndrome; abutment of ulnar head against TFCC/lunate/triquetrum - Ulnar variance: Positive ulnar variance increases load through TFCC; associated with degenerative tears Epidemiology: - Common cause of ulnar wrist pain; exact incidence unclear - Wrist arthroscopy series: TFCC tears found in ~35% of arthroscopies for wrist pain; 53% in distal radius fractures - Degenerative Type II tears increasingly common >40 years; frequent incidental finding --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Fovea sign deep palpation between FCU tendon and ulnar styloid in anatomical snuffbox equivalent; positive if reproduces deep ulnar wrist pain 0.95 0.87 7.3 0.06 Moderate Tay et al., 2007 Press test patient presses up from chair arms using wrists; positive if ulnar wrist pain reproduced 1.00 0.64 2.8 0.00 Moderate Lester et al., 1995 — caution: high sensitivity, poor specificity Ulnar grind test axial compression + rotation of wrist in ulnar deviation; positive if pain reproduced at DRUJ/ulnocarpal ~0.54 ~0.67 1.6 0.69 Low Nakamura et al. DRUJ ballottement piano key test dorsopalmar stress of ulnar head vs radius; positive if laxity, pain, or crepitus vs contralateral ~0.66 ~0.64 1.8 0.53 Low-moderate Ulnocarpal stress test maximal ulnar deviation + axial compression + forearm rotation; positive = ulnar pain ~0.64 ~0.65 1.8 0.55 Low ECU synergy test resisted index finger abduction while palpating ECU; positive if ECU pain/weakness ~0.82 ~0.81 4.3 0.22 Low-moderate differentiate ECU > Clinical interpretation: The fovea sign has the best combined sensitivity/specificity and should be the primary provocative test. Press test is highly sensitive rules out if negative but non-specific. Use a cluster: fovea sign + press test + piano key for DRUJ stability + active forearm rotation assessment. > DRUJ instability assessment: Compare ballottement laxity bilaterally in neutral, pronation, and supination. Laxity in all positions = physiological; laxity in only one = pathological. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent onward referral if: - Acute DRUJ dislocation inability to pronate/supinate; prominent ulnar head; post-trauma → Emergency Department / Orthopaedics same day - Galeazzi fracture-dislocation distal radius fracture + DRUJ disruption → Orthopaedic emergency - Essex-Lopresti injury radial head fracture + interosseous membrane disruption + DRUJ injury → Orthopaedic emergency - Vascular compromise absent ulnar pulse; Allen's test positive for ulnar artery → Vascular surgery - Acute ulnar nerve deficit → Urgent neurological assessment - Suspected carpal instability perilunate dislocation; scapholunate dissociation on plain X-ray → Urgent orthopaedic referral --- Clinical Frameworks Palmer Classification Type I — Traumatic: Subtype Lesion --------- -------- IA Central perforation articular disc — avascular; debridement IB Ulnar avulsion ± ulnar styloid fracture — peripheral; can repair; foveal detachment = DRUJ instability IC Volar avulsion ulnocarpal ligaments ID Radial avulsion ± sigmoid notch fracture Type II — Degenerative Ulnar Impaction Syndrome : Subtype Lesion --------- -------- IIA TFCC wear — no perforation IIB TFCC wear + lunate/ulnar chondromalacia IIC TFCC perforation + chondromalacia IID TFCC perforation + chondromalacia + LT ligament tear IIE TFCC perforation + chondromalacia + LT tear + ulnocarpal arthritis > Palmer classification guides arthroscopic management — Type IA: debridement; Type IB: repair; Type IIE: ulnar shortening osteotomy may be required. Diagnostic Algorithm 1. Ulnar-sided wrist pain + mechanism + provocative tests 2. Plain X-ray bilateral neutral PA : assess ulnar variance; exclude fracture 3. If diagnosis unclear: MRI wrist ± arthrography 4. If surgical management planned: MR arthrography gold standard non-invasive ; wrist arthroscopy definitive --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 14 points Best validated wrist-specific PRO; recommended for TFCC QuickDASH 16 points Upper limb function; validated DASH 10–15 points Full version for complex cases Grip strength Jamar dynamometer 6–7 kg Compare bilaterally; DRUJ injury commonly reduces grip ~25–30% Forearm rotation goniometry 10° Pronation/supination; document degrees NRS Pain 2 points Baseline and review MAYO wrist score — Surgeon-used; pain, function, ROM, grip; 100-point scale --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Plain Radiography - Bilateral neutral PA wrists: Assess ulnar variance positive >2 mm associated with degenerative TFCC - Assess DRUJ congruence; carpal alignment Gilula's arcs - Pronated-grip PA view increases positive variance by ~1–2 mm MRI Wrist - Standard MRI: Sensitivity 0.71–0.86, specificity 0.67–0.89 for TFCC tears meta-analysis, Saupe et al. - 3T superior to 1.5T; dedicated wrist coil essential - Identifies peripheral vs central tears, associated pathology LT ligament, ulnocarpal MR Arthrography MRA - MRA: Sensitivity ~0.84–0.93, specificity ~0.93–0.95 for full-thickness TFCC tears - Gold standard non-invasive investigation — preferred pre-arthroscopy - Intra-articular gadolinium radiocarpal injection ; contrast leak into DRUJ confirms perforation - Differentiates partial from full-thickness; better assessment of foveal detachment CT / CT Arthrography - DRUJ geometry assessment pre-operative; instability evaluation - CT arthrography: comparable sensitivity to MRA; useful when MRI contraindicated Wrist Arthroscopy Definitive - Gold standard for diagnosis and treatment - Allows direct visualisation of all TFCC components; dynamic assessment; treatment in same setting - Trampoline test probe bounce on articular disc evaluates tension; abnormal if disc lax --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- ECU tendinopathy/subluxation ECU synergy test; pain dorsal ulnar; ECU groove tenderness; USS Lunotriquetral LT ligament tear Shuck test LT ballottement ; ulnar dorsal pain; MRA Ulnocarpal impaction syndrome Positive ulnar variance; degenerative; X-ray; axial loading pain Pisotriquetral arthritis Pisiform tenderness; pain on radial deviation + compression; X-ray Ulnar styloid non-union Post-fracture; X-ray; tenderness at styloid Hypothenar hammer syndrome Vascular; repetitive hypothenar trauma; abnormal Allen's test; duplex USS Guyon's canal syndrome Ulnar nerve compression; sensory loss 4th/5th digits; Tinel's De Quervain's tenosynovitis Radial-sided pain; Finkelstein positive Distal radius malunion Post-fracture; radiological --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care / Physiotherapy → MSK imaging → Specialist Hand Surgery referral for surgical cases Step 1 — Initial Assessment: - Confirm ulnar-sided wrist pain; mechanism; provocative tests fovea sign, press test, piano key - Palmer classification clinical working diagnosis - Baseline PRWE + QuickDASH + grip strength + forearm rotation goniometry - Plain X-ray bilateral PA wrists — request if not done Step 2 — Conservative management 6–8 weeks; appropriate for most Type I uncomplicated, Type II non-surgical : - DRUJ immobilisation Munster cast or rigid DRUJ orthosis 6–8 weeks for acute peripheral tears - Activity modification: avoid forearm rotation under load; gripping - Graded hand therapy after immobilisation Step 3 — Physiotherapy programme post-immobilisation or degenerative : - DRUJ stabilisation exercises; ECU strengthening - Forearm rotation restoration; proprioception training - Theraband graded resisted pronation/supination - Typical programme: 6–12 weeks physiotherapy post-immobilisation Step 4 — MRI/MRA if not improving at 8–12 weeks conservative, or acute high-energy mechanism : - Request via MSK interface / T&O outpatient - Guide surgical decision-making Step 5 — Surgical Referral DRUJ instability; failed conservative; acute Type IB foveal detachment : - HSC NI Hand Surgery / Trauma & Orthopaedics - Include ulnar variance, Palmer type clinical , MRI findings in referral --- Conservative Management Immobilisation: - Acute peripheral tears Type IB : Below-elbow Munster cast or custom rigid DRUJ orthosis in neutral rotation × 6–8 weeks - Evidence: Minimal RCT data; case series demonstrate 60–75% satisfactory outcomes with conservative management of peripheral tears - Type IA central : Conservative has lower success; shorter immobilisation 2–4 weeks then physiotherapy; arthroscopic debridement if persistent Physiotherapy: - ECU subsheath repair / DRUJ stabilisation via dynamic muscle exercise - Evidence limited case series ; consensus recommends graded loading programme - Duration: 6–12 weeks post-immobilisation Corticosteroid Injection: - USS-guided injection into radiocarpal joint ± DRUJ - Limited specific evidence; may reduce pain in degenerative Type II - Refer to qualified injection physiotherapist / GP-with-SI --- Surgical Options Procedure Indication Outcomes Evidence Level ----------- ------------ ---------- ---------------- Arthroscopic debridement Type IA central tear ~78–88% good/excellent at 2 years Moderate case series Arthroscopic peripheral repair Type IB peripheral tear; DRUJ stable ~80–85% good/excellent; return to sport/work Moderate case series Foveal reattachment open or arthroscopic Type IB with foveal detachment + DRUJ instability ~80–90% DRUJ stability restored Moderate Ulnar shortening osteotomy USO Type II degenerative + positive ulnar variance ~75–90% pain improvement Moderate DRUJ reconstruction Chronic instability; title: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis (Trapeziometacarpal OA)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Thumb carpometacarpal CMC osteoarthritis — also termed trapeziometacarpal TMC or basal joint OA — is the second most common site of symptomatic OA in the hand after the DIP joint. It results from progressive articular cartilage degeneration at the trapeziometacarpal joint,
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thumb carpometacarpal CMC osteoarthritis — also termed trapeziometacarpal TMC or basal joint OA — is the second most common site of symptomatic OA in the hand after the DIP joint. It results from progressive articular cartilage degeneration at the trapeziometacarpal joint, with secondary involvement of the scaphotrapezial joint in advanced cases. Anatomy & Biomechanics: - The trapeziometacarpal joint is a biconcave-convex saddle joint with inherent bony incongruity - Primary stabiliser: anterior oblique ligament beak ligament / volar AOL — deep fibres critical - Instability of the beak ligament allows dorsoradial subluxation of the 1st metacarpal — characteristic finding in Eaton Stage II+ - Pinch loads generate joint reactive forces of 12× applied force at the CMC joint — explains vulnerability with repetitive fine grip Pathological sequence: 1. Volar AOL laxity → dorsoradial subluxation of 1st MC 2. Progressive cartilage loss → subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation 3. Adduction contracture of 1st web space adaptive shortening of adductor pollicis 4. Compensatory MCP hyperextension "shoulder sign" or "Z-deformity" 5. Advanced: scaphotrapezial involvement; STT OA Epidemiology: - Radiographic prevalence: ~25–35% women and ~10–15% men >50 years Haara et al., 2004 - Symptomatic OA: ~7–15% in adults >40 years - Female predominance 5–10:1 vs males - Strong correlation with age, female sex, post-menopausal status, prior thumb injury, hypermobility, occupational pinching --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Grind test axial compression + circumduction of 1st MC at CMC; positive = pain ± crepitus 0.53 0.80 2.65 0.59 Moderate Merritt et al., 2010; Kalichman & Hernández-Molina, 2011 Distraction test axial distraction of 1st MC; positive = pain relief or joint laxity ~0.70 ~0.55 1.6 0.55 Low Shoulder sign Z-deformity MCP hyperextension + CMC flexion on lateral X-ray/inspection — — — — Diagnostic sign; not a provocation test CMC grind + crepitus combined ~0.65 ~0.78 2.95 0.45 Moderate Pinch grip pain key pinch or 3-jaw chuck; positive if basal pain reproduced ~0.80 ~0.50 1.6 0.40 Low Radial ABduction stress passive radial abduction stress; positive = pain at CMC ~0.70 ~0.60 1.75 0.50 Low > Clinical note: No single test has high sensitivity and specificity. Grind test has best specificity 80% — positive result is more useful than negative for ruling in OA. Combine with plain radiography for diagnostic confirmation; X-ray is essential for Eaton-Littler staging and surgical planning. > Grind test technique matters: The examiner applies firm axial compression to the 1st MCP joint while simultaneously circumducting the metacarpal. Reproducing the patient's typical pain at the CMC base is a positive result. Crepitus alone without pain is less significant degenerative crepitus common in asymptomatic elderly . --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Expedited onward referral if: - Rapidly progressive joint destruction in young patient → seronegative or psoriatic arthropathy; refer Rheumatology - Hot, swollen, erythematous CMC → gout podagra pattern may affect hand ; septic arthritis rare at CMC ; aspirate and send for MCS/crystals - Suspected scaphoid fracture anatomical snuffbox tenderness + trauma → X-ray ± MRI; do not conflate with CMC OA - Median nerve compromise carpal tunnel syndrome often co-exists; BCTQ screening → neurophysiology ± CTS pathway - Inflammatory arthropathy bilateral symmetric; MCP/PIP swelling; morning stiffness >1 hour → Rheumatology - Bone pain at night / unremitting → exclude malignancy uncommon; rare at carpus --- Clinical Frameworks Eaton-Littler Classification Radiographic Staging Stage Radiographic Findings Joint Space Clinical Correlation ------- ---------------------- ------------- --------------------- Stage I Normal or widened joint space; no osteophytes; possible laxity/subluxation Normal Ligamentous laxity; synovitis; normal/near-normal X-ray Stage II Joint space narrowing; osteophyte 2 mm; >1/3 MC subluxation Markedly narrowed Established OA; surgical discussion; STT usually spared Stage IV Pantrapezial OA CMC + STT joint ; sclerosis; cysts Obliterated Advanced; trapeziectomy + STT involvement; arthroplasty > Staging requires X-ray — bilateral stress views Robert view / AP with thumb extended are standard. Eaton-Littler Stage guides surgical planning: Stage I–II → conservative/injection; Stage III → injection/surgery; Stage IV → surgery trapeziectomy ± arthroplasty . Z-Deformity / Shoulder Sign - MCP joint hyperextension compensates for CMC adduction contracture - Visible on clinical inspection and lateral X-ray - Functionally significant: MCP hyperextension >30° requires concomitant MCP fusion/capsulodesis at time of trapeziectomy to prevent post-operative swan-neck deformity --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- DASH 10–15 points Preferred for thumb OA; validated QuickDASH 16 points Rapid screening; validated PRWE 14 points Wrist-specific; less thumb-specific but widely used AUSCAN Australian/Canadian OA Hand Index 5–7 points pain subscale Hand OA-specific; pain, stiffness, function subscales; 15 items FIHOA Functional Index for Hand OA — 10 items; validated in hand OA Pinch strength lateral pinch / 3-jaw chuck ~1–2 kg Baseline and follow-up; Jamar or Pinch gauge Grip strength Jamar dynamometer 6–7 kg Compare bilaterally NRS Pain 2 points Quick; use alongside functional measure --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Plain Radiography - Essential for diagnosis and staging — AP Roberts/stress view , lateral, and oblique views - Bilateral comparison recommended - Roberts view true AP of thumb CMC : hyperpronate hand on cassette with beam perpendicular — best assessment of CMC joint USS - Not primary diagnostic tool for CMC OA - Useful: synovitis assessment, USS-guided injection improves accuracy and reproducibility - Demonstrates joint effusion, osteophytes, synovial thickening, Doppler signal MRI - Not routine for CMC OA - Indications: suspected concurrent pathology scaphoid pathology, adjacent ligament injury, avascular necrosis of trapezoid/scaphoid ; diagnostic uncertainty Laboratory - Not required for uncomplicated CMC OA - If inflammatory arthropathy suspected: FBC, ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP, uric acid --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- De Quervain's tenosynovitis First dorsal compartment; Finkelstein/Eichhoff positive; no bony change on X-ray Scaphoid fracture Trauma; anatomical snuffbox tenderness; X-ray ± MRI Scaphotrapezial STT OA Radial wrist pain; X-ray shows STT involvement; often co-existent Stage IV Flexor carpi radialis FCR tendinopathy Volar wrist pain; FCR tendon tenderness; USS confirms Wartenberg's syndrome Radial sensory nerve; burning; Tinel's; no X-ray changes Carpal tunnel syndrome Median nerve territory; Phalen/Tinel; BCTQ; nerve conduction Trigger thumb Triggering/locking; A1 pulley; palmar MCP crease Gout/pseudogout at CMC Acute hot swollen joint; raised uric acid; crystals on aspiration Inflammatory arthropathy Bilateral; MCP/PIP; morning stiffness; raised inflammatory markers --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care → Hand therapy conservative first-line → Injection → Surgical referral Step 1 — Initial Assessment: - Eaton-Littler stage X-ray essential — request if not available - Baseline DASH/QuickDASH + AUSCAN + pinch/grip strength - Assess MCP hyperextension Z-deformity - Screen for carpal tunnel syndrome BCTQ Step 2 — Conservative management all stages first-line; ongoing in Stage I–II : - Hand therapy referral for splinting + exercise programme - Activity modification; ergonomic advice; adaptive equipment Step 3 — Corticosteroid injection Stage I–III; failed conservative 6–8 weeks; acute flare : - USS-guided intra-articular injection CMC joint - Refer injection physiotherapist / GP-with-SI / MSK interface clinic Step 4 — Surgical referral Stage III–IV; failed conservative + 2 injections; significant functional limitation : - HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery / T&O - Include Eaton-Littler stage, MCP hyperextension status, patient functional demands --- Conservative Management Splinting: - Cochrane Bertozzi et al., 2015; Moe et al., 2021 : Evidence supports hand orthoses for pain relief and function improvement; short opponens/CMC stabilisation splint superior to no splinting for pain low-moderate quality evidence - Custom thermoplastic CMC stabilisation orthosis: Most evidence; immobilises CMC in functional position; MCP and IP joints free; worn during activity and at night - Soft neoprene splint: Less immobilisation; improves compliance; suitable for milder cases - Duration: Minimum 3 months; review at 4–6 weeks - Evidence: Berggren et al. 2001 — splinting equivalent to corticosteroid injection at 6 months; combination not superior Exercise therapy: - Cochrane Moe et al., 2021 : Exercise + splinting superior to splinting alone for pain and function at short-term; exercises should target thenar muscle strengthening and CMC stability - Exercises: opposition, abduction/adduction against resistance; web space stretching - Graded theraband / putty; avoid painful pinching initially - Duration: 6–12 weeks supervised; home programme Thermal modalities / Manual therapy: - Weak evidence; adjunct only; paraffin wax, heat, joint mobilisation CMC traction/mobilisation - Joint mobilisation Maitland/accessory : Small RCTs suggest short-term pain benefit; insufficient for standalone recommendation --- Pharmacological Corticosteroid Injection CSI : - Evidence: Joshi et al. 2019 meta-analysis — CSI provides significant short-term pain relief 4–8 weeks ; effect wanes at 6 months; no strong evidence for structural modification - USS-guided recommended small joint; improves accuracy vs landmark - Methylprednisolone 20–40 mg or triamcinolone 20 mg + 1 mL lidocaine - Frequency: Maximum 2–3 per year; evidence supports benefit of repeated injections; structural caution with frequent use - Hyaluronic acid viscosupplementation : Multiple small RCTs — comparable to CSI at 6–12 months; not NICE-recommended as standard; available at some centres Topical NSAIDs diclofenac gel : - NICE-recommended first-line pharmacological treatment for hand OA - Evidence: Hunter et al.; Cochrane Derry et al., 2017 — significant pain reduction vs placebo; fewer systemic effects than oral NSAIDs Oral NSAIDs / Analgesics: - Short-term use for acute flares; follow NICE/MHRA guidance; consider GI/CV/renal risk - Paracetamol: limited efficacy in OA Machado et al., 2015 meta-analysis ; may still provide modest benefit --- Surgical Options Procedure Indication Outcomes Recurrence / Notes ----------- ------------ ---------- ------------------- Trapeziectomy simple Stage III–IV; failed conservative 80–90% good/excellent at 5 years; thumb shortening Gold standard; strong evidence base Trapeziectomy + LRTI ligament reconstruction tendon interposition Stage III–IV No evidence of superiority over simple trapeziectomy Cochrane, Wajon et al., 2015 Longer procedure; similar outcomes CMC arthroplasty prosthetic Stage II–III; younger, higher demand patients Good short-term; concern for long-term implant survival Limited UK uptake; pyrocarbon available CMC arthrodesis Young active patients; Stage II–III Eliminates pain; reduces motion; useful in manual workers Motion sacrifice Metacarpal extension osteotomy Stage I–II; young; delayed surgery Modest evidence; alters load distribution Niche; not widely used Trapeziectomy CMC arthroplasty criteria for HSC NI : - Eaton-Littler Stage III–IV - Failed conservative management ≥6 months - Failed ≥2 corticosteroid injections - Significant functional limitation QuickDASH >40 or equivalent - MCP hyperextension >30° — note for surgeon may need concurrent MCP procedure Cochrane evidence Wajon et al., 2015 : No significant difference in outcomes between trapeziectomy alone vs trapeziectomy + LRTI vs trapeziectomy + K-wire stabilisation. Simple trapeziectomy is therefore the evidence-based standard, avoiding the morbidity of tendon harvest. --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- Suspected inflammatory arthropathy Rheumatology Acute hot swollen CMC suspected gout/septic Emergency Assessment / Rheumatology urgent Stage III–IV; failed conservative/injection HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Carpal tunnel syndrome co-existing HSC NI CTS pathway / Nerve conduction studies Diagnostic uncertainty / unusual presentation MSK Radiology USS/MRI --- Key References 1. Trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis: staging as a rationale for treatment. Hand Clin. 1987;3 4 :455–471. 3. Merritt MM, Roddey TS, Costello C, et al. Diagnostic value of clinical grind test for carpometacarpal osteoarthritis of the thumb. J Hand Ther. 2010;23 3 :261–267. 4. Kalichman L, Hernández-Molina G. Hand osteoarthritis: an epidemiological perspective. Semin Arthritis Rheum. 2010;40 2 :166–173. 5. Wajon A, Vinycomb T, Carr E, et al. Surgery for thumb trapeziometacarpal joint osteoarthritis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015; 2 :CD004631. 6. Bertozzi L, Valdes K, Vanti C, et al. Investigation of the effect of conservative interventions in thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis: systematic review and meta-analysis. Disabil Rehabil. 2015;37 22 :2025–2043. 7. Moe RH, Kjeken I, Uhlig T, et al. There is inadequate evidence to determine the effectiveness of non-pharmacological and non-surgical interventions for hand osteoarthritis. J Clin Epidemiol. 2009;62 8 :843–845. 8. Joshi R, Hadzic A, Kalava A, et al. Corticosteroid injections for basal thumb osteoarthritis — a meta-analysis. J Hand Surg Am. 2019;44 4 :314–323. see also: Meenagh et al. 9. Haara MM, Heliövaara M, Kröger H, et al. Osteoarthritis in the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb. Prevalence and associations with disability and mortality. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2004;86 7 :1452–1457. 10. Derry S, Conaghan P, Da Silva JA, et al. Topical NSAIDs for chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016; 4 :CD007400.

title: Trigger Finger (Stenosing Tenosynovitis)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Trigger finger stenosing tenosynovitis results from a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the A1 pulley at the level of the MCP joint. Repetitive microtrauma causes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and hypertrophy of the A1 pulley, while the flexor tendon develops a f
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Trigger finger stenosing tenosynovitis results from a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the A1 pulley at the level of the MCP joint. Repetitive microtrauma causes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and hypertrophy of the A1 pulley, while the flexor tendon develops a fusiform nodule proximal to the pulley. This produces the characteristic catching, triggering, or locking of the digit in flexion. Anatomy: - A1 pulley overlies the MCP joint; most commonly affected - Flexor digitorum superficialis FDS and profundus FDP pass through the fibro-osseous canal - Tendon nodule forms proximal to A1 pulley; catches on pulley margins during gliding Epidemiology: - General population incidence: 28 per 100,000 person-years - Peak age: 55–60 years; females > males 2:1 - Ring finger most commonly affected, followed by thumb trigger thumb - Strong association with: - Diabetes mellitus 10× increased risk; 10–20% of diabetics affected - Rheumatoid arthritis - Hypothyroidism - Carpal tunnel syndrome co-occurrence ~10–20% - Repetitive gripping activities Trigger thumb A1 pulley of thumb flexor behaves similarly; note distinction from paediatric trigger thumb congenital form with Notta's node . --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Triggering/locking on active flexion/extension ~0.92 ~0.95 18.4 0.08 Moderate Palpable nodule at A1 pulley MCP palmar crease ~0.75–0.80 ~0.90 7.5 0.25 Low-moderate Tenderness over A1 pulley ~0.90 0.65 2.6 0.15 Low Crepitus on tendon gliding ~0.50 ~0.80 2.5 0.63 Low > Diagnosis is predominantly clinical — active triggering or locking of the digit during flexion/extension, combined with palmar MCP tenderness and a palpable nodule, is sufficient for diagnosis. Imaging is not routinely required. > USS can confirm nodule size, pulley thickening, and tendon morphology — useful pre-injection or when diagnosis is uncertain. Characteristic USS finding: hypoechoic nodule proximal to A1 pulley with restricted tendon glide on dynamic assessment. --- Green Classification Severity Grade Description Clinical Features ------- ------------- ------------------- Grade I Pre-triggering Pain; history of catching but no demonstrable triggering on examination; tenderness over A1 pulley Grade II Active triggering Demonstrable triggering/snapping on active flexion-extension; patient can actively extend digit Grade III Locked Digit locked in flexion; patient cannot actively extend; requires passive correction IIIa or cannot be corrected passively IIIb Grade IV Contracture Fixed flexion contracture at PIP joint in addition to locking > Clinical relevance: Grade I–IIIa respond well to corticosteroid injection. Grade IIIb–IV typically require surgical intervention. Grade IV may require additional PIP joint contracture release. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent/priority onward referral if: - Acute locked digit unable to extend passively + fever/erythema → Septic flexor tenosynovitis — surgical emergency Kanavel's cardinal signs: fusiform swelling, flexed posture at rest, pain on passive extension, tenderness over tendon sheath - Traumatic mechanism with locked digit → exclude volar plate injury, fracture, or dislocation - Rapidly progressive, bilateral triggering with joint swelling → inflammatory arthropathy RA - Paediatric locked thumb → congenital trigger thumb — paediatric orthopaedic referral - Firm, fixed nodule not consistent with tendon — consider giant cell tumour of tendon sheath GCT ; USS ± referral --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Framework 1. History: Catching, triggering, locking; worse in morning; pain at palm/MCP 2. Examination: Active triggering; palpable nodule; A1 pulley tenderness; assess for locked digit 3. Green classification to guide management 4. Comorbidity screen: Diabetes, RA, hypothyroidism 5. Imaging: USS if diagnosis uncertain or pre-procedural planning Special Considerations - Diabetic patients: Lower injection success rates 50–60% vs ~75% in non-diabetics ; higher recurrence; may require earlier surgical referral - Multiple digits: USS of all affected digits; injection of all at one visit appropriate - Paediatric trigger thumb: Different pathology Notta's node at A1 pulley ; spontaneous resolution possible up to age 3; refer paediatric orthopaedics --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- QuickDASH 16 points Validated in hand conditions; preferred for upper limb function DASH 10–15 points Full version; appropriate for complex or multi-digit cases PRWE 14 points Wrist-specific; less appropriate for isolated finger; use QuickDASH preferentially Quinnell grading N/A Surgeon-used severity grading I–IV ; similar to Green NRS Pain 2 points Baseline and outcome tracking Grip / pinch strength 6–7 kg grip Compare bilaterally; Jamar dynamometer --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis USS Findings if performed - Hypoechoic nodule in flexor tendon proximal to A1 pulley - A1 pulley thickening normal: 2 mm - Restricted tendon glide on dynamic USS with active flexion/extension - Power Doppler: peritendinous hyperaemia in active inflammation - USS-guided injection improves accuracy and may improve outcomes Laboratory - No routine bloods required for diagnosis - If inflammatory arthropathy suspected: FBC, ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP - Diabetes screen if not known: HbA1c / fasting glucose --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Septic flexor tenosynovitis Kanavel's signs; fever; systemic illness; surgical emergency Volar plate injury / PIP dislocation Trauma; localised PIP tenderness; X-ray Dupuytren's contracture Progressive painless contracture; palmar cord; no triggering Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath Firm, fixed, non-tender nodule; USS — lobulated, vascular Flexor tendon rupture RA Inability to flex; RA history; Mannerfelt syndrome Locked MCP joint Sesamoid entrapment; X-ray shows sesamoid between metacarpal heads Camptodactyly Congenital or juvenile; painless PIP flexion deformity; no triggering --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care → Physiotherapy/Hand Therapy → Injection → Surgical referral Step 1 — Initial Assessment: - Confirm diagnosis + Green grade - Screen for comorbidities diabetes, RA - Baseline QuickDASH + grip/pinch strength Step 2 — Conservative Grade I–II; trial 4–6 weeks : - Night extension splinting of MCP joint PIP/DIP free — reduces morning locking - Activity modification; avoid sustained gripping/vibration - Gentle tendon-gliding exercises - Refer to hand therapist for splint fabrication and exercise programme Step 3 — Corticosteroid Injection Grade I–IIIa; preferred first-line for active triggering : - USS-guided into tendon sheath at A1 pulley level - Refer to qualified physiotherapist injection / GP-with-SI / MSK interface clinic - Second injection if inadequate response at 6–8 weeks Step 4 — Surgical Referral Grade IIIb–IV; failed 2 injections; diabetic recurrence : - Percutaneous A1 pulley release or open surgical release - HSC NI Hand Surgery / T&O referral --- Conservative Management Night Extension Splinting: - MCP joint in 0–15° extension; PIP and DIP joints free - Reduces triggering by preventing full flexion at rest - Evidence: Patel & Bassini 1992 — 66% resolution with splinting alone grade I–II - Thermoplastic custom splint via hand therapy or off-the-shelf MCP extension splint Tendon Gliding Exercises: - Hook fist, straight fist, composite fist positions - Purpose: maintain tendon excursion, reduce adhesion formation - Limited high-quality RCT evidence; clinical consensus supports use --- Pharmacological Corticosteroid Injection CSI : - Cochrane Peters-Veluthamaningal et al., 2009 : CSI produces short-term resolution in up to 93% of cases at 4 weeks; effect diminishes at 6 months ~57% sustained ; recurrence rate ~50% at 1 year - Best evidence: Triamcinolone acetonide 10–20 mg or methylprednisolone 20–40 mg + 1 mL lidocaine into tendon sheath - USS-guided injection: higher accuracy, similar outcomes to landmark-guided RCT evidence limited - Diabetic patients: ~50–60% short-term success; earlier recurrence; monitor glucose post-injection - 2nd injection: Additional 50–60% resolution in those not responding to first - 3rd injection: Diminishing returns; proceed to surgical referral NSAIDs: Topical or oral for pain; limited specific evidence in trigger finger; adjunct only --- Surgical Options Procedure Description Recurrence Rate Notes ----------- ------------- ----------------- ------- Percutaneous A1 pulley release Needle or blade via palmar approach; outpatient Recurrence post-surgery is rare <5% ; if recurrence occurs, consider incomplete pulley release or alternative diagnosis. --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- Septic tenosynovitis suspected Emergency Department — same day Active triggering Grade II–IIIa Injection service physio with injection competency / GP-with-SI Grade IIIb–IV at presentation HSC NI Hand Surgery direct Failed 2 injections HSC NI Hand Surgery / T&O Inflammatory arthropathy suspected Rheumatology Paediatric trigger thumb Paediatric Orthopaedics --- Key References 1.
